The aim of Synthese Library is to provide a forum for the best current work in the methodology and philosophy of science and in epistemology, all broadly understood. A wide variety of different approaches have traditionally been represented in the Library, and every effort is made to maintain this variety, not for its own sake, but because we believe that there are many fruitful and illuminating approaches to the philosophy of science and related disciplines.

Special attention is paid to methodological studies which illustrate the interplay of empirical and philosophical viewpoints and to contributions to the formal (logical, set-theoretical, mathematical, information-theoretical, decision-theoretical, etc.) methodology of empirical sciences. Likewise, the applications of logical methods to epistemology as well as philosophically and methodologically relevant studies in logic are strongly encouraged. The emphasis on logic will be tempered by interest in the psychological, historical, and sociological aspects of science. In addition to monographs Synthese Library publishes thematically unified anthologies and edited volumes with a well-defined topical focus inside the aim and scope of the book series. The contributions in the volumes are expected to be focused and structurally organized in accordance with the central theme(s), and should be tied together by an extensive editorial introduction or set of introductions if the volume is divided into parts. An extensive bibliography and index are mandatory.

## Introduction

**Juan M. Durán and Giorgia Pozzi**

In 2004, Paul Humphreys observed that the influence of computational methods in many areas of the sciences was transforming their theory development and practice. The core argument, according to Humphreys, was that human abilities could no longer be considered the ultimate criteria of epistemic success. An exclusively anthropocentric epistemology, as offered by the diverse forms of empiricism in the philosophy of science, is no longer an attainable position. In 2009, he called this the anthropocentric predicament and advocated for an epistemology that addresses the displacement of humans from the center of production of knowledge. Here lies, to our mind, the basis for many of the debates that will follow in the intersection between the philosophy of science and algorithms. In this sense, this book largely builds on Humphreys’ work. But it is also in great debt to the many philosophers who have extensively worked in the philosophy of computer science and received less recognition over these recent years—Amnon Eden, Raymond Turner, Aaron Sloman, Paul Thagard, Zenon Pylyshyn, Margaret Boden, Nils Nilsson, and so many others.

We have divided this volume into seven parts, each including a handful of chapters from scholars in the field. With this division, we intend to articulate key debates in the intersection between the philosophy of science and machine learning (ML). This is done, of course, to the extent possible and without any pretense of being exhaustive. Now, as the reader will quickly note, several chapters exceed the exclusivity of the philosophy of science and ML, encroaching into areas such as epistemology, ethics, and the sociology of science, as well as scientific modeling and mathematics. Beyond this minor deviation from the title, the book offers a variety of viewpoints on core issues pertaining to the philosophy of science—and related topics—that are at the basis of current debates on ML. There are not, we must recognize, unifying themes across chapters. Rather, the reader will find a wealth of common ideas and concepts of mutual dependence. The value of this book lies, therefore, not so much in its organization but in the merits of each contributing chapter. We take the opportunity to praise the authors for their magnificent work, as well as their commitment to reviewing their chapters and those of others to a great extent. It goes without much dissension that much more can and must be discussed in the future. Our hope is that this volume will pave the way for and motivate a more systematic discussion of central topics at the intersection of the philosophy of science and ML.

As mentioned, the volume is divided into seven different parts. The first five deal with theoretical issues in connection with ML. Issues about epistemic opacity, knowledge and justification, explanation and understanding, and scientific modeling and representation are at the center of attention. The questions addressed in these parts cover a wide range of old and new philosophical concerns: what is epistemic opacity, and how can explanation and understanding be intelligibly articulated within ML? Can ML outputs be justified and if so, what is a suitable epistemology? What forms of representation—if any at all—can we claim from ML? The last two parts in the volume—parts six and seven—complement the previous whole by looking into scientific practice with and by ML. Part 6 focuses on the role of ML in scientific practice and on which values do and should influence it. Questions here revolve around whether scientists are transitioning into a novel form of scientific inquiry through ML and, if so, how, under what conditions, and with which foreseeable implications. Moreover, questions pertaining to scientific values and inductive risk take a prominent place. For example, questions along the following lines receive full attention: what role do epistemic and non-epistemic values play in constructing and evaluating ML? How can inductive risk in ML be effectively evaluated and managed? Part 7, on the other hand, works toward visualizing the philosophical nuances required for analyzing ML for its applicability in scientific fields. Of particular interest are the applicability of ML in astrophysics and particle physics, neuroscience, climate science, and public health. Two goals are anticipated within these parts. On the one hand, as it was mentioned before, they showcase ML in different fields of scientific inquiry. On the other, they exemplify how previously discussed theoretical issues, such as explanation and understanding, relate to scientific practice with ML.

Before entering into a brief description of each part and chapter individually, we would like to entertain some ideas of what comes next. We predict that the debates addressed here are likely to continue in the foreseeable future due to a number of outstanding issues that were not able to be addressed here. Now, while this might sound like an easy prediction, we also include in it debates that are rather absent in the literature. These include objectivity in ML, emergence, replicability, underdetermination, and the—possibility of a—demarcation problem in the context of ML. We could also raise the stakes a bit higher and mention that ML seems to be configuring novel, possibly never seen before, modes of scientific inquiry; that ML seems to depart from syntactic and semantic accounts of models and theories, possibly requiring an account of its own; and why the computation—as opposed to mere modes of inference—and representation of the temporal dynamic of ML these systems displace—or threatens to displace—humans from every the center of production of knowledge. We hope the reader recognizes Humphreys’ direct influence on this shortlist.

In what follows, we break down each part to its main goals, as well as provide a brief description of each chapter’s main interest.

## Epistemic Opacity

The opacity of algorithms is at the heart of virtually every issue pertaining to ML. Moral philosophers, political philosophers, and epistemologists all seem to have opacity in mind when dealing with their arguments. Interestingly, the concept is still very much up in the air, and its philosophical use sometimes lies on purely intuitive grounds. This is partly because, we conjure, opacity works as the motivating starting point for other, perhaps more interesting philosophical issues that presumably do not require any fine-grained definition. Now, this might be an unfortunate argumentative tactic, as the very notion of epistemic opacity is currently under much dispute and far from being intuitive.

This part of the book tries to capture the many complexities lurking behind the concept of epistemic opacity and address the current debates that pertain to it. It also intends to serve as a primer conceptualization for much of the chapters that follow.

The chapter by **Claus Beisbart** provides a solid basis for approaching the complexities of epistemic opacity in ML. In a nutshell, the chapter investigates the specific ways in which ML is considered opaque. This is done by examining statements from scientists and commentators who highlight the significant challenges in achieving certain epistemic goals regarding ML, such as predicting its outcomes. Beisbart then proceeds to contrast these observations with Humphreys’ theoretical concept of epistemic opacity. The chapter goes on to explore whether Humphreys’ notion fully explains the opacity issues in ML, or whether there is more to it. The chapter concludes with the following thesis: while Humphreys-style opacity applies to some aspects of ML, it is not the sole source of their opacity. Other factors, like the absence of comprehensive higher-level descriptions of ML, for instance, also play a significant role for the epistemic opacity of ML. Beisbart proposes two—seemingly disjoint—approaches to understanding opacity: as an “umbrella term,” broadly enough to encompass the difficulties in reaching various achievements in ML, or as a specific issue that accounts for why we struggle with diverse epistemic achievements. The exploration proposed by Beisbart provides a nuanced understanding of the concept of opacity in ML, offering a foundation for further discussion on the topic.

**Nico Formanek** proposes a turn in the rather standard treatment that opacity has found in the literature. That is, the author neither argues for or against opacity as a sui generis foundational concept of specific fields, nor for extending, restricting, or otherwise analyzing the definition. Formanek’s core interest, instead, lies in the practical effects that opacity has in the concrete scientific uses of ML. This argumentative maneuver brings the opacity debate to a rather unanticipated new light, one where the historical record furnishes cases where the gradual acceptance and habituation to levels of incompleteness and uncertainty have been central to overcoming practical opacity in past technologies. By understanding this process, the chapter proposes that developers and users of ML can develop a similar habituation. The expectation is that, over time, as users and developers become accustomed to the inherent opacity in ML, they will develop practical strategies to manage it effectively.

Finally, **Jack Casey’s** chapter begins with noticing a similarity found in debates between computer-assisted proofs and ML, namely, that the former are taken to be unsurveyable methodologies while the latter are epistemically opaque. A proof is unsurveyable if it is impossible for a rational agent to understand the proof in its entirety, while an ML is epistemically opaque if it is impossible for a rational agent to know all the relevant epistemic elements of the algorithm. This similarity, Casey argues, has been standardly cast under the same umbrella, that is, computer-assisted proofs and ML are both taken to be epistemically opaque. Nothing new admits the author. However, what has not yet been considered and that constitutes Casey’s main case is that concerns about epistemic opaqueness might result in being importantly dissimilar for either methodologies. Casey then builds the argument that epistemic opacity is a matter of degree. To Casey’s mind, the level of comfort with a given degree of epistemic opacity is largely determined by one’s commitments to scientific (anti-)realism. In this sense, if one holds realist commitments, then one’s tolerance for epistemic opacity is lower than holding anti-realist commitments. These ideas, then, bridge the scientific realism and anti-realism debate with computer-assisted proofs and ML.

## Justification

When Humphreys presented and discussed (essential) epistemic opacity, he was thinking of a problem of justification of the algorithm and its output. This particular focus is, surprisingly, passed over by many philosophers, who rapidly cash out opacity as a problem pertaining to explanation, understanding, and other epistemic functions. But as Humphreys put it, opacity prevents human agents from “examin[ing] and justify[ing] every element of the computational processes that produce the output of a[n . . . ] artifacts of computational science” (Humphreys, 2009, 618).

Why is, then, justification important in the context of ML? Justification typically refers to forming beliefs in the right way, or whether beliefs have been formed properly. In this way, a central concept in theories of justification is concerned with what makes a belief rational, credible, or warranted. Claims about having justification for believing that ML’s outputs are true, scientifically valid, or represent a fact in the world—you pick your commitment—have multiple repercussions for philosophical studies of ML, both for theoretical and practical philosophy. For starters, it is at the basis of different concepts of knowledge that pervade the literature on ML—philosophical and otherwise. Moreover, justification is also integral to debates about trust and trustworthy ML, debates with a more practical flavor. Interestingly, questions about the justification of ML outputs also seem to be present in the diverse commitments (e.g., factivity conditions) adopted by explanatory AI. Through its chapters, this part of the book laid out the basis for future debates on justificatory ML.

**Juan M. Durán** motivates the chapter by asking the question, “what is a reliable algorithm?” As Durán intends to answer it, the question is about epistemic justification. The chapter then proceeds in two directions. First, it distinguishes between internal-to-the-algorithm and external-to-the-algorithmic epistemologies. The former refers to showing “the inner workings of the algorithm,” largely driven by diverse transparency methods (e.g., transparency reports, some forms of explanatory AI); the latter describes external factors, metrics, practices, and cultures of research that confer reliability to the algorithm but are not inherent to its internal workings. With this distinction in place, Durán lays out a newer version of his Computational Reliabilism (CR), understood as an external-to-the-algorithmic epistemology that builds on the best epistemic efforts for the justification of the algorithm’s output. Most of the chapter is geared toward fleshing out CR, its integral parts (i.e., type- and token-reliability indicators), and to what extent an individual is justified in believing algorithms’ outputs.

The chapter by **Ramón Alvarado** is engineered around a critical view of CR, as discussed in earlier versions—most prominently, in discussions on computer simulations. Alvarado presents three core objections to CR. First is the “challenge of warrant transmission and reliability-crediting properties.” This objection, as admitted by Alvarado, is of a general kind, and not necessarily targeted to CR. At its core, the issue is to know how and to what extent any process, evidence, reason, and the like confer epistemic reliance on an algorithm. The second objection is the so-called “challenge of the indispensability of endogenous features in artifactual reliability.” Alvarado’s strategy is to question whether reliability indicators, intrinsic to CR, are sufficient to increase the degree of warrant we have to believe in ML outputs. Artifacts, it is argued, are endogenous to the algorithm (i.e., internal to its workings) and thus central to the justification of ML outputs. Finally, there is the “challenge of error-related opacity” which aims at shedding light on an equally important but less discussed epistemic issue related to how a process can fail. After presenting these objections, Alvarado expresses the hope that these observations serve as a starting point to alleviate the limitations previously identified.

Finally, **Carlos Zednik** and **Philippe Verreault-Julien** propose to interlock justification with explainable AI (XAI). They begin by asserting that justification requires decisions to align with relevant norms and that XAI has the potential to uncover the series of reasons influencing ML’s outputs, such as identifying spurious correlations and highlighting relevant patterns. By adopting a framework from the philosophy of action, they aim to cover three key issues: first, differentiate between the various types of reasons that may be provided for an ML’s outputs; second, assess how these diverse types of reasons contribute to the author’s interpretation of justification; and finally to evaluate the capacity of current XAI methods to identify and describe said reasons. The heart of Zednik and Verreault-Julien’s chapter is, then, to pinpoint some XAI methods that are suitable for identifying and clearly articulating the reasons that justify ML-driven decisions. The authors also complement their argument by offering insights into how and why some of the methods proposed are limited.

## Scientific Explanation (XAI)

Arguably one of the most popular topics in ML nowadays is explanatory AI (XAI). There are a number of good reasons for this. To some, XAI is the key to making ML more transparent, and thus increasing epistemic, cognitive, and morally relevant achievements (e.g., reliability, trustworthiness, credibility, accountability); to others, XAI provides sensitive and valuable answers to how—and even why—a given ML output was rendered; yet to others, XAI is the path to understanding the behavior of ML, following the footsteps of the much accepted philosophical idea that understanding is the goal of explanation. There are, of course, more reasons for engaging in philosophical discussions on XAI. Is there a (objective) logic of scientific explanation exclusive to ML? Do we admit factivity conditions for XAI? What would the plurality of scientific explanation in ML look like? Is XAI just a few algorithmic techniques that intend to answer how ML outputs are rendered but with no conceptual relation to the philosophical treatment of scientific explanations? Some of these reasons are addressed here, and some of the questions are answered. Under all of these headings, it is undoubted that XAI is central to the philosophy of science just as much as it is to ML in its diverse scientific applications. This part of the book navigates through these choppy waters, searching for precision in the debate, as well as novel interpretations.

**Andrés Páez**’s contribution is an attempt to break with a growing trend of linking models of scientific explanation with ML. To this end, Páez argues that claims that ML is scientifically explainable are either trivial or false, and that, ultimately, these efforts misrepresent the goals of XAI. They are trivial, the author argues, if an explanation is understood as a set of causes, taken to be either entities or physical states of the computer, that aim to account for a prediction. Claims about ML being scientifically explainable are false, on the other hand, if it is always possible to offer an “explanatory text,” a truthful description of the source of the prediction, thereby satisfying the factivity condition on scientific explanation. Páez splits the chapter into two halves. The first half is devoted to justifying the author’s claims about the triviality and falseness of scientific explanations in ML. The second half advocates for the use of labels such as “interpretable machine learning” and “understandable AI” instead of subsuming these under the umbrella term “XAI.” By doing this, Páez argues, we not only sidestep many of the misconceptions on the goals and purposes of XAI methods that furnish current literature but, more importantly, we recenter our attention on what is achievable, namely, understanding. Páez finalizes proposing a pragmatic account of understanding where conditions of satisfaction for understanding an ML are fleshed out in terms of the agent’s success in using the system.

The chapter by **Stefan Buijsman** links XAI with mathematics and mathematical explanation. In this vein, Buijsman proposes to shift the analysis of XAI from scientific explanations—to this author’s mind mainly driven by causal explanations—to non-causal explanations as analyzed in the literature on mathematical explanations. Buijsman’s key argumentative maneuver consists of taking that ML are mathematical objects. Once this is established—with some caveats, as the author points out—the theoretical apparatus provided by non-causal mathematical explanations follows suit. The chapter also contains a debate on counterfactual and interventionist explanations, today at the center of the many analyses on XAI. Of particular interest to the author are those mathematical equations that are standardly conceived as symmetrical, as opposed to causal relations—recall the canonical objection to the Deductive-Nomological model of explanation. This raises the question of whether counterfactual dependence in the mathematical case is appropriately asymmetrical. The answer to this question, as it should be expected, is complex and with many angles. However, Buijsman favors the idea that the asymmetry of many of the standard explanations found in the ML literature can be accounted for in virtue of concrete implementations of ML.

Finally, **Tim Räz** explores the connections between ML interpretability and— scientific and mathematical—explanations. Through this exploration, the author proposes a pluralistic approach where different notions of interpretability and different notions of—scientific and mathematical—explanations converge. While the former is required for explaining ML phenomena, the author argues, the latter benefits from understanding the nature of explanations. This convergence, however, should be taken as a mutual and prolific way to show their interconnection. In this sense, the chapter introduces perspectives on interpretability and explanation emphasizing a balanced approach between extreme views. It suggests, furthermore, that while a single, homogeneous notion of interpretability is unnecessary, an excessive proliferation of different notions should be avoided. Interpretability should be accepted to be context- and audience-dependent with a psychological dimension, but not entirely subjective nor detached from facts.

## Scientific Understanding and Interpretability

We seek to understand scientific theories and hypotheses, the gravitational pull, and the side effects of taking a drug. Philosophers of science have debated the nature of understanding, its scope, and its relation to other cognitive achievements (justification, truth, knowledge, explanation) for a long and very prolific time. It is only natural, one could hyperbolically say, that philosophical studies on ML gravitate toward a philosophical analysis of understanding. Now, the pull seems to exceed mere epistemic work and also include the impact that understanding the behavior and outputs of ML have (or could have) on society at large, economic implications, and a host of ethical and moral considerations. Thus, not only epistemic functions such as explanations are linked to understanding, but also its social, moral, and political implications are the driving force of much of the literature on this central concept. The chapters in this part of the volume are geared toward bridging epistemological concerns in connection with understanding, with moral and societal concerns linked to ML.

**Emily Sullivan** and **Atoosa Kasirzadeh**’s main goal is to push back on the trend in explainable AI that suggests actionable recourse explanations are the ethical gold standard for AI explanations. Instead, they argue that understanding should be the chief aim of explanations of ML decisions. The strategy begins with laying out the so-called recourse explanations, that is, explanations of ML decisions that give recommendations to the end users and data subjects on what actions they could take to get a different model decision in the future. Sullivan and Kasirzadeh refer to this as the “recourse-first approach” to explanation and define it as explanations that provide end users and data subjects with reasons that are actionable and feasible for change. Sullivan and Kasirzadeh argue that the recourse-first approach faces several conceptual pitfalls. Of main interest to these authors are the problems of hidden assumptions, deflecting responsibility, and explanation hacking. A suitable solution, as proposed by Sullivan and Kasirzadeh, is to advocate for an “understanding-first approach,” where users get explanations that aim at understanding the AI decisions. The value of the understanding-first approach is that end users are in the possession of informed self-advocacy against ML decisions and does not face the conceptual pitfalls that we see with the recourse-first approach.

**Eva Schmidt’s** chapter offers a further perspective on the connection between explainability and understanding in ML. In this chapter, Schmidt presents and discusses conditions for understanding through explanations in terms of stakes. More precisely, the author argues that whether the belief involved in an arguable case of understanding is sufficiently justified for outright understanding why depends on what is at stake in the particular circumstances considered. This pragmatic perspective is supported by comparing two situations that are identical, except that in one of them, a decision support system (specifically, the well-known COMPAS algorithm) is used in making a harmless decision, whereas in the other, it is used in making a life-determining decision. The COMPAS system has been used to determine the likelihood of defendants to re-offend. A connection with debates on pragmatic encroachment and inductive risk is established to explain how understanding is sensitive to the stakes of a particular situation. Overall, this connection aims to shed light on how non-epistemic values have an influence on whether explainable AI (XAI) methods suffice to generate outright understanding in context.

## Scientific Models and Representation

Debates about scientific models and representation seem to be underrepresented in the philosophical literature on ML, thus constituting, to our mind, a non-negligible research gap that needs timely attention. This is particularly the case given the heavy philosophical weight that these concepts pull over others previously discussed such as understanding, explanation, and the formation of beliefs.

Rafael Alvarado and Paul Humphreys made early efforts on representation, linking these concepts back to forms of opacity: with transparent representations “we represent the states of a system in a way that is open to explicit scrutiny, analysis, interpretation, and understanding by humans, and transitions between those states are represented by rules that have similar properties” (Alvarado & Humphreys, 2017, 740). Opaque representations are simply defined as non-transparent representations. While these authors are more interested in debates on the multiple meanings of “Big Data,” these initial thoughts furnish a solid basis for the chapters included in this part of the volume.

Now, given the scarcity of these debates in the specialized literature, this part of the book not only attempts to shed light on these authors’ positions but it holds the more ambitious aim of setting an agenda on the relevance of these debates. With these intentions in mind, three chapters populate this part of the volume.

**Phillip Hintikka Kieval** takes note that much of the current philosophical work on the use and applicability of ML in the sciences appeals to one or another form of representation. Under this heading, researchers are inclined to assume that the epistemic value of their deep learning models stems from their capacity to represent the world, preferably to represent it accurately. But Kieval proposes a turn on this growing tendency, one that rescues non-representationalist ideas according to which scientific models are tools for mediating our epistemic activities. With these ideas in mind, the author elaborates on an artifactualist approach for ML in the sciences, which aims to understand their epistemic worth in terms of the material practices of construction and application. More precisely, the argument pivots on the researchers’ skills for modeling. Thus considered, the design and construction of deep learning models in science involve iterative processes dependent upon the skill and tacit knowledge of researchers, and which ultimately scaffolds into genuine forms of understanding between the researcher’s means of construction and application and their epistemic ends. To Kieval’s mind, deep learning models provide diverse epistemic functions, including prediction, exploration, and manipulation. But they do not necessarily do so, unlike standardly believed, through scientific representation.

**Timo Freiesleben** begins by identifying assumptions underlying the standard narrative about the representational qualities of artificial neural networks (ANN). One central assumption he identifies is that humans rely on concepts—higher-order representations—when engaging in various tasks. For instance, humans perceive images as composed of objects and interpret texts according to grammatical structures. According to Freiesleben, the standard narrative further assumes that ANNs are able to perform similar tasks because they develop similar concepts to those used by humans. The central question Freiesleben poses is whether ANNs actually learn human-like concepts, and if so, whether these concepts are localized in individual units within the network. According to Freiesleben, it is believed among the literature, that by sharing concepts, images, and tasks, ANNs learn something similar to what humans learn—and that is more than just performing a task, but rather conceptual learning. Freiesleben challenges this view, or at least significantly qualifies it. While he acknowledges that ANNs are capable of performing complex prediction tasks and may, in doing so, learn human as well as non-human concepts, he argues that these concepts are not stored in individual units. These findings circle back to the beginning of the chapter, now with a negative twist: the actual forms of representation in ANN differ in important ways from the standard narrative, particularly on issues about the representational qualities of human concepts and ANN.

Finally, in their chapter, **Chiara Manganini** and **Giuseppe Primiero** notice that the concept of validity has typically been spelled out by the literature on deterministic scientific simulations in terms of the relationship between the mathematical model underlying the target system and the computational model used. However, with ML entering the game, the authors argue that this picture needs to be reconsidered. This is because the behavior of said target systems is now being primarily represented by a computational model—as opposed to a mathematical one—that is inherently opaque due to its high complexity. They go on to define three formal relations of probabilistic simulation: Weak Simulation, Weak Bisimulation, and Weak Approximate Simulation and show how these can help us to assess the ability of an ML model to correctly represent real-world phenomena.

## Scientific Practice and Scientific Values in ML

The use of ML opens up new paths for scientific inquiries. It is often assumed that their ability to process vast amounts of data at incredible speed grounds their scientific merits. However, questions emerge regarding their impact on diverse scientific endeavors. This is due to the limited understanding of how ML produces knowledge and how they are possibly displacing humans from the center of scientific inquiry. The goal of this part of the book is twofold. First, it aims to inquire into the ways in which the design and use of ML generally affect scientific inquiry. This is done by critically questioning whether scientific pursuits based on ML uphold current accepted epistemic and conceptual standards. Moreover, this part of the book focuses on what can be said about scientific debates that involve systems about which there is often limited knowledge. Second, since ML is used in socially salient fields to carry out predictive tasks (e.g., in judicial systems and in the public health domain), the generalizations that allow predictions are not immune to philosophical concerns such as inductive risk. When assessing this risk, valueladen considerations necessarily play a relevant role. More precisely, the evaluation of whether a certain risk is acceptable in a particular situation is not free from epistemic, societal, and moral considerations. This part of the volume thus brings to the fore discussions regarding the role of values in ML-mediated scientific contexts and the extent to which inductive risk is associated with ML’s design, use, and output.

In their chapter, **Sahra A. Styger, Marianne de Heer Kloots, Oskar van der Wal, and Federica Russo** address a topic at the heart of epistemic opacity, explainability, and algorithmic bias, which the authors deem crucial to scientific practice with ML, namely, the question of whether these systems are epistemically displacing humans from the process of scientific inquiry. Thus, the authors take as a starting point this canonical epistemological problem identified by Humphreys in computational science. The authors address this question from the perspective of the philosophy of techno-science and empirical research carried out utilizing ML in neuroscience as an example. They base their analysis on the consideration of ML design practices, thus broadening the discussion beyond mere ML outputs. In doing so, they show that humans are very much involved in the first crucial steps of the design and development of ML and are thus not displaced; they rather uphold a central stage in their role as epistemic agents. A key contribution of this chapter is that humans are not passively undergoing the changing modes of scientific inquiry brought about by ML but are instead actively involved in the choices connected to, among others, the degree of automation these systems (should) acquire. Moreover, through a case of ML in neuroscience, the authors show that human displacement in scientific inquiries is not an all-or-nothing occurrence but rather comes in degrees, depending on the level of system automation. This take on the issue of knowledge displacement opens the possibility for humans to acquire new roles in the process of scientific inquiry.

**Milou Jansen and Koray Karaca’s** chapter examines values and inductive risk in ML, with a special focus on ML used for optimizing decision-making processes in the public domain. Starting from the idea that the evaluation of ML’s inductive risk is a necessarily value-laden procedure, the authors highlight the mutual influence of epistemic and societal value judgments. To show the relevance of their considerations, a case study pertaining to an ML is analyzed, which is used to increase the livability of Amsterdam’s urban environment. More precisely, the ML is used to classify citizens’ reports of malfunctions in public spaces (e.g., a streetlight not working or similar issues) and allocate these to the correct department within the city government of Amsterdam. To this end, the authors first define what inductive risk amounts to in relation to the different ML modeling stages (e.g., methodology choice, data gathering, etc.). Afterward, they advance the claim that the acceptance of an ML also implies the acceptance of the uncertainties and risks connected to it. Therefore, the evaluation leading to the acceptance—or not—of a certain ML should entail epistemic assessments as well as ethical and societal ones. While epistemic values play significant and confirmative roles in the process of knowledge production, the authors claim that this also holds true for non-epistemic values in ML modeling. Indeed, while relevant social factors are often implicit in the evaluation of ML in terms of model performance and outcome, the study by Jansen and Karaca also shows that these factors play a crucial role and should acquire a central place in ML’s assessment procedures.

**Emanuele Ratti’s** chapter takes a further perspective on the problem of inductive risk. Differently from other chapters, the focus here is not on the analysis of the background assumptions that lead to the acceptability—or not—of uncertainty and risk with ML. Rather, the author brings attention to the assumption of the so-called Uniformity of Nature (UoN) as the central component for ML inductive strategies. This amounts to the fact that inferences of future observations are warranted based on past observations under the assumption that there is, indeed, a uniformity between past and future. By considering the use of ML in biology, the author argues that the UoN assumption is to be considered widely unproblematic in the natural sciences. However, this is not the case when ML is used in different domains that pertain to the prediction of human behavior. For example, the author takes note of these difficulties in political science. So, while UoN can be seen as an unproblematic epistemic norm in the natural sciences, the same cannot be said when it is applied to contexts in which human agency plays a role. In said contexts, the author maintains, a UoN assumption can be ethically controversial. Through the analysis of the oftendiscussed case of the COMPAS algorithm, it is shown that a defendant’s future behavior is predicted based on the previous conduct of individuals sharing similar salient characteristics (e.g., socio-economic status, educational background). Thus understood, the author indicates, a UoN assumption is in place. It is then claimed that assuming UoN in cases similar to COMPAS can be detrimental to human agency. Ratti argues that this is because the evaluation of individual agents’ future behavior merely in terms of what they (or similar subjects) have done in the past might constrain an agent’s freedom of action.

## ML in the Particular Sciences

The use of ML is quickly gaining dominance in diverse fields of science. This part of the book takes a closer look at five promising fields where the use of ML is the driving force of its progress and recent success: astronomy, neuroscience, climate science, particle physics at the Large Hadron Collider, and public health. The chapters included in this part provide novel philosophical challenges related to ML in these particular scientific domains, ranging from their practical use to the acceptance of ML results by the respective communities. This includes a broad range of (classic) epistemological, methodological, and conceptual issues, such as understanding, representation, and scientific progress.

**Helen Meskhidze’s** chapter focuses on ML applications in astrophysics. The chapter considers novel approaches in the so-called “physics-informed machine learning,” PIML for short. Approaches in PIML aim to include physical laws and domain-specific knowledge in ML, with the aim of rendering more accurate predictions and increasing these systems’ interpretability. Through the consideration of two case studies pertaining to astrophysical shocks and gravitational fields around small bodies, the role of PIML methods on the overall transparency and interpretability of the ML is assessed. In the first case study (i.e., astrophysical shocks), it is argued that there is no noteworthy increase in interpretability through PIML (also due to the specificity of the ML’s goal). However, in the second (i.e., gravitational fields around small bodies), it is maintained that PIML shows more promising results in terms of transparency and interpretability compared to standard neural networks. The main argument hinges on the fact that the possibility of adjusting PIML methods contributes to the transparency and, thus, the interpretability of the system.

**Florian Boge and Henk de Regt’s** chapter addresses challenges related to the use of ML, in particular Deep Neural Networks (DNN), in the field of particle physics. This chapter focuses on issues pertaining to scientific understanding, which emerge from two relevant scientific enterprises related to discovery. The first is connected to the possibility of DNNs discovering novel concepts. However, since concepts are an essential part of theories that, in turn, enable understanding, limitations in assessing how ML generates concepts pose considerable constraints to our theoretical understanding. The second issue pertains to DNNs’ recognition of anomalous phenomena (i.e., phenomena that deviate from accepted theory) that would otherwise remain inaccessible to humans. Also in the case of anomalous phenomena, noteworthy challenges to understanding are likely to emerge. This is because the discovery of novel phenomena without a theoretical basis would not be well understood. The authors critically address both points and conclude that hybrid approaches that combine ML and theory are realistic in the context of ML-supported discovery of phenomena in particle physics.

The chapter by **Barnaby Crook and Lena Kästner** advances considerations related to the increasing use of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) as models of cognitive and perceptual systems in neuroscience. The authors refer to arguments advanced in the literature defending the claim that the high level of predictive accuracy afforded by ANNs cannot contribute to the goal of understanding biological neural systems. Crook and Kästner argue against this often-defended claim and maintain that the use of complex and epistemically opaque ANNs need not hamper our understanding of the human brain. In supporting this argument, a distinction is made between two forms of understanding. The first is model understanding, which is challenging to achieve due to the ANNs’ complexity. The second is what the authors call model-induced understanding of phenomena. Through the latter, Crook and Kästner aim to show that scientific understanding can be achieved by complementing findings from standard neuroscientific research with the insights gained through ANNs and post-hoc interpretability methods. Combining these different epistemic perspectives in an iterative re-engineering process can, according to the authors, serve as a base for neuroscientists to understand and explain neuroscientific phenomena.

**Greg Lusk’s** chapter offers an analysis of the role of Neural Networks (NNs) in climate science. Starting from the consideration of ML applications that have started to gain ground in this scientific field already in the 1990s and are thus currently standardly adopted, the chapter aims to inquire into the novelty of NN methods in climate science and how these might substantially affect their epistemology. To this end, the chapter considers how NNs impact central epistemic functions such as understanding, representational transparency, and explanation in the philosophy of climate science. Furthermore, the chapter considers how NNs can complement systems that have a considerable theory-driven component and whether data-driven

NNs could eventually substitute theory-based methods of climate projection. It is further argued that purely NN-based climate projections are unlikely to be successful. This is the case because there is a lack of observational data on climate timescales. Moreover, inferences made from historical data are not necessarily warranted, as climate change implies that the future climate will exceed what can be derived from historical data patterns. This also represents a considerable issue that supports the idea that it is unlikely that theory-informed climate modeling will be discarded in favor of purely NN-based models.

**Thomas Grote and Oliver Buchholz’s** chapter focuses on the deployment of ML in the context of public health. The authors explore why, unlike the increasing use of ML in clinical medicine, the implementation of ML in public health remains limited. One identified reason is the gap between predictions and interventions. Particularly in domains that are subject to considerable change, such as in the context of epidemiology, predictions based on historical data are often considered not sufficiently robust or informative to shape future interventions in public health policy. However, contra skeptic positions, the authors argue that even purely predictive ML can be successfully integrated into public health. They do so through the consideration of a case study from health economics. This study analyzes how ML can spot inefficiencies in the allocation of medical testing by investigating physicians’ tendencies to generally overtest low-risk patients while under-testing high-risk ones in diagnosing heart attacks. Drawing on this case, the authors analyze how predictive models can support our understanding of inefficient medical testing and facilitate the improvement of public health outcomes. Grote and Bucholz also highlight some limitations of ML, particularly related to the fact that MLs are most efficient for narrowly defined tasks for which appropriate intervention can be known in advance.

## References

Humphreys, P. (2004). Extending ourselves: Computational science, empiricism, and scientific method. Oxford University Press.

Humphreys, P. (2009). The philosophical novelty of computer simulation methods. Synthese, 169, 615–626.
