**Part I Epistemic Opacity**

# Chapter 1 In Which Ways Is Machine Learning Opaque?

**Claus Beisbart**

**Abstract** Machine learning models are often said to be opaque: They are supposed to lack transparency and are compared to black boxes. But in which ways are ML models opaque? This chapter aims to help answer this question. To establish a basis for my investigation, I first collect a few statements about the opacity of machine learning (ML) from working scientists and authors who comment on ML. The content of the statements can be summarized by saying that scientists face difficulties in reaching specific epistemic achievements regarding ML, e.g., they struggle to predict their outcomes accurately. This empirical basis is contrasted with a theoretical account, namely the well-known notion of epistemic opacity proposed by Paul Humphreys. My research question then is to what extent epistemic opacity à la Humphreys applies to ML and to what extent it can account for the problems that researchers discuss under the label “opacity of ML”. As a heuristic, an analogy with diseases proves helpful: The question is whether Humphreys-style opacity provides a good diagnosis for the symptoms discussed under the heading “opacity of ML”. My answer is that epistemic opacity à la Humphreys does apply to some forms of ML and that this is a partial, but not the only, cause for what people describe as opacity. There are other partial causes, for example, that researchers currently lack informative higher-level descriptions of ML models. This leaves us with two options to clarify the idea of opacity. We can either take “opacity” to be an umbrella term for the difficulties in reaching various achievements regarding ML. Alternatively, we can reserve the term for a more specific problem that stands out as a crucial factor in explaining why we struggle with these achievements.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">C. Beisbart (🖂) Institut für Philosophie, Universität Bern, Bern, Switzerland e-mail: [claus.beisbart@unibe.ch](mailto:claus.beisbart@unibe.ch)</span></small>

## 1.1 Introduction

It is now common lore that machine learning (ML) is opaque: ML models seem to be intransparent or black boxes, as it is often put, and this is supposed to constitute a problem. For instance, Burrell (2016, 1) considers “the issue of opacity as a problem for socially consequential mechanisms of classification and ranking”. But what exactly does it mean to say that ML is opaque? In which ways is ML opaque? And why exactly is this a problem? This chapter aims to help answer these questions and to clarify the opacity of ML.

In a sense, the opacity of ML is a phenomenon in the real world: ML applications have a feature that people refer to as “opacity”. From this perspective, an inquiry about the opacity of ML can be expected to describe and explain the phenomenon. However, the phenomenon is introduced using a term, viz., the word “opacity”, and is conceptualized using a concept with this name. Accordingly, we only make progress in understanding the phenomenon if we have a clear grasp of the concept. For this reason, this chapter will focus on the concept of opacity, as applied to ML or computer-based methods (see below for further qualifications). This kind of focus on a concept is typical of philosophical inquiry, which specializes in conceptual work. Still, clarifying the concept of opacity is only fruitful if ML itself and related phenomena are taken into account. Therefore, in this chapter, I will also look at ML itself and its features. The concept of opacity is obviously related to the notions of explainability and interpretability. However, in this chapter, I will not consider the latter notions.

My investigation of the opacity of ML will draw on two sources. One source is talk about opacity, mainly in the sciences, but also in everyday life (Sect. 1.2). I draw on this source because an explication of opacity should be faithful to how people think and talk about opacity (see Carnap, 1950/1962, Chap. [1](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_1)). It will turn out that the opacity of ML is often articulated by saying that humans lack specific abilities or achievements regarding ML, or have at least difficulties in reaching them. I will thus analyze important achievements that matter to the opacity of ML. My second source is theoretical work by philosopher Paul Humphreys. He has proposed a notion of epistemic opacity that has been extensively discussed in the philosophy of science, but so far, with a focus on computer simulation rather than ML. I will thus introduce Humphreys’s account of epistemic opacity in Sect. 1.3. The question then is whether Humphreys-style opacity applies to ML and whether it covers the concerns that people express using the term “opacity”. I will answer this question in Sect. 1.4. In Sect. 1.5, I will draw my conclusions.

Before I start, let me mention a challenge for my project. ML comprises various kinds of methods, models, or algorithms. They have in common that their crucial assumptions or rules are learned from data rather than fixed in advance (Alpaydin, 2020, Sect. 1.1). However, they differ in other respects, and this may lead to differences regarding their opacity. There is thus the danger of overgeneralizing claims about opacity. In this chapter, I cannot do justice to all kinds of ML. However, I will try to keep in mind that there are several types of machine learning, and I will consider neural networks, decision trees, and clustering algorithms as examples of

ML. These examples have not been selected because they are particularly opaque, but rather to represent the plurality of ML approaches.

Let me briefly introduce the examples. A neural network is a model of interconnected neurons. Typically, information from an input layer of neurons can be propagated through the network to an output layer. The interconnections between the neurons are described using parameterized functions. The parameters are optimized using labeled training data such that the output layer reproduces known labels for a range of inputs. Here, the labels may, e.g., classify masses from mammograms as benign or malignant. After some training and validation, the network is applied to new inputs to infer labels for previously unlabeled data (see, e.g., Samala et al., 2017).

Like neural networks, decision trees are optimized to reproduce labels, e.g., classifications, for training data. The crucial idea is to organize the data into a hierarchical structure of types, subtypes, and so on. New data, then, are classified through a series of decisions that determine to which type, subtype, etc., the data belong (see, e.g., Loh, 2011 for an overview, and Carliles et al., 2010 for an application in astrophysics).

Finally, clustering algorithms identify clusters in a space in which objects are represented as points. No prior information on cluster membership is provided, so we are talking about unsupervised learning. Roughly, objects that are close to each other in some sense are grouped into the same cluster (see e.g., Madhulatha, 2012 for a review). If the underlying space is real space, then the clusters are agglomerations of objects, e.g., clusters of galaxies. If the space is a feature space, by contrast, the clusters represent types of objects, e.g., certain types of stars. There are several methods of clustering, such as k-means clustering, where the definition of exactly k clusters is intended to minimize the intra-cluster spread of objects (see, e.g., Jain, 2010). This method was, for example, used in astronomy to classify stellar spectra (Garcia-Dias et al., 2018).

ML differs from other computer-based methods, notably from the method of computer simulation. In a computer simulation, a digital computer is used to obtain (approximate) solutions to model equations that scientists have come up with. Since the model equations refer to the temporal behavior of a system, the computer effectively obtains a series of state descriptions when solving the equations. The outputs of computer simulations are often visualized using animations (see Humphreys, 2004, 110 for a characterization of computer simulations; see also Durán, 2020). Since Humphreys-style opacity was first proposed in the context of computer simulations, while this paper is concerned with ML, my investigation will also shed light on the question of how ML differs from computer simulation.

## 1.2 Some Talk About the Opacity of ML

To start our inquiry, it is useful to examine how people talk about the opacity of ML. I have collected a few statements on the opacity of ML by conducting a Google Scholar search using the words “machine learning opaque”. I have also searched for what might count as a definition of the opacity of ML. I have bracketed philosophical works at this point to obtain an independent perspective.

Opacity is commonly associated with black boxes and is contrasted with transparency (e.g., Lipton, 2018, 12; Woods, 2018; Pearl, 2020). In his oft-quoted paper, Lipton (2018, 12) defines transparency as “some sense of understanding the mechanism by which the model works.” Following Belle and Papantonis (2021) define transparency as “a human-level understanding of the inner workings of the model” (3). Opacity may then be characterized as a lack of understanding of the working of a ML model. This characterization fits quite well with Wood’s (2018, 148) complaint that in “artificial intelligence algorithms [ . . . ] the relationships between the variables used to derive their predictions are obscure.” Woods adds to this that the algorithms “often fail to provide insight to the underlying systems,” where he seems to refer to real-world target systems studied with ML (Woods, 2018, 128).

Sociologist Burrell (2016, 1) gives the characterization of opacity a slightly different twist:

[Some algorithms] are opaque in the sense that if one is a recipient of the output of the algorithm (the classification decision), rarely does one have any concrete sense of how or why a particular classification has been arrived at from inputs. Additionally, the inputs themselves may be entirely unknown or known only partially.

Here, the focus is on the inputs and outputs. I assume that the term “inputs” refers specifically to the types of inputs used to train a model, rather than to a single input that triggers a classification or prediction. After all, the former input (the training data) is much more comprehensive than the latter, and thus more difficult to know. Also, many ML models (and ML models are the focus of Burrell’s paper) are characterized by the fact that they rely on training data.

The output is also at the center of what Michalsky (1986, 8) calls the “predictive opacity of self-changing systems”: “Predicting the behavior of machines that can learn inductively is considerably more difficult than predicting the behavior of machines without such an ability.” I take it that the behavior manifests in the outputs that are produced in response to inputs; it is thus difficult to predict the outputs of a ML program.

In a short statement titled “The limitations of opaque learning machines,” Pearl (2020, 15) explains the importance of transparency as follows:

Once you unleash it on large data, deep learning has its own dynamics, it does its own repair and its own optimization, and it gives you the right results most of the time. But when it doesn’t, you don’t have a clue about what went wrong and what should be fixed. In particular, you do not know if the fault is in the program, in the method, or because things have changed in the environment. We should be aiming at a different kind of transparency.

The focus of this passage is on scientists’ abilities to work with a ML model.

These quotations provide some insight into what working scientists and commentators mean by the opacity of ML. To summarize the content of the statements, we may say that they mention things that humans do not do in connection with ML models:

(a) Know the training data (Burrell, 2016);

(b) Know relations among variables (Wood, 2018), understand the workings of the model (Belle & Papantonis, 2021 following Lipton, 2018);

(c) Predict the behavior/the outputs of the models (Michalsky, 1986);

(d) Have a sense of/understand why an outcome was produced (Burrell, 2016);

(e) Pin down mistakes if results are wrong (Pearl, 2020);

(f) Understand the system that is investigated (Wood, 2018);

To simplify terminology, I will say that the items on the list represent (epistemic) achievements. The first four achievements concern the training data (a), the model (b), and the output (c-d), respectively. The other achievements (e-f) are related to working with the model, particularly concerning the target system (f). Opacity then means that humans fall short of these achievements. Often, it is added that humans cannot (easily) reach these achievements.<sup>1</sup>

The achievements most often mentioned are kinds of knowledge and understanding. The other achievements are related to inferences. For instance, to predict an output, scientists must infer it. Now, understanding is often spelled out in terms of abilities, at least some of which are inferential (see, e.g., Grimm, 2006; Hills, 2016; see also Baumberger et al., 2016). Accordingly, we can subsume all the achievements on the list under a broad notion of understanding and the notion of knowledge.

Some of the statements talk about “a sense (of understanding)” (Burrell, 2016, Lipton, 2018). It is not entirely clear what is meant here—for instance, is Lipton talking about understanding in a particular sense of the word, or about what people call “sense of understanding”—the feeling that you have understood something? In what follows, I will bracket a merely subjective feeling of understanding because it may be deceptive and should not be confused with understanding itself (Trout, 2002).

Of course, the above list of quotations is based upon a tiny sample and cannot be expected to be exhaustive. Still, the achievements mentioned seem pretty typical for what is discussed under the heading of opacity. What is typical, too, is that the lack of achievements is seen as a problem, at least prima facie.

What people mean by “opacity” concerning ML is consistent with the meaning of “opacity” in ordinary language. There, the term “opaque” has two meanings, viz. “(of glass, liquid, etc.) not clear enough to see through or allow light through” and “(of speech or writing) difficult to understand; not clear” (Oxford Learner’s Dictionary, n.d.)

Some of the above problems, articulated under the label “opacity of ML,” consist of a lack of understanding; therefore, opacity is here meant in the second sense listed in the dictionary. Other problems refer to a lack of knowledge. This lack of knowledge may either be an aspect of a lack of understanding, which brings us back to the second meaning of the term. Alternatively, we may say that “opaque” is used in the first sense, but in a metaphorical way, where seeing is meant to stand for knowing. ML models are then opaque either because their inner workings are difficult to “see” (b) or because they do not let us “see target systems through them” (cf. point f above).

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">1 There is a general ambiguity when it comes to what people can (easily) do. A large fraction of the literature focuses on what humans can do without any help or by hand (e.g. Tymoczko, 1979). Dissenting voices suggest that it is more relevant what humans can do using instruments, particularly computers (e.g. Teller, 1980). In this paper, I too focus on what humans can do without any help.</span></small>

## 1.3 Paul Humphreys’s Notion of Epistemic Opacity

Can we provide a more systematic account of the opacity of ML? To answer this question, it is helpful to draw on a second source, viz., existing philosophical work on opacity. This section aims to explain the concept of epistemic opacity, as developed by philosopher Paul Humphreys. This notion of opacity has been extensively discussed in the context of computer simulations. In the next section, I will then apply this notion to machine learning (ML). (Note, by the way, that something like the opacity of computer-based methods has been noted before Humphreys; for instance, Moor, 1985 speaks of invisibility and of “invisible complex calculation”, 274).

Humphreys (2009, 618) defines epistemic opacity as follows:

a process is epistemically opaque relative to a cognitive agent X at time t just in case X does not know at t all of the epistemically relevant elements of the process.

He calls a process “essentially epistemically opaque” if the required knowledge is impossible for the agent due to their nature (ibid.).

In what follows, I will reserve the term “epistemic opacity” to epistemic opacity as defined by Humphreys (although I do not think that the qualification “epistemic” is beneficial here because even the ordinary language notion of opacity is related to knowledge, understanding, and the like). To simplify the presentation, I will occasionally omit the qualification “epistemic” in this section. Note, too, that Humphreys and a coauthor have defined a different notion of opacity, viz., representational opacity (Alvarado & Humphreys, 2017; see also Facchini & Termine, 2022 for different kinds of opacity). In this chapter, I do not consider representational opacity much because it applies to representations, and it can be debated to what extent, and in which sense, ML models represent (see Chap. [12](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_12) by Kieval in this volume).

Humphreys’s definition of epistemic opacity is valuable and helpful in many respects. First, what may be opaque according to the definition is a process. In computer simulations, the process under investigation is the so-called core simulation, i.e., the process that leads from the input to the output (Humphreys, 2004, 147, see also 110 and 127). However, other processes may also qualify as opaque. This is advantageous because my goal in this paper is to apply the notion of opacity to ML, and when a ML model is run on a computer, this forms a process too.

Second, according to Humphreys’s definition, opacity consists in a lack of knowledge. This is in agreement with one of the ordinary language meanings of “opacity”.

Third, what is unknown is the entirety of the steps in the process under consideration, not just a single step. It is at least possible to know about an arbitrary step in a simulation. So-called debuggers focus on such steps. The problem behind epistemic opacity is instead that there are too many steps. There are several reasons why computer simulations contain a vast number of computational steps. High resolution requires more time steps and possibly a smaller grid size, and thus more calculations. Also, many computer simulations trace very complex models with a large number of parameters. So, ultimately, for Humphreys, opacity is a problem of large numbers and the corresponding high complexity. It is interesting in this respect that Humphreys (2004, 148) notes some computational processes to have irreducible complexity, which means that their complexity is unavoidable: Roughly, there is no shorter way to provide complete information about the process than listing all of its steps (Humphreys, 2004, 148 and Humphreys, 2020, 16 mentions high speed as another source of opacity, but I doubt that this is a separate issue).

Fourth, the definition stresses that the entirety of the relevant steps is unknown. In this way, Humphreys avoids the objection that opacity is not a problem because knowledge of all elements is futile: some steps may not matter after all. Humphreys grants this; as he explains, neglect of certain details is often advantageous because understanding is facilitated (Humphreys, 2004, 148). Accordingly, the steps in the process do not need to be individuated in too fine a manner. Still, even if the steps are individuated in a reasonable way, the entirety of the steps is not, or cannot be, known if opacity is present.

Fifth, epistemic opacity is relativized to an agent and to a time. Accordingly, what may be opaque to one agent may not be opaque to another agent, or the same agent at a later time. Humphreys uses an analogy to illustrate this. In a proof of a mathematical theorem, a step may be relevant for one agent but trivial for another (Humphreys, 2009, 618). The relativity of opacity is a plus because it helps to avoid over-generalization.

Sixth and finally, by defining essential epistemic opacity, Humphreys effectively introduces a distinction between two kinds of opacity: In a weak sense, opacity is a lack of knowledge of the relevant details. In a stronger sense, opacity means that such knowledge is impossible. An option that falls between these extremes is that the relevant knowledge is difficult for humans to attain. In what follows, I will focus on this middle path, both for epistemic opacity and opacity of ML (see Beisbart, 2021 for a similar move). In practice, it often doesn’t really matter whether we talk about a difficulty or an inability.

Although Humphreys’s definition of opacity contains several valuable insights, it also raises some questions. Fortunately, they have largely been answered in the literature.

A first question is how we can talk about opacity sans phrase if the definition relativizes opacity to an agent (and to a time for non-essential opacity). An obvious answer is that opacity sans phrase is opacity for every human agent at all times (cf.

Boge & Grünke, forthcoming; they use essential opacity and quantify over agents to obtain what they call fundamental opacity).

Second, it may be asked what exactly is meant by knowing the epistemically relevant elements. What are the elements, and to what kind of things are they relevant? Further, what sort of knowledge is missing—knowledge that there are the steps, how they have been finished, or whether they were correct? Humphreys seems to leave these questions deliberately open and only gives the following examples of relevant elements: “justification for moving from one step in the process to another, the representational correctness of semantic elements of the process, and the defeasibility of the process” (Humphreys, 2020, 15). So, one way to think about epistemic opacity is to refrain from specifying the missing knowledge and to think of the definition as a kind of template that can be applied to discuss various types of ignorance. This aligns well with what Zednik (2021) does when classifying what various stakeholders are interested in knowing about ML methods. Later in this chapter, I will argue that the resulting take on opacity is an interesting option, but that Humphreys’s definition is not ideal in this respect.

An alternative option is to spell out in more detail what sort of knowledge or epistemic access is missing. Durán and Formanek (2018) take this approach (see also Durán, Chap. [4](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_4) in this volume). As indicated in Humphreys’s first example mentioned in the last paragraph (the other examples are less clear), they consider the process to be a justification, e.g., an argument that leads from premises to a conclusion. One can thus ask whether the justification is correct (e.g., a valid argument). Opacity, then, is defined in terms of the difficulty of checking, or the inability to check, that the justification is correct. Similarly, the process can be viewed as a calculation, and we may ask whether the calculation is correct. Opacity would then be a related difficulty or the inability to check the correctness of the calculation.

Taken in either of these ways, opacity is assimilated to unsurveyability, as introduced by Tymoczko (1979). For Tymoczko, the proof of the Four Color Theorem by Appel and Haken is unsurveyable. To complete their proof, Appel and Haken wanted to check that each configuration from a large, so-called unavoidable set is reducible in a mathematical sense. This check requires too many steps to be completed by a human person in a reasonable time and was thus delegated to a computer. What the computer did is not surveyable because humans cannot check by hand whether the result obtained by the computer is correct. Computer simulations are unsurveyable in a similar way because humans cannot check the correctness of the calculations by hand.

If epistemic opacity is essentially unsurveyability, how significant a problem is it? As Durán and Formanek (2018) argue, researchers can be justified in believing the results of simulations, even though these results are opaque. Durán and Formanek explain this by introducing computational reliabilism (see also Chap. [4](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_4) by Durán and Chap. [5](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_5) by Alvarado in this volume). Independent of this position, the central point is as follows: A step-by-step check of the computer simulation is not necessary to check the correctness of the calculations or the validity of the argument. There are alternative methods, often called methods of verification, that at least make a case that the justification/calculation is correct (see Rider, 2019). For instance, scientists compare the output of a computer simulation with analytically known benchmark solutions or examine whether the outputs converge to a value by sequentially refining the grid resolution.

To summarize this section, according to Humphreys, a process is epistemically opaque to an agent if, and only if, the agent has difficulties knowing the epistemically relevant elements. We can either leave it to the discussion of specific examples to clarify what exactly knowledge of epistemically relevant elements entails. Alternatively, we can answer this question by further developing the definition. A natural way of doing this is to refer to the difficulty in checking the process as justification or calculation: The process is then epistemically opaque if it is unsurveyable, i.e., if there are too many steps to be checked. In the machine learning literature, this is sometimes called lack of simulatability (Lipton, 2018, 12–13). There is no doubt that computer simulations are epistemically opaque, either in the broad sense or in the sense of unsurveyability.

## 1.4 The Opacity of ML and Epistemic Opacity

We now have material from two sources on hand—first, a couple of statements that articulate problems about ML by using the term “opacity”, and, second, the idea of epistemic opacity, as defined by Humphreys. It is thus time to establish a connection between them or to let the two sources coalesce. There is a natural way of doing this: Epistemic opacity à la Humphreys is used to articulate a sense in which computer simulations are opaque. In principle, it has a broader scope because its definition can be applied to every process. ML involves processes too, notably the process of training and the process in which the ML model is applied to new input (our focus will be on the latter). We may thus hope that, in one of its interpretations, Humphreys-style opacity applies to ML as well, and that the resulting epistemic opacity of ML encompasses what people mean when they talk about the opacity of ML. In the remainder of this paper, I will investigate whether this is the case.<sup>2</sup>

There is no doubt that Humphreys-style opacity applies to many ML models. Typical ML applications involve a vast number of computations. This is true both for the training phase and the application of the trained model. The reason is that many ML models involve a large number of variables and parameters. For a recent example, consider the work done by Samala et al. (2018). They tried to reduce the number of parameters in a deep convolutional network trained for classifying medical images. Even their reduced model contains 19'084 neurons. There are more than 20 million parameters. For one classification task, more than 6 million addition and multiplication operations are required. Accordingly, it is impossible for a human to know or to check each computational step. Thus, ML applications are unsurveyable, and they are epistemically opaque in the broader sense if the computational steps of the computer are epistemically relevant.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">2 Zednik (2021) too applies Humphreys’s notion of opacity to ML. But, as indicated above, he is working with a very broad notion of epistemically relevant elements and concentrates on knowledge. So what he does, basically, is to specify the knowledge that several types of stakeholders are interested in, but typically lack, when it comes to ML. My take on opacity is broader because I do not restrict myself to knowledge. Note however, that my understanding of epistemic opacity is narrower than his since I stress the aspect of complexity.</span></small>

But how is this epistemic opacity related to the problems that people articulate using the label “opacity”, i.e., to the lack of achievements (a-f) above? Epistemic opacity is undoubtedly in the same ballpark as the problems that scientists discuss regarding ML. The reason is that epistemic opacity is a lack of knowledge, and the achievements that are lacking regarding ML include knowledge as well or are closely related to it. It is also common to epistemic opacity and opacity attributed to ML that they can come in various strengths: knowledge or related achievements can be absent, difficult, or even impossible. As said before, in this chapter, I concentrate on medium strength (difficulty), but for the sake of simplicity, I will often also talk of the lack of some achievements.

Despite the commonalities, the collected statements about ML cover a broader range of problems than can be captured using Humphreys’s epistemic opacity. For instance, Humphreys’s definition doesn’t cover a lack of knowledge of the training data (point a above). There is also a more general mismatch between Humphreys’s account of opacity and the statements collected in Sect. 1.2: While some of the latter focus on understanding, e.g. the understanding why some outputs have arisen, Humphreys’s definition does not mention understanding (although Humphreys slips into talk about understanding when commenting on opacity; e.g. Humphreys, 2004, 148).

Still, this need not be the end of the story for an attempt to reduce the opacity of ML to epistemic opacity. The statements collected above, one may say, mention various phenomena for which “opacity” suggests itself as an umbrella term. Humphreys’s definition of epistemic opacity, by contrast, has the ambition to dig deeper and to identify a kind of feature that explains other problems. That Humphreys does indeed try to give a general diagnosis is suggested by the following statement (Humphreys, 2009, 618–619):

Many, perhaps all, of the features that are special to simulations are a result of this inability of human cognitive abilities to know and understand the details of the computational process.

Admittedly, this passage refers only to computer simulations, and, when commenting on the opacity of ML, Humphreys (2020) uses a broader notion of opacity. However, it is still a legitimate question how the problems expressed using the term “opacity” relate to his epistemic opacity. It is interesting in this respect that, when Boge (2022) and Zednik (2021) discuss the opacity of ML, they do so within the confines of epistemic opacity à la Humphreys.

To illustrate the central idea here, we may compare the opacity of ML to a disease. The problems discussed under the label “opacity” (i.e., that humans lack the achievements listed above) form various symptoms. Humphreys’s definition may then provide a diagnosis of the symptoms or explain them.

Of course, tokens of diseases do not have a single cause. For example, when Sam experiences certain symptoms, say fever and coughing, this may go back to a genetic predisposition for a particular disease, to his habits plus a trigger such as an infection. Similarly, if a ML model is opaque, this may stem from a complicated interplay of causes. Still, in either case, there may be a main cause or a main contribution to the explanation. If epistemic opacity à la Humphreys is the main explanation of why scientists lack the achievements mentioned above, then we can say that the opacity of ML largely reduces to epistemic opacity.

To determine whether this is indeed the case, I will now analyze whether epistemic opacity is the main explanation for why humans struggle with reaching the achievements mentioned above. Since (f) is somehow special because it refers to the target system, I bracket it and concentrate on (a-e). In simple cases, our difficulty in reaching a certain achievement may be an instance of epistemic opacity. In other cases, epistemic opacity may at least be an essential part of the explanation of why we struggle with the achievement. To be fair, it wouldn’t be much of a problem if opacity à la Humphreys weren’t central to the explanation of why humans struggle with one or the other achievement. After a closer investigation, some symptoms may be traced back to different diseases. Introducing an etiological (cause-based) definition of a disease often has the effect that alleged cases of the disease no longer fall under the disease category. Still, the cause mentioned in the definition should account for a majority of the symptoms or the most important ones. The question now is whether this requirement is fulfilled and whether Humpreys’s notion of opacity can explain the most important symptoms.

## (a) Know the training data

Scientists typically do not know the inputs that were used for training a decision tree or a neural network, at least not in detail. The reason is that the training data is too massive to be known. For instance, Samala et al. (2018) utilize a network that was initially trained on 1.2 million images; subsequently, additional images were incorporated into the training. Things are different with clustering algorithms. Properly speaking, the latter do not involve training data, and the data used to build clusters can often be visualized in a way that allows humans to obtain an overview of the data. I will thus concentrate on ML models that are trained.

If humans lack knowledge of the training data, this cannot be explained in terms of epistemic opacity as defined by Humphreys. The training data cannot instantiate the latter because it is not a process. Furthermore, the training data is prior to all processes running during the phases of machine learning (both the training process and the process of applying a trained ML model). Thus, it would be strange to explain lack of knowledge of the training data via lack of knowledge of the process (although it is true that some processes, in particular those of training, involve the training data, so knowledge of the training data may be obtained from knowledge of those processes; still, this is a very unnatural way to learn about the training data). Accordingly, Humphreys-style opacity is not a diagnosis of the first problem, not even a partial one. The background is that epistemic opacity was first introduced with an eye to computer simulations, which do not undergo training using data.

## (b) Know relations among variables/understand the workings of the model

Consider now knowledge of the relationships between the variables of the model (which I now assume to be the learned model). For both decision trees and networks (but not for clustering algorithms), scientists do not know the relationships between the variables of the models. For instance, for a typical neural network, scientists do not know the exact functions that mediate the interactions between neurons. These functions have been “learned”, i.e., obtained using an optimization procedure. Each single function can, in principle, be known, but scientists cannot keep their entirety in mind.

Admittedly, scientists tend to have some general knowledge of the architecture of their decision trees and neural networks. For instance, they may know the number of layers of neurons or the shape of the functions connecting the neurons. However, scientists do not know the precise model that the machine has constructed. Contrast this with other models used in the sciences, e.g., that of a double pendulum or models from fluid dynamics. These models can be written down using a few equations, e.g., the Navier-Stokes equations. The relationships between the variables are all known and relatively simple. There are only very few parameters in the model. Accordingly, sometimes, analytical results about the model are known. Network models are different. Since they have extremely many parameters, they form a very broad class of models that is more difficult to overview (note though that there are now ML models that take physical knowledge into account. In these models, more is known about the relationships between variables; see e.g. Cuomo et al., 2022 for a review).3

How is all this connected to epistemic opacity as defined by Humphreys? Relationships between variables are not elements of a process, since elements of something are its proper parts, whereas a relationship between variables is not a proper part of a process. Thus, we are not talking of an instance of epistemic opacity (things are different if one opts for an extremely broad understanding of “element”, assimilating “element” to “aspect”). Furthermore, if the process of applying a ML model to new input has many unknown elements, this is the consequence of unknown relationships between variables, and not the other way round. Thus, epistemic opacity is not the explanation of the problem, not even in part, but rather a “downstream” consequence of the fact that the relationships among the variables are unknown.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">3 Admittedly, there are some scientific models that are closer to ML models than the scientific models I have considered in this paragraph. For instance, the models on which computer simulations are built can become very complicated. Further, many computer simulations contain parameters that are calibrated to data of the target system. Accordingly, the resulting computer simulations are based upon some learning too, the details of which may not be understood by the scientists. Still, the variables used in computer simulations allow for an interpretation in terms of the target system, which is more difficult with much ML.</span></small>

Turn now to the problem that the model or its working is not understood. This point applies to both neural networks and decision trees. There are at least two facets to the problem. First, as we have just seen, the model is not known in that the relationships between its variables are not known, so how can one understand the workings of a model about which one does not know much? Still, it may be objected that the model is, in principle, accessible (unless the program code is secret): scientists may learn how the neurons of an artificial network are connected or which decision rules a decision tree has learned. However, there is a second problem: Even if scientists knew the relationships among the variables, the model or its workings would not be intelligible to them. To argue for this point, we can draw on work by de Regt and Dieks (2005). They call a theory intelligible to a scientist if she can anticipate the consequences of the theory without doing exact calculations (p. 151). This account of intelligibility can also be applied to models. Many neural networks and decision trees are not intelligible in this sense because scientists lack a “feeling” for the model: they cannot infer what the model implies without doing the precise calculations (here and elsewhere, “inference” is meant in a comprehensive sense; it may not feel like going through an argument). They might do so if they had a sense of the properties to which a network model is most sensitive; however, scientists often cannot identify the features to which the model is most sensitive. Additionally, they lack sufficient experience with the model to make reasonable predictions about its behavior for specific inputs. (As this example shows, the most significant consequences of the model refer to the outputs. Since I will get to the prediction of outputs in the discussion of the next achievement, I will not elaborate on this issue here.)

This lack of understanding is quite far from Humphreys-style opacity. First, the achievement that humans lack in this regard does not refer to a process, but rather to features and consequences of a model. Second, the central problem is not a lack of knowledge, but rather the difficulty of running, or the inability to run, certain inferences. Finally, the problem is not that there are too many steps (epistemically relevant elements) in some calculations, because the definition of intelligibility excludes going through many steps. A crucial part of the problem is rather that there is no higher-level description that enables a more intuitive grip on the model (but see Buckner, 2019 for attempts to characterize the workings of neural networks at a higher level). Additionally, at least for today, scientists lack experience with these models, which means they lack implicit expert knowledge of what the model implies.

## (c) Predict the behavior/the outputs of the models

Predicting the output of a ML model is sometimes possible. For instance, if a neural network or a decision tree has the task of classifying masses from mammograms, and a new image is shown to experts, they can determine with high probability whether the mass is benign or not. Assuming the ML model works well, they can thus predict the outcome of the ML model. The outcomes of clustering algorithms can also often be predicted, at least in a rough outline. For instance, in a visual representation of a galaxy catalogue, the human eye can detect clusters of galaxies.

Still, there are cases in which humans are not good at predicting the outputs of ML models, for instance, when ML models are used to predict the weather (see e.g. Lam et al., 2023 and Price et al., 2025). It is also challenging to predict the output of ML models when the input falls outside the range of the training data used (this is the issue of generalizability; see, e.g., Zhang et al., 2017 and Zhang et al., 2021).

Why is it difficult to predict the outcomes of some ML models? Part of the reason is epistemic opacity à la Humphreys. If scientists knew all epistemically relevant elements of the process run on the computer (more precisely, if they knew in advance the outcomes of all computations done by the computer), they would be able to predict the outcome. However, there are too many computational steps, making this knowledge difficult, if not impossible, as implied by epistemic opacity.

Now, scientists do not need to know all the steps in the calculations performed by the computer to make predictions about the outputs. As indicated, there can, in principle, be alternative routes to predicting the outputs. The problem, however, is that, frequently, all these routes are closed, often for reasons that do not stem from epistemic opacity. Therefore, epistemic opacity is not the main cause of our difficulty in predicting outcomes. Let me explain.

As for a first route, scientists may, in principle, know the ML model and calculate the output of the model themselves. In practice, this is not possible for two reasons. First, as we have seen (point b), scientists do not know the model. As indicated above, this point may, with some goodwill, be taken to instantiate epistemic opacity, namely, if we allow that the relations between the variables are the epistemically relevant elements. But there is a second problem. Even if the scientists knew the model, they would have a hard time calculating its solution for the given input. The reason is that the model is extremely complicated. So, the problem is not only that some kind of knowledge is missing, but also that humans cannot perform many calculations in a short time.

Now, at least some aspects of an output may be predicted without a detailed knowledge of a model. For instance, in many models in physics, e.g., in hydrodynamics, energy is known to be conserved. For other models, scientists know that the behavior is composed of certain oscillations. This allows scientists to predict certain aspects of the model output if they can assume that the computer program correctly evaluates the model.

This second alternative route to prediction, however, is also closed for many ML models. The reason is that ML models are not sufficiently well studied and well understood, as we have shown under point b. Whereas many features of the behavior of, say, the Ising model are known, this is not (yet) the case with ML models.

A third alternative route for predicting outputs or certain aspects thereof would begin with the training data. For instance, it may be foreseeable that a classifier classifies a certain mass as benign because the mass is very similar to other masses that are labeled as benign in the training data. However, such a prediction is only possible based on knowledge of the training data, which is often too massive to be known (see above). Furthermore, the prediction may prove incorrect in some cases. So-called adversarial examples are cases in point (Szegedy et al., 2013; Kurakin et al., 2018). These are based upon inputs that are correctly classified. The adversarial examples change the inputs in a way that is barely perceptible to humans, but leads to a different machine classification. Thus, for adversarial examples, the machine outcomes differ from what humans predict.

To summarize our findings on predicting the behavior of outputs: If ML models make detailed predictions, then it is difficult for humans to anticipate the predictions. Part of the reason is epistemic opacity: If scientists knew all epistemically relevant elements in advance, they could make a prediction. Still, there are additional important reasons why the outputs of ML models are difficult to predict: ML models are not the kind of models that humans can currently work with (see Chap. [12](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_12) by Kieval and Chap. [13](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_13) by Freiesleben in this volume; this point is also captured using the notion of representational opacity by Alvarado & Humphreys, 2017). Additionally, it is practically impossible to predict the output based on the training data.

## (d) Have a sense of/understand why an outcome was produced

For neural networks and decision trees, scientists often do not understand why a particular output was produced, or why it has certain features (this kind of problem is central for the account of opacity proposed by Beisbart, 2021). It’s different again for clustering algorithms, which is why I will not address them here.

But what exactly is the problem for neural networks and decision trees? According to a recent account of understanding why something is the case (Hills, 2016), understanding why specific outputs have been produced would imply a cluster of abilities, including the abilities to explain why the outputs have arisen, and to draw inferences about slightly modified inputs and outputs. The second ability would mean that scientists can answer “what-if” questions for counterfactual conditions (this ability is mentioned explicitly by Pearl, 2020; in what follows, I neglect inferences back from perturbed outputs to inputs).

In some sense, scientists know the crucial parts of an explanation of the output: the input that was used to produce the output, and the computer program or the model. But this knowledge is very shallow and does not suffice for understanding why a specific output has arisen. For one thing, the scientists do not really know the model. They can point to “this” model, but they do not know it in detail (point b). For another thing, scientists cannot run counterfactual inferences about slightly perturbed inputs and thus fall short of an ability that is central to understanding according to Hills (in this volume, Chap. [8](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_8) by Buijsman also stresses the importance of counterfactuals for explaining and understanding ML models). This inability to run inferences about slightly perturbed inputs is related to the inability to predict in detail the outcomes of runs of the model: Clearly, if scientists could predict outcomes of the model, they also could run the required inferences about perturbed inputs. Accordingly, humans struggle with making inferences about counterfactual inputs partly because they cannot predict outputs based on actual inputs (note, however, that there may be other possibilities for inferring outcomes for perturbed inputs, e.g., by tracing the effects of perturbations). As we have seen above (point c), there are various reasons for this latter inability; epistemic opacity is only one of them, and it does not stand out in this context. On a more general note, reasoning about counterfactual scenarios moves further away from epistemic opacity, as this reasoning does not refer to an actual process anymore, as it figures in Humphreys’s definition.

## (e) Pin down mistakes if the results are wrong

The results of an ML model are incorrect, for instance, if it misclassifies benign masses as malignant or if its forecasts turn out to be wrong. A single incorrect result isn’t too much of a problem because ML models are only intended to provide the correct result with high probability. Still, if the fraction of wrong results is too high or if an important class of inputs is misclassified, this is a problem for a ML model.

Suppose, then, that a row of results of a ML model are wrong. According to Pearl (2020), pinpointing the source of the error is challenging. Pearl mentions three possibilities: either there is a bug in the program, the model is incorrect, or the new inputs differ markedly from the data used to train the model. Additionally, a hardware failure may have led to the mistake. What scientists face here is a degeneracy, an underdetermination problem, or an instance of holism (see Lenhard & Winsberg, 2010 for a similar point regarding computer simulations). There are several possible explanations of what has gone wrong, and scientists struggle to determine the correct explanation.

Pearl is correct that such degeneracy is common; his point applies to all kinds of machine learning models (and also to computer simulations; Lenhard & Winsberg, 2010). Still, the degeneracy can sometimes be broken. For instance, scientists may know, or discover, that the new inputs are significantly different from the training data. A precondition for this is that the training data is known. As we have seen before (point a.), the training data is often not known in detail. Still, sometimes a rough characterization of the training data is sufficient to help scientists see that new inputs differ markedly from the training data.

If scientists knew the model and understood its workings, then they might be able to tell whether the problem derives from the model. However, as we have seen before, scientists often do not know the model. Moreover, they lack an understanding of its workings. In particular, they often do not understand to which kinds of features from the input the model is really sensitive. We may put this again by saying that they lack a higher-level description of what the model does.

If the incorrect results are due to a new type of input data or a bug in the program, this can be determined by examining the computational process. At this point, epistemic opacity à la Humphreys becomes relevant: Since scientists do not know, or cannot check, all epistemically relevant steps in the computational process, they cannot find out where a hardware failure or a bug has led to the wrong result.

Note, though, that epistemic opacity is, once more, not the only cause of the problem. What is an issue, too, is a lack of knowing the training data, and a lack of understanding the model, which is not only a matter of epistemic opacity.<sup>4</sup>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">4 As mentioned before, according to Humphreys (2020, 15), one example of epistemically relevant elements is “the representational correctness of semantic elements of the process”. This example seems to gesture at a possible representational inaccuracy of the conceptual model. If epistemic opacity is supposed to cover the examination of accuracy, it is of course more relevant to the identification of mistakes. Still, representational inaccuracy is not naturally discussed at the level of the process that is running when the ML model is evaluated.</span></small>

To summarize this section: For some of the problems that working scientists summarize under the label “opacity”, Humphreys-style opacity is part of the diagnosis. If scientists knew all epistemically relevant elements, they would be in a better position to predict the outputs of ML models, explain them, and understand them. However, knowing the epistemically relevant elements is not sufficient for all achievements on the list; for instance, running certain inferences requires more than just knowing about the process by which the ML model is numerically evaluated. Nor is lack of epistemic opacity always necessary for avoiding the difficulties that humans encounter regarding ML. For instance, the outputs of ML models may, in principle, be inferred from a detailed knowledge of the training data. That such an inference is not possible in practice is not a matter of epistemic opacity à la Humphreys. In sum, then, epistemic opacity is neither sufficient for all problems that people summarize under the label “opacity of ML,” nor is it necessary for each problem of this kind.

A significant problem with many ML models is not only that they are extremely complicated in their details, but also that scientists lack good higher-level descriptions of such models. This differs from some computer simulations that are also epistemically opaque. Although such simulations also involve extremely complex computational processes, they are built upon domain-specific conceptual models, the core of which are sometimes a few laws of nature. It is thus easier to characterize those simulations at a higher level of description. Accordingly, scientists can describe their simulations in terms of physical, biological objects, and assumptions. For instance, they can say that individuals from a population interact in these specific ways. In fact, all computer simulations have an interpretation in terms of a target system; accordingly, domain knowledge about the relevant type of system can be applied to the simulation. By contrast, scientists who work with ML models cannot describe the model’s working using their domain knowledge (although domain knowledge about networks may help them understand the model).

This result aligns with recent findings by Boge (2022). Boge argues that DNNs are opaque in two dimensions, which he calls h-opacity and w-opacity, respectively. While h-opacity is supposed to be continuous with epistemic opacity of simulations, w-opacity is distinctive of ML. Here, w-opacity roughly is a lack of knowledge or understanding of what the ML model learns. In my terms, he is referring to the lack of a higher-level description of the ML model. But I think it is not helpful when Boge tries to mold w-opacity in the form of Humphreys-style opacity. It stretches things too much if we say that the higher-level features, the lack of which is decisive for w-opacity, are elements of a process. This is because elements of a process are parts of it rather than its features.

## 1.5 Conclusions

Where does all this leave us? To conclude, I will expand on the analogy between the opacity of ML and diseases.

Working scientists discuss a broad range of problems related to ML under the heading of “opacity.” These problems primarily consist of a lack of epistemic achievements on the part of humans concerning ML, or difficulties, if not outright inabilities, to attain these achievements. If we want to systematize the problems a bit, we can group them into clusters or draw some distinctions. For instance, some of the achievements refer to the target systems, while others do not.

In an analogous way, people discuss a broad range of symptoms affecting various kinds of people under headings like “cold”. The symptoms include coughing, a sore throat, fever, etc. If we want to systematize the symptoms a bit, we can group them into clusters or draw some distinctions.

Whenever a method is found to be opaque for a particular person in some sense, this is often due to an interplay of various causes, some more proximal and some more distal. In the same way, whenever a person has a cold in some sense, this goes back to an interplay of various causes. To provide a more systematic account of opacity or colds, we may ask how the different symptoms of opacity or colds relate to one another and how they are explained. Maybe some symptoms cause others, or there are common causes for symptoms. In the case of ML, it would be attractive to explain the symptoms using features of ML methods themselves.

Concerning opacity, the symptoms consist of a lack of specific achievements, or related difficulties, if not an inability to reach these achievements. The relevant achievements are clearly interconnected. For instance, explanatory understanding requires the ability to draw inferences about slightly modified inputs, which is clearly given if scientists can predict outputs. Further, if we try to explain why humans lack the achievements, some features of ML arise again and again, e.g., the large number of computational steps or the lack of an informative higherlevel description. Still, a neat theory of opacity is unlikely. One reason is that our difficulties in achieving specific tasks have multiple causes. This is because tasks related to ML can be accomplished in different ways. For instance, in principle, there are several ways to explain the outputs of ML models. The deeper reason is that ML models can be described at different levels, e.g., as performing computations, as evaluating a model, or as projecting examples from the training set, etc. (an analogous point is made by Barberousse et al., 2009 regarding computer simulations). Accordingly, we may explain the outputs in terms of computations, in terms of a model, or in terms of an inductive inference from the training data.— For similar (but not exactly the same) reasons it is unlikely that we come up with a neat theory of what people take to be colds (well, if colds are not confused with influenza, they have in common that they go back to viruses; still, many different viruses can produce a cold, and a general theory on who can be how affected by which type of cold is unlikely).

This leaves us with two options for clarifying the concept of opacity. We can either remain at the level of symptoms and try to summarize them using a definition. Alternatively, we can select one or two important causes and refer to them (and possibly their consequences) as opacity.

If we choose the first option, it will be challenging to provide a clear-cut clarification of opacity with necessary and sufficient conditions. Human achievements and related difficulties or inabilities to reach them are not the sorts of things that allow for a systematic account. Additionally, people may disagree on when precisely the lack of an achievement constitutes a problem, and different types of stakeholders perceive different kinds of problems as more or less severe (Zednik, 2021). It is more likely that “opacity” is an umbrella term for all types of problems that are similar or loosely connected (a similar point has been made for many concepts; see Murphy, 2002, Chap. [2](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_2), for an overview).

Perhaps, epistemic opacity, as defined by Humphreys, was originally intended to capture the use of “opacity” as an umbrella term for various interrelated symptoms. This is suggested by the fact that Humphreys doesn’t define what knowledge of the relevant elements is. Still, if opacity à la Humphreys is meant to encompass all kinds of epistemic problems that agents face regarding ML, it doesn’t seem ideally suited for this purpose. One reason is that it focuses on knowledge, while there are other achievements that one may want to attain regarding ML, such as understanding or the ability to run certain inferences. That such achievements are difficult to obtain should also be covered by an account of opacity. A second problem with Humphreys’s definition is the focus on a process and its elements. Some problems with the epistemic access to ML models are not naturally described as relating to the process in which a computer simulation is run. For instance, if scientists don’t know the training data or the relations between the variables, this is not ignorance about the process. Humphreys’s emphasis on the elements of the process leads readers to the high number of computational steps. This is undoubtedly a significant problem, but it is not the only one.

If we nevertheless want to explicate what opacity of ML is in a broad sense, the notion of understanding suggests itself as a better alternative, precisely because it is pretty vague. Recent research in philosophy has tried to say a bit more about understanding, and we can become clearer by focusing on what some philosophers call “objectual understanding” (see Beisbart & Räz, 2022 for this proposal). The latter is an understanding of some object or topic, and it comprises a grasp of the connections among various parts of the object/topic (see, e.g., Kvanvig, 2003, 192). A precondition for this is that we know some of the parts, and grasping the connections then manifests in various abilities, particularly in inferential skills. The opacity of a ML model may thus be defined using the difficulty for humans in understanding the model, its training, its behavior, and its target (a similar definition for the opacity of computer simulations is also possible).

The other option is to identify opacity with a specific cause that is responsible for a range of symptoms. This parallels etiological definitions of diseases, where the latter are identified and individuated using their primary cause (see, e.g., Broadbent, 2009 for discussion). An advantage is that such a definition is more specific. At least under a natural interpretation, Humphreys-style opacity focuses on one cause, viz., computational complexity. I have argued, however, that such a definition does not do justice to various symptoms that have been discussed under the label “opacity”. The vast number of steps is important, but if it only forecloses some routes to achieving certain tasks, we cannot call it the main cause for the symptoms (a similar problem is also discussed for diseases, see e.g., Broadbent, 2009).

All in all, then, we face a choice between a broad account of opacity that covers various kinds of difficulties with ML models and a narrower account that tries to identify a specific cause of the symptoms. We confront similar choices in medicine, where a disease or a group of diseases can be identified using either symptoms or causes.

Since human difficulties in reaching certain achievements change over time and depend on various factors, such as the tools available and the stock of knowledge that has already been obtained, opacity is contingent upon several circumstances. This makes a general theory of opacity even more unlikely. But it also leaves hope that at least some symptoms associated with opacity can be overcome.
