# Chapter 6 Can XAI Justify?

**Carlos Zednik and Philippe Verreault-Julien**

**Abstract** AI systems are increasingly being used to drive high-stakes decisionmaking in domains such as medical diagnosis, credit approval, and human resources. Ensuring that AI-driven decisions are properly justified is crucial. Justification implies that decisions align with relevant norms. However, the opacity of many AI systems hinders this kind of justification since it makes it difficult to determine which features influence these systems’ outputs and whether they have learned to track spurious correlations rather than relevant patterns. Although explainable AI (XAI) offers potential solutions by uncovering the reasons for AI systems’ outputs, its role in justification remains underexplored. This chapter adopts a framework from philosophy of action to differentiate between the different types of reasons that may be given for an AI system’s outputs, assess how these types of reasons contribute to justification, and evaluate the capacity of current XAI methods to identify and describe such reasons. Overall, while the chapter shows how XAI methods could be used to identify reasons with which to justify AI-driven decisions, it also highlights some of these methods’ current limitations.

**Keywords** Xai · Justification · Reasons · Motivation · Explanation · Opacity

## 6.1 Introduction

AI systems facilitate decision-making in domains as varied as medical diagnosis, credit approval, and human resources. In many of these domains, the stakes are high: the decisions being made can profoundly impact human well-being. For this reason, it is important that AI-driven decisions<sup>1</sup> are justified. Roughly, for a decision to be justified means that it demonstrably accords with relevant norms (Malgieri & Pasquale, 2024). In medicine, for example, diagnoses should conform with received medical knowledge; in banking, creditworthiness should be assessed based on financially relevant attributes such as income as opposed to irrelevant ones such as hair color; in human resources, hiring decisions should be fair rather than discriminatory and be motivated by business reasons rather than by nepotism.<sup>2</sup>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">Both authors have contributed equally.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">C. Zednik (🖂) · P. Verreault-Julien Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, Netherlands e-mail: [c.a.zednik@tue.nl](mailto:c.a.zednik@tue.nl); [philippe@pvjulien.net](mailto:philippe@pvjulien.net)</span></small>

Justification is important in these domains because it allows for decisions to be adequately contextualized, evaluated, and if necessary, challenged (e.g. Baum et al., 2022; Durán & Formanek, 2018; Ferrario & Loi, 2022; Symons & Alvarado, 2022; Vredenburgh, 2022; Widdau & Zednik, 2022). If skin cancer is diagnosed on the basis of skin discolorations that are known to be medically irrelevant, then this may be a reason to mistrust the accuracy of the diagnosis. If creditworthiness is assessed on the basis of relevant features such as income, this can be used by a credit applicant to effect different assessments in the future (e.g., by securing a higherpaying job before re-applying). If a hiring decision is known to violate principles of non-discrimination, this may be grounds to challenge the decision and possibly even seek legal retribution. For all of these reasons and more, decision-makers in highstakes domains should be able to provide information to demonstrate that AI-driven decisions are justified.

Although justification is important, the fact that many state-of-the-art AI systems are opaque threatens the ability to justify the decisions they inform (e.g. Chap. [1](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_1) by Beisbart and Chap. [2](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_2) by Formanek, in this volume; Durán & Formanek, 2018; Humphreys, 2009; Krishnan, 2020; Maclure, 2021). Because of their opacity, it often remains unknown which features these systems actually consider when generating a particular output, whether they have learned to track features that can be considered problematic, or how to best effect a different outcome in the future. In addition to causing other harms such as reducing end-user trust and posing an obstacle for effective debugging, opacity therefore makes AI-driven decisions hard to justify.

Insofar as opacity is a problem, explainable AI (XAI) might be considered a solution (Doshi-Velez & Kim, 2017; Zednik, 2021; cf. Durán, 2021). Indeed, a variety of sophisticated analytic methods can be used to uncover the features being considered by a particular AI system, the representations being learned, and the inputs that determine particular outputs, among other information. Nevertheless, questions arise about whether the insights garnered from these methods suffice for the purposes of justifying. Can explainable AI contribute to the justification of AI-driven decisions? If so, how? Moreover, what, if any, are the limitations?

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">1 The term ‘AI-driven decision’ is here used as a catch-all term for any kind of action that is significantly influenced or determined by an AI system’s outputs. Paradigmatically, this may be a decision to, e.g., grant a loan or hire a candidate, but it may also include an action-guiding classification or prediction. Notably, although in many real-world applications such decisions are made through complex and interactive processes that involve both humans and machines, for simplicity of argument here these complexities will be ignored.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">2 See also Chap. [10](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_10) by Sullivan and Kasirzadeh in this volume for a related discussion of ‘core’ reasons.</span></small>

In what follows, we adopt a framework from the philosophy of action to distinguish between the different kinds of reasons that one might give for an AI system’s behavior. Then, we analyze the extent to which these kinds of reasons figure in justification, and evaluate the extent to which current methods from explainable AI can be thought to identify and describe such reasons. In general, although we propose that XAI methods can sometimes provide relevant insights, they are also limited in important ways. Most notably, in addition to technical limitations such as a lack of robustness and interpretability, explainable AI cannot itself provide insight into the kinds of normative reasons that are ultimately needed for justification. Therefore, although explainability is often helpful, it cannot be considered generally sufficient for justification.

## 6.2 Reason & Justification

## 6.2.1 Justifying Human Actions

When people act, we often ask for the reasons that favor their actions. We want to gain insight into why people act, what motivates their actions, and whether they have good reasons for doing as they do. Consider an example discussed by Alvarez (2017): Othello’s murder of his wife, Desdemona. Iago, Othello’s ensign, manipulates circumstances and people to make Othello believe that his wife has been unfaithful. This leads Othello to a state of intense jealousy and anger. Othello confronts Desdemona in their bedchamber, refusing to believe her protests of innocence. In a state of emotional turmoil, he smothers her, only to learn afterwards that Desdemona has indeed been faithful all along, and that Iago had deceived him.

What are the reasons for Othello’s murderous action? According to Alvarez, what motivates Othello–the motivating reason–is the putative fact that Desdemona was unfaithful. Motivating reasons are reasons that, for the agent, favor actions, and for which the agent acts.

Notably, in this case, the putative fact that motivates Othello’s action cannot also explain the action. Since Desdemona has not actually been unfaithful, it is merely a putative fact, rather than an actual fact. As a result, what explains Othello’s murderous action–the explanatory reason–must instead be a psychological fact:

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">3 In the following, we broadly follow Alvarez’s (2017) externalist treatment of reasons for action, but want to remain agnostic with respect to the ontology of reasons, and in particular, whether motivating reasons are only facts about mental states (psychologism) or whether they can also include external objects, states, and events (non-psychologism).</span></small>

Othello’s having a belief that Desdemona has been unfaithful. This belief is what makes a difference to whether or not Othello acts in the way he acts.<sup>4</sup>

Two noteworthy clarifications about motivating and explanatory reasons. First, there is often a close representational connection between the psychological fact that explains an action and the (putative) fact that motivates it. In the current example, the belief that explains Othello’s murder represents the (putative) fact that Desdemona has been unfaithful. Second, not all explanatory reasons are psychological facts. Although Othello’s false belief is the most immediate or proximate explanation of his action, Iago’s deceptive scheme is also explanatorily relevant. Indeed, the latter explains the former, which in turn explains the action. The etiology—viz. the causal history—of beliefs and other difference-making psychological states may thus provide explanatory reasons that supplement the relevant psychological facts.

Of course, we are not only interested in understanding why Othello kills Desdemona, but also in determining whether he is justified in doing so. Normative reasons favor an action, but from a perspective external to the agent. Although there is widespread agreement that normative reasons are facts (e.g. Raz, 2009), for a reason to be considered normative it need not appeal to fundamental moral principles. Rather, it only needs to appeal to relevant rules or standards—more generally, norms—that can be shared with others. To say that a reason normatively counts in favor of an action implies that others could not reasonably reject it (Scanlon, 1998). Since in most social contexts unfaithfulness does not warrant murder, there is no normative reason for the killing. Thus, Othello’s action is unjustified.

## 6.2.2 Justifying AI-Driven Decisions

The tripartite distinction between explanatory, motivating, and normative reasons can, we contend, also be fruitfully applied to AI systems.<sup>5</sup> More generally, the language of reasons can be used to make sense of these systems’ outputs and the decisions to which they contribute, with the goal of determining whether these decisions are justified. Indeed, in many contexts it has already become commonplace to request reasons to explain or justify certain AI-driven decisions. Consider, for example, the American Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) (2022), which recently published a circular clarifying compliance requirements with the Equal Credit Opportunity Act:

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">4 Although we here appeal to a notion of difference-making, we remain agnostic with respect to whether difference-making should be understood in strictly causal terms. There are good reasons to believe that explanatory reasons may also provide non-causal explanations (see e.g. Reutlinger & Saatsi, 2018), but our argument doesn’t hinge on the existence of such explanations.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">5 See Baum et al. (2022) and Cappelen and Dever (2021, 162ff.) for a similar suggestion. Notably, it is not necessary to think of AI systems as genuine agents in a philosophically “thick” sense in which they are equated with persons, nor to think of these systems’ behaviors as genuine “actions”. Nevertheless, these terms will be used here for matters of convenience.</span></small>

Whether a creditor is using a sophisticated machine learning algorithm or more conventional methods to evaluate an application, the legal requirement is the same: Creditors must be able to provide applicants against whom adverse action is taken with an accurate statement of reasons.

Similarly, the German Institute for Standardisation (DIN, 2023) recently published a national standard which specifies some of the requirements for an AI system to be considered trustworthy:

[ . . . ] when the stakes are high (as in the case of an AI system used for medical diagnosis), user trust might additionally require knowledge of the reasons for a particular output, prediction, or decision, because this kind of knowledge allows a user to question, challenge, or influence the system’s behavior.

Although these and many other documents (e.g., HLEGAI, 2019) make frequent appeals to reasons, the term remains ambiguous. In particular, these documents don’t clearly describe the nature of the reasons to be provided, leaving unclear whether these reasons should be motivating, explanatory, and/or normative.

To illustrate the different kinds of reasons that might be given for AI-driven decisions, consider the kinds of financial risk-assessment systems that are targeted by the CFPB and that are used to predict the likelihood that a particular individual will default on a loan. Suppose that Jimmy applies for a loan to buy a car. A financial risk-assessment system predicts his risk of default on the basis of input data such as Jimmy’s income, gender, employment status, education history, marital status, and number of dependents, among others. Given this data, the AI system might output the following: “Applicant has a 70% chance of defaulting”. On the basis of this prediction, Jimmy’s bank denies the application. Having read the CFPB’s circular, Jimmy then asks the bank for a statement of reasons. But what kinds of reasons might actually be given?

The bank could provide explanatory reasons. Just as Othello’s belief explains the murder, it is the AI system’s computational states and processes—the values of internal variables and parameters, mathematically interlinked to systematically transform inputs into outputs—that explain the system’s assessment. Indeed, the computational states and processes in such a system can be fruitfully viewed as analogues of the psychological states and processes of human agents.<sup>6</sup> Of course, as in the human case, here too it is possible to supplement the “psychological” facts of the system with etiological facts about the training data, learning algorithm, architecture, and objective function that help explain the values of the system’s internal variables and parameters. Ultimately, however, it is the variables and parameters themselves–together with the system’s inputs–that explain the system’s outputs for any particular input.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">6 To be clear, the analogy is epistemic rather than ontological. It need not be assumed that an AI system’s computational states and processes are similar physically or even functionally to the psychological states and processes of human agents, but only that they play a similar role, as theoretical posits, in an observer’s descriptions, predictions, explanations, and/or justifications of that systems’ outputs. This is in line with a widespread but nevertheless contentious habit, within the AI community, of using mentalistic terms to describe AI systems’ internal processes, as well as with several classic and contemporary philosophical treatments thereof (e.g. Papagni & Koeszegi, 2021; Zerilli et al., 2019; Zednik, 2021).</span></small>

Although explanatory reasons may help Jimmy better understand the system’s behavior, these are not the reasons that regulators typically require, nor the reasons that Jimmy actually wants. Instead, Jimmy wants to know the reasons that, for the system, counted in favor of the assessment. Was it Jimmy’s relatively low income that led to the poor evaluation? Was it his high level of student debt? Perhaps, more problematically, was it Jimmy’s gender or immigrant background? Even though it is the system’s computational states and processes that bring about the system’s evaluation, these states and processes are not what motivate the system to make the evaluation. Instead, what motivates the system is the particular set of features or patterns that the system has learned to detect, track, and represent. In particular, these may include the combined feature of having a relatively low income and high student debt, as well as the learned correlation between this combined feature and a high likelihood of default. In order to answer Jimmy’s request for reasons, the bank should not describe the computational states or processes that explain the assessment, but rather the features or patterns that motivate it.

Knowledge of motivating reasons is important because it is these reasons that allow Jimmy to ask whether or not the decision to reject his application is justified. More precisely, Jimmy would like to know whether the motivating reasons are appropriate in the sense of according with relevant norms. Do the relevant features or patterns constitute good reasons to predict that he has a 70% chance of default? In order to answer this question, Jimmy must evaluate the system’s motivating reasons in light of relevant laws, norms, or values. Since Jimmy has an immigrant background, he is concerned that the AI system might have invoked this particular feature–instead of, or in addition to, other features–when producing its output. However, by knowing the system’s motivating reasons–i.e. his low income and high student debt–Jimmy is able to determine that the AI-driven decision conforms with the norm of not basing financial decisions on protected attributes such as race, sex, or geographic origin. Put differently, the decision accords with the norm of non-discrimination. Because of this accordance, Jimmy is likely to consider the decision justified.

## 6.2.3 The Interplay of Reasons

Before proceeding, it is worth reflecting on the subtle differences and interdependencies between motivating, explanatory, and normative reasons. In particular, three aspects are worth highlighting. First, while some reasons are internal to a system, others are external. Explanatory reasons that relate to a system’s computational states and processes (or analogously, an agent’s psychological states and processes) are internal to the system; they are the system’s states and processes. However, other explanatory reasons may be external. In particular, reasons that cite the etiology of a system’s states and processes are likely to be at least partially external, because they are likely to refer to the environment in which the system has been trained or developed. Motivating reasons are also internal in the sense of being (putative) facts that, for the system, count in favor of the action. Nevertheless, these facts will typically be about environments outside of the system which the system has learned to represent and respond to–the training environment, or the environment from which inputs are acquired. Finally, normative reasons are always wholly external to the system (Henin & Le Métayer, 2022) because they pertain to moral, legal, epistemic, or social rules or standards of evaluation in which the system’s behavior unfolds.

Secondly, while in most typical cases justification is likely to require consideration of explanatory, motivating and normative reasons, in some cases only normative reasons matter. Indeed, normative reasons are always essential–these are the kinds of reasons that provide the evaluative component that is necessary for making normative assessments. Normative reasons show why some action is right or wrong, e.g. from a legal or ethical perspective. Nevertheless, normative reasons are not always sufficient for justification. In Kantian or (versions of) virtue ethics, for example, motivations determine whether or not an action is done for the right reasons or reflect a person’s character and virtues. Helping an elderly person cross the street in the expectation of a reward would thwart its moral value. In contrast, other moral frameworks like utilitarianism downplay the relevance of motivations for normative assessment. Likewise, in the law, motivations tend to be less important in civil law than in criminal law and can be unnecessary to, e.g., establish guilt.

Like some areas of ethics and law, in the case of AI systems it might be argued that the overall reliability of a system is relevant for justification, and that therefore, explanatory or motivating reasons may not be needed (see e.g. Durán & Formanek, 2018; see Chap. [4](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_4) by Durán, in this volume). However, here it is important to distinguish epistemic justification from other kinds of justification. Even if we accept that reliability may be sufficient for epistemic justification (which is controversial), it is unlikely to be sufficient for the purpose of moral justification (Durán & Jongsma, 2021; Smart et al., 2020). To bridge that gap between epistemic and moral justification, some (e.g. Maclure, 2021; Smart et al., 2020) emphasize the importance of integrating human oversight around these systems’ outputs. In addition to such oversight, however, regulatory frameworks such as the ones identified above place strong requirements concerning the relevance of AI systems reasons, in addition to their overt behaviors. In practice, knowing reasons plays an important role in justification.

All that being said, how exactly do explanatory or motivating reasons contribute to justification? As suggested previously, justification of AI-driven decisions involves showing that these decisions conform to relevant norms (Henin & Le Métayer, 2022; Malgieri & Pasquale, 2024). As indicated above, in some cases only showing that the system’s behavior conforms to a norm might be sufficient (e.g., by ensuring that the outputs are “fair” in some statistical sense). In some other cases, however, we might not only be concerned with the outcomes themselves, but must also confirm that these outcomes are reached for the right motivating reasons. To illustrate the importance of motivation, consider again the case of Othello. Had

Othello’s murderous action been motivated by the putative fact that Desdemona posed an immediate threat to his own life and that killing her was his only viable course of action, then there might have been a normative reason for the action: self-defense. In that context, to assess whether a given reason is a good reason we first need to know what the motivation is. Likewise for AI systems, it may not always be sufficient to justify an AI system’s behavior by appealing to its overall reliability. For instance, a system trained to visually classify images of huskies may be very reliable in a statistical sense. Nevertheless, probing that classifier’s motivating reasons may show that, in fact, it classifies huskies on the basis of a whiteness in the image background (Lapuschkin et al., 2019; Ribeiro et al., 2016). Regardless of its statistical reliability, there is a clear sense in which the classifier’s outputs are not justified because its decisions are reached for the wrong motivating reasons. Although justification itself ultimately depends on the presence or absence of normative reasons, demonstrating that a particular decision is justified may also require knowledge of motivating reasons. Explanatory reasons, especially external ones, can also help assess whether an AI-driven decision is justified. For example, imagine that in the loan-application case we discover that one reason that explains the decision is the presence of bad labeling or inappropriate sampling in the training data. As a result, the system might have learned a spurious correlation between applicant-features and likelihood of default. Again, the presence of that explanatory reason undermines the justification; the learning process was not reliable.

Thirdly, although normative reasons are often taken to fall under the realm of the moral or the legal, there are other sources of normativity that are potentially relevant for the justification of AI-driven decisions. Since knowledge is often viewed as a constraint on practical reasoning (e.g. Hawthorne & Stanley, 2008; Mueller, 2021; see also Buijsman & Veluwenkamp, 2022), a lack of epistemic reasons qua normative reasons (Sylvan, 2016) may imply that an action is unjustified. Epistemic norms may specify the explanatory or motivating reasons that would be relevant to know for the purpose of justification. In particular, AI behavior based on false motivating reasons may be unjustified. That financial risk assessment should not rely on protected classes is a legal (and probably ethical) norm. However, as the example of the husky-classifier shows, in the context of AI-driven decision-making, epistemic norms can also be relevant. In particular, for a system’s motivating reason to be considered good, that reason will typically need to be (approximately) true. To illustrate, consider the motivating reason for Jimmy’s loan rejection, viz. that applicants with low income and high student debt are likely to default. One normative reason that counts in favor of the system’s decision is that it is reached without appealing to protected attributes. However, this motivating reason is only appropriate if it is also true. Suppose that having a low income and a high student debt doesn’t actually make people more likely to default. Indeed, student debt might actually be an indicator of high education and future career prospects. On this supposition, would the decision to reject Jimmy’s loan application still be justified? Insofar as there are no legal requirements of accuracy, we may want to say that the prediction is justified in a legal sense. However, the prediction is clearly not justified in an epistemic sense, because the decision is grounded in a false belief. Epistemic norms also play a role in helping us assess whether the output or its use in a decision was justified.

## 6.3 Opacity as a Threat to Justification

The previous section was written as if the reasons for an AI-driven decision are always transparent to an external observer. Given knowledge of relevant motivating, explanatory, and normative reasons, it should be possible to determine whether or not a particular AI-driven decision is justified. That said, it is now widely accepted that many state-of-the-art AI systems are opaque (e.g. Chap. [1](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_1) by Beisbart and Chap. [2](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_2) by Formanek, in this volume; Burrell, 2016; Creel, 2020; Lipton, 2018). Opacity negatively affects many different kinds of stakeholders, depending on their unique tasks or purposes with respect to a particular system, as well as on their prior knowledge and expertise (Zednik, 2021). For example, expert developers tasked with debugging an AI system can be negatively affected insofar as opacity prevents them from knowing the nature of a bug or how to fix it. Moreover, non-expert endusers who receive an opaque AI system’s outputs will be unlikely to trust these outputs if they are not given clear and comprehensible information about how these outputs were generated. More relevant to present concerns, opacity also affects stakeholders who are tasked with justifying AI-driven decisions, because it threatens their ability to know relevant motivating and explanatory reasons.

## 6.3.1 Opacity and Motivation

Consider again the kinds of financial risk-assessment systems introduced above. State-of-the-art systems of this kind are typically based on classifiers that have been trained using sophisticated machine learning techniques. These techniques are applied to large repositories of previous applicants’ demographic, financial, and behavioral data to identify statistical correlations between, e.g., age, income, and the likelihood of default (World Bank, 2019). The power and utility of these techniques derives from the fact that they regularly uncover predictive features and statistical patterns that were previously unknown even to domain experts. Notably, in addition to being unknown, these features and patterns are often also highly unintuitive and intricate. For the system that is eventually used to process Jimmy’s application, for example, although no single demographic or financial attribute in the training data might indicate (from the perspective of a domain expert) a high likelihood of default for applicants with Jimmy’s profile, it is nevertheless possible that a very subtle and previously unrecognized combination of attributes is statistically correlated therewith. Moreover, it may be that seemingly irrelevant features such as the number of letters in an applicant’s first name, or the color of an applicant’s hair, might reliably predict the likelihood of default. However unintuitive or intricate these features and patterns may be, Jimmy’s bank is likely to use machine learning to uncover and use them for financial gain.

The fact that machine learning facilitates decisions that ground on such unintuitive and intricate features and patterns has led to gains in efficiency and accuracy in many different domains even beyond finance. At the same time, it is also the source of great risk. Because the relevant features and patterns may be so unintuitive and intricate, they might not be easily described and understood by human observers, regardless of their level of technical expertise or domain knowledge. More precisely, it may be difficult for human observers to interpret these patterns using concepts from natural language or from an appropriate technical domain such as finance or medicine. From the perspective of these domains, it can be exceedingly difficult to make sense of what the relevant AI systems are actually doing, why they are doing it, and how they work.

Lack of interpretability undermines the ability to justify AI-driven decisions because it threatens our ability to understand the motivating reasons that favor these decisions. To better understand the link between interpretability and motivating reasons, it is worth delving a bit deeper into what it is that makes an AI system interpretable. Roughly, interpretation involves associating elements of the system with features or patterns in the environment or problem domain that are recognized or understood by a human observer. For example, activity in a particular unit of an artificial neural network might be associated with the presence (or absence) of a particular object or attribute in the input (e.g., low income, or high student debt). In many respects, this kind of interpretation is similar to attributing representational contents to the system’s variables, parameters, or architectural elements (Zednik, 2021); a neural unit that is associated with low income represents that particular feature.<sup>7</sup> That said, this kind of attribution of representational content—and thus, interpretation—is difficult if the relevant content is unintuitive and intricate, because a human observer will have difficulty identifying and describing that content in the first place. As the degree of unintuitiveness and intricacy increases, the degree of interpretability decreases.

Recall now that a motivating reason—a reason that favors an action for an agent or a system—can be viewed as the representational content of a particular internal (e.g. psychological or computational) state or process. On this view, interpretation is tantamount to identifying a system’s motivating reasons. Accordingly, an inability to interpret is tantamount to an inability to identify the motivating reasons that favor a particular course of action, for a system. The fact that a system may be making decisions about Jimmy’s creditworthiness on the basis of a highly unintuitive and intricate feature or pattern that is difficult for a human observer to comprehend suggests that this observer will have great difficulty in knowing the reasons that motivate the system’s decisions. Insofar as knowledge of motivating reasons can facilitate justification, opacity in the sense of a lack of interpretability makes it harder to determine whether or not an AI-driven action is justified.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">7 ‘Representation’ is here used in the relatively loose sense of carrying information. For present purposes, no more specific commitments are made (or need be made) about the specific conditions in which informational content may actually be considered representational (cf. e.g. Ramsey, 2007). See also Chap. [12](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_12) by Kieval and Chap. [13](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_13) by Freiesleben in this volume for discussions about representation in humans versus machines.</span></small>

## 6.3.2 Opacity and Explanation

There is another way in which state-of-the-art AI systems can be opaque. In addition to not knowing how to meaningfully interpret a system by attributing representational contents, it may be hard for human observers to identify the corresponding representational vehicles. Consider again the fact that financial riskassessment systems are based on classifiers that are trained using techniques from machine learning. Many of these techniques work by fine-tuning the parameters of high-dimensional nonlinear systems—for example, the connection weights of a deep neural network with a large number of layers and units, or the decision criteria in a random forest consisting of a large number of decision trees of arbitrary depth. Because the number of parameters in such systems is high, and because the interactions between these parameters are nonlinear, it is difficult for a human observer to describe the way in which individual system elements contribute to the system’s behavior (Humphreys, 2009). When Jimmy applies for a loan and his application is denied, no bank employee—no matter their level of technical expertise or domain knowledge—is likely to be in a position to know which elements— input variables, intervening variables, or system parameters—actually contribute to the denial, how exactly they contribute, and how these elements might have to be modified in order for the decision to be reversed.

This kind of opacity can be likened to a lack of knowledge about explanatory reasons. Recall that in the case of Othello’s murder, the explanatory reason for the action is a psychological state (a belief) that has the motivating reason (the putative fact that Desdemona has been unfaithful) as its representational content. Even if it appears that the financial risk-assessment system motivates its decision on the simple fact that Jimmy has a relatively low income (i.e., even if the system can be interpreted), it may still be difficult to know where in the system that fact is represented, and how (or even if) that fact actually contributes to the final decision to deny. More specifically, insofar as any representational content is likely to be distributed across a large number of variables and parameters—i.e., insofar as the representation is distributed (Hinton et al., 1986)—it can be difficult for a human observer to identify and clearly delineate the vehicle of this representational content and to specify that vehicle’s causal contribution to the system’s output as a whole. Because of this difficulty, it can be difficult to confirm that the relevant representational content—i.e. the motivating reason—is in fact the reason that favored the system’s action.

Like a lack of knowledge about motivating reasons, a lack of knowledge about explanatory reasons can therefore be viewed as an obstacle for determining whether or not an AI-driven decision is justified. Lacking knowledge of explanatory reasons increases the uncertainty about a particular system’s motivation. Because such uncertainty poses an obstacle to evaluating the system’s motivation against a relevant norm, it also interferes with the ability to determine whether or not that system’s behavior is justified.

## 6.4 Uncovering Motivating and Explanatory Reasons

The preceding sections suggest that, although knowledge of motivating and explanatory reasons helps (and may in some cases be necessary) to justify AI-driven decisions, opacity challenges our ability to acquire this kind of knowledge. Can this challenge be met?

The explainable AI (XAI) research program is dedicated to overcoming opacity that results from the increased use of machine learning. Specifically, its aim is to apply statistical, mathematical, or computational methods to meet different stakeholders’ epistemic needs (Zednik, 2021; see also Chap. [7](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_7) by Páez and Chap. [10](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_10) by Sullivan and Kasirzadeh, in this volume).8 Insofar as opacity is an obstacle to justifying the behavior of AI systems in high-stakes domains, it is worth asking whether any of these methods may be able to overcome opacity in the sense of providing insight into motivating and explanatory reasons. Although this is not the occasion to provide a comprehensive overview of XAI methods, there is reason to believe that some of these methods are well-suited for uncovering motivating and explanatory reasons.

## 6.4.1 Feature-Importance Measures

Methods from the broad family of feature-importance measures are designed to identify features within the input space that are particularly important with respect to a specific output. Insofar as Jimmy’s demographic and financial data are entered into the financial risk-assessment system, such methods can be used to determine which particular data points are most important for the decision that his application should be denied. Notably, these methods can be tailored to the type of input data being processed. For domains that center on visual images (e.g. medical image classification), they can be used to construct heatmaps to highlight pixels or pixelregions that are deemed particularly relevant for a classification. In contrast, for domains that center on tabular data (e.g. financial decision-making), they might be used to group or rank the most high-importance table elements.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">8 The application of such methods to opaque AI systems is often termed post hoc explanation. An alternative to post hoc explanation has been termed inherent interpretability (Rudin, 2019). The aim of this alternative approach is to replace current machine learning techniques that yield opaque systems with alternative techniques that avoid opacity altogether. The latter approach will not be considered here, in part because of lingering doubts about the resultant systems’ predictive power, as well as about the legitimacy of claiming that any system can be considered “inherently” interpretable.</span></small>

Because they identify relevant features in the input, feature-importance measures appear well-suited for identifying motivating reasons. The features or patterns that are deemed particularly important for a decision can also be thought of as features or patterns that the system has learned to detect, track, or more generally, represent. Thus for example, if the method of Shapley Additive Explanation (Lundberg & Lee, 2017) highly ranks the INCOME and STUDENT\_DEBT fields in Jimmy’s application, this may be viewed as evidence for claiming that the values in those particular fields favor the denial for the system: Jimmy’s income is too low and the amount of student debt is too high.

Beyond motivating reasons, some feature importance measures can also be used to characterize explanatory reasons. For example, Layerwise Relevance Propagation (LRP, Montavon et al., 2019) uses the “blame attribution” subroutine from the backpropagation learning algorithm to identify the particular input elements that bear the greatest causal responsibility for a specific output. Thus, LRP provides evidence for the claim that the features being highlighted do not only motivate the system’s behavior, but also explain that behavior. That said, it is worth emphasizing that not all feature-importance measures are equally attuned to detecting a system’s causally relevant states and processes. In particular, unlike LRP, SHAP highlights input elements that correlate statistically with particular outputs whether or not they also play a causal role in the production of those outputs. Therefore, whereas all feature-importance measures appear well-suited for revealing motivating reasons, only some of them are also likely to reveal explanatory reasons.

## 6.4.2 Surrogate Modeling Methods

The heterogeneous family of surrogate modeling methods aims to develop relatively simple models to replicate a more complex AI system’s behavior. For methods such as Linear Model-Agnostic Explanation (Ribeiro et al., 2016), the behavior is replicated locally (i.e., for a subsection of the input domain) using a simple linear approximation. In contrast, for methods such as tree-extraction (Wu et al., 2018), the behavior is replicated globally (for the input domain as a whole) using a decision tree with relatively few decision criteria.

Like feature-importance measures, surrogate modeling methods can also be thought to provide insight into motivating reasons. That said, whereas featureimportance measures are most useful for identifying features in the input data, surrogate modeling methods can also be used to identify higher-order features that a system has learned to detect without those features being explicitly contained in the input. For example, a decision tree extracted from a financial risk assessment system might have, as one of its decision criteria, a feature that might be interpreted as “high job security”. Although this feature might not be explicitly contained in the training or input data, it is possible that this feature nevertheless partitions the training set in a way that might be used for the purposes of assessing financial risk: farm workers and postdoctoral researchers (who typically have limited-term contracts) may be more likely to default on a loan than farm owners and department chairs (who typically have permanent contracts). Insofar as the decision tree with a JOB\_SECURITY criterion adequately replicates the original system’s behavior, that criterion might be viewed as a motivating reason for that system’s decision.

As was the case for feature-importance measures, different surrogate modeling methods vary in the extent to which the motivating reasons being uncovered can also be considered explanatory. In particular, there is no guarantee that the criteria of an extracted decision tree actually correspond to causally relevant latent variables in the AI system being modeled. Therefore, although the motivating reasons identified by such a method might be plausible and illuminating to a human observer, these reasons might not actually explain the system’s behavior. That said, current research has recently attempted to improve these methods so that the variables of the surrogate model also track the causally-relevant variables of the system being modeled. In particular, causal abstraction analysis (Geiger et al., 2021) yields a low-dimensional causal network whose nodes are aligned with causally-relevant variables (or variable groupings) of a high-dimensional neural network. In that sense, whereas traditional tree-extraction may yield motivating reasons that may or may not also be explanatory, causal abstraction analysis is more likely to yield both.

## 6.5 Limits of XAI

The previous section shows how different XAI methods may be used to overcome some of the negative effects of opacity by providing insight into motivating and explanatory reasons. Since knowledge of these kinds of reasons facilitates justification, these methods can play an important role in justifying AI-driven decisions in many different domains. That being said, it is important to be wary of some of the characteristic limitations of state-of-the-art explainable AI. Although some of these limitations may already be familiar from a growing body of critical discussions, what remains less well-understood is the particular way in which these limitations relate to justification.

## 6.5.1 Residual Lack of Interpretability

Whereas feature-importance measures and surrogate models may be able to reveal the kinds of features or patterns that might potentially be referenced by motivating reasons, they do not always do so in a way that actually facilitates justification. In particular, although the features and patterns being revealed may be viewed as contents which the AI system has learned to detect, track, or more generally represent, they may still not be interpretable in the sense of being recognizable to a human observer. Recall that interpretability is tied to an observer’s ability to identify and describe elements of the system using concepts from natural language or a relevant technical domain such as medicine or finance. Although several XAI methods are capable of revealing the features being detected, these methods do not guarantee that the features are in fact interpretable in this sense. For example, a heatmap developed using LRP could highlight an amorphous blob or a seemingly random collection of distributed pixels (Rudin, 2019). Similarly, the individual criteria in an extracted decision tree need not be as meaningful or familiar as an applicant’s level of job security. Although these features may well play an important role in motivating decisions for the system, it will be difficult for a human observer to actually characterize and understand that motivation.

This residual lack of interpretability–even after the application of XAI methods– is problematic for the purpose of justifying a relevant AI system’s behavior. This is because it prevents a human observer from evaluating the system’s motivating reasons against relevant norms. Insofar as most such norms are formulated using concepts from natural language or from the technical domain to which these norms pertain, the evaluation of a system’s motivating reasons is hindered if those reasons cannot be described using concepts from that same domain. For example, if the decision on Jimmy’s loan application actually turns out to be made on the basis of an unintuitive or intricate feature such as the sum total of letters in Jimmy’s first name divided by the timestamp value (in milliseconds) at which Jimmy’s application was submitted, then it will be difficult to know which norm to use to evaluate the correctness or appropriateness of this feature for the purposes of financial decisionmaking. Is it appropriate to decide on an individual’s creditworthiness on the basis of such an intricate numerical value, given that there is no explicit rule declaring that doing so is inappropriate, whether or not this particular feature is reliably correlated with the likelihood of default?

## 6.5.2 Verification and Validation

A second issue concerns the verification and validation of XAI methods as epistemic tools. Verification (in this particular context) involves ensuring that a given measure or model does in fact do what it is supposed to do: consistently identify motivating or explanatory reasons. In contrast, validation consists in assessing whether the XAI method adequately represents its target: the original AI system. Current XAI methods are still notoriously limited in both respects.

Consider verification first. Even if XAI methods can be used to identify interpretable motivating reasons, it may not always be clear that these reasons are actually motivating the system’s actions, as opposed to being mere computational artifacts of either the XAI method being used, or the AI system to which that method is applied. More generally, it may be difficult to verify that a given XAI measure or model does in fact do what it is supposed to do. Verification is a problem because many XAI methods lack robustness (Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola, 2018). For one, small and irrelevant changes in the input have been known to yield significant changes in XAI methods’ results. Even more problematic, different runs of the same XAI method can sometimes yield different explanations, and different XAI methods regularly, when applied to one and the same system, disagree. This indicates that XAI methods might not always be doing what they are supposed to be doing, viz. providing consistent explanations across similar inputs and unchanged systems.

Validation is a problem because we often don’t know whether the motivating reasons being identified are true of either the training environment or the real world. XAI methods often approximate an AI system’s actual behavior in order to provide interpretable representations. But whether those representations are accurate is by and large an open question. The problem is twofold. First, it is often unclear when one can be sure that a particular reason has been adequately described. More generally, there is a lack of widely shared and accepted standards for evaluating the goodness or accuracy of the information that an XAI method delivers. Applying one method as opposed to another often involves making trade-offs between different criteria such as faithfulness or predictive accuracy. For instance, suppose a surrogate model makes similar predictions to the original AI system 95% of the time, but another more accurately represents causally-relevant motivating reasons. Absent evaluation standards for comparing the quality of different methods, it is difficult to know which method is better (though cf. Durán forthcoming for one promising proposal).

The second problem is that, even if we can be confident that a particular method accurately represents the reasons that motivate the system’s output, whether those facts are indeed facts or merely putative facts is often difficult to assess.9 But this is often essential for the purpose of justification. In particular, false motivating reasons would violate the epistemic norm of truth. For the behavior of AI systems to be justified, their motivating reasons should reflect facts about the world.

## 6.6 Normative Opacity and Normative Discovery

The preceding discussion might be taken to suggest that knowing a system’s motivating and explanatory reasons is the main obstacle to justifying its behavior. Furthermore, it can give the impression that XAI cannot play a role in our normative practices. In this section, we would like to push back against these two ideas.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">9 In a different context, Sullivan (2022) discusses this particular validation problem as ‘link uncertainty’, viz. an uncertainty concerning the empirical validation of a deep neural network and its target phenomena. See also, e.g., Humphreys (2009) for a related discussion of the semantic opacity of computer simulations.</span></small>

## 6.6.1 Normative Opacity

Although explainable AI is well-suited—within limitations—for providing insight into a system’s motivating and explanatory reasons, justification also requires reference to normative reasons. In order to justify a particular AI-driven action, the system’s motivating and explanatory reasons must be evaluated against relevant norms. As discussed previously, however, normative reasons are external to the AI system itself. Normative facts—if there are any such facts—are facts about abstract evaluative principles, rather than facts about the AI system itself. Insofar as the methods being developed in explainable AI are designed to extract information about the system itself rather than about its socio-technical context, these methods will be unable to reveal the normative reasons that are needed to ultimately determine whether the system’s behavior is justified.

Current methods from XAI can, despite some limitations, alleviate the lack of interpretability and explainability. They cannot, however, alleviate a lack of normative clarity—or, equivalently, a prevalence of normative opacity. Indeed, whereas for some systems, deployed by certain stakeholders in certain contexts, it is relatively clear which norms their actions should be compared against, in other contexts it is not. One issue we are currently facing with using AI systems is the lack of established moral and legal norms: it is unclear what normatively counts in favor of the behavior of AI systems.

Governmental and nongovernmental organizations are responding to this lack of normative clarity by drawing up regulatory frameworks to govern the development and deployment of AI systems. In October 2023, the White House issued an executive order that instructed federal agencies to develop guidelines to assess the risks of AI systems. The EU introduced a legislation draft in April 2021, the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act), whose aim is to govern the use of AI systems by anyone in the EU. Other states are also developing various governance regimes that will institute legal norms, and national as well as international standardization organizations are engaged in efforts to specify good practices in the development and deployment of AI systems. All these frameworks will provide norms against which to assess the behavior of AI systems. Among others, we can expect upcoming regulations to require impact assessments. The behavior of an AI system may then be justified if, for instance, it doesn’t unduly interfere with people’s autonomy. Or, a behavior that would be too risky may be prohibited.

But there is normative unclarity also beyond the regulatory domain. In particular, many epistemic norms remain unclear. Although systems for algorithmic medical diagnosis now regularly achieve levels of accuracy that are higher than those of human doctors, in many cases medical knowledge is still insufficiently developed to confirm or disconfirm the correctness of any individual diagnosis. Similarly, although experts in the financial sector may have over a century of expertise with which to evaluate the quality of an AI-assisted decision on a particular loan application, that expertise is far from perfect. In these domains and others, the epistemic norms are unclear. As long as this unclarity persists, it will be difficult to justify AI-driven decisions even if motivating and explanatory reasons can be identified.

As a result, even if XAI methods deliver the relevant explanatory or motivating reasons, we might still not be in a position to evaluate whether the system’s behavior is justified. Explanatory or motivating reasons aren’t sufficient for the purpose of justification. A lack of normative clarity is also an obstacle. To assess justification, we need to have appropriate normative reasons external to the system. No amount of XAI can deliver those reasons.

## 6.6.2 Normative Discovery

An unappreciated potential role for XAI is helping in normative discovery. In the context of scientific discovery, Zednik and Boelsen (2022) argue that XAI methods can help scientists refine target phenomena, identify experimental starting points for causal inference, or generate possible explanations, thereby aiding them in discovering (even if not quite predicting or explaining) empirical facts. Could XAI play an analogous role in the discovery of norms or normative facts?

According to some views in moral philosophy, an action is morally justified if the normative reasons coincide with the motivating reasons (Markovits, 2010). But if the reasons don’t coincide, a lack of justification is not the only possible conclusion; an alternative conclusion is that new norms need to be articulated, or existing norms revised. To illustrate, consider the case of anti-discrimination laws. Wachter (2022) argues that machine learning systems cluster people into new forms of groups. Contrary to traditional groups that are typically formed on the basis of self-identified characteristics, algorithmic groups are based on patterns in the data. For that reason, they can be quite diverse, unconventional, and even obscure. These groups may include attributes like being a Star Wars fan, dog owner, and tennis news reader–but also seemingly obscure attributes such as frequent-mouse-clickers or more-than-100-open-brower-tabs-users.

Although some groups receive the protection of anti-discrimination laws (e.g. women), these laws don’t protect these new algorithmic groups. According to Wachter, there is thus a gap between the protection offered to traditional groups and these new algorithmic groups. In turn, “[t]his gap necessitates rethinking and reinterpretation of legal doctrine resulting in the inclusion of those new algorithmic groups under the law” (Wachter, 2022, 8). To address that concern, Wachter proposes that the new algorithmic groups should receive the protection of the law since these harms are similar to those addressed by existing laws. This would ensure the spirit of the law is followed.

Traditionally protected groups often have so-called immutable characteristics, i.e. features that people cannot reasonably change (e.g. sex or race). Wachter introduces the notion of ‘artificial immutability’, viz. the idea that characteristics assigned by AI to individuals often act de facto immutable traits.

Wachter’s concerns are to a large extent independent of any specific explanatory or motivating reasons AI systems may have. In fact, that AI systems are opaque and often uninterpretable counts in favor of reinterpreting the law. But suppose that, at least in some cases, XAI could deliver motivating reasons grounded on belonging to an algorithmic group. What if the reason to deny Jimmy a loan is that he is a banjo-loving, PC-user, high-frequency-mouse-clicking, Diplomacy-player? Although appropriate XAI methods may reveal that the financial risk-assessment system is deciding on his creditworthiness on the basis of Jimmy’s membership in just such an algorithmic group, whether or not that decision is in fact justified will require the development or discovery of relevant norms. Insofar as XAI methods play an important role in discovering these kinds of algorithmic groups, they might ultimately inspire the articulation of normative frameworks with which to evaluate such AI systems’ outputs.

## 6.7 Conclusion

AI-driven decisions are used in many different high-stakes domains. Although these decisions merit justification, the opacity of the AI systems involved poses a considerable obstacle. Explainable AI is a research project whose goal is to reduce the systems’ opacity. But can the methods from XAI help justify AI-driven decisions?

Justifying AI-driven decisions requires reasons. In this chapter, we use the distinction between explanatory, motivating, and normative reasons to spell out the way in which different reasons contribute to justification. Moreover, the distinction allows us to clarify the role of XAI for that purpose. While normative reasons are essential, they stem from norms external to the AI systems themselves, and are for this reason beyond the purview of Explainable AI. What XAI can potentially do, however, is to provide insight into a system’s explanatory and motivating reasons, and in this sense, contribute to justification.

That being said, current XAI methods, although useful, still face significant hurdles. Although many of these methods help to identify features and patterns that can be viewed as a system’s motivations, these features and patterns may remain uninterpretable. Moreover, it is not always clear whether the motivations identified through the use of explainable AI are the system’s actual motivations and are thus responsible for the outputs. Finally, and perhaps most significantly, normative opacity poses an obstacle that XAI cannot overcome. For this reason, although XAI can be viewed as a promising research program that can sometimes help, it is by no means guaranteed to yield the insights that are needed to justify AI-driven decisions.
