# Chapter 11

# Stakes and Understanding the Decisions of Artificial Intelligent Systems

![](images/page_236_image_2.jpg)

**Eva Schmidt**

**Abstract** Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to overcome the opacity of black box systems, i.e., to make them understandable to suitable stakeholders. In this chapter, I investigate how understanding depends on how much is at stake in a context. I support the intuition that understanding is sensitive to the stakes with a pair of cases. I further use this pair of cases to spell out how exactly the stakes affect understanding, particularly, outright understanding why. To do so, I connect discussions of the concept of understanding with debates on pragmatic encroachment and on inductive risk. I zoom in on one necessary condition on understanding specifically, viz. the epistemic justification condition, according to which the beliefs involved in understanding have to be supported by sufficient evidence and have to cohere sufficiently well. I argue that, where the stakes are high, there are more stringent standards for sufficient evidence and coherence, and that this explains the stakes-sensitivity of understanding.

**Keywords** Understanding · Explainable artificial intelligence · Pragmatic encroachment · Inductive risk · Epistemic justification · Evidence · Coherence

## 11.1 Introduction

As artificial intelligent (AI) systems become more and more widespread, their decisions and recommendations increasingly impact people’s lives. The predictions of modern AI systems are often more accurate than those of human decision-makers; but this tends to come at the price that they are epistemically opaque—not even their developers can understand how the systems work or produce particular outputs. This is the so-called black box problem (e.g. Bathaee, 2018, Zednik, 2021): Where AI systems substantially contribute to high-stakes decisions, it seems especially important that we understand why they provide certain outputs or how they function; but this information tends to be unavailable especially for modern, powerful AI systems.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">E. Schmidt (🖂) TU Dortmund, Dortmund, Germany e-mail: [eva.schmidt@tu-dortmund.de](mailto:eva.schmidt@tu-dortmund.de)</span></small>

Against this backdrop, the last decade has seen an explosion of interdisciplinary work on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). The point of much of this research has been to alleviate the opacity of AI systems by providing explanations either locally of individual outputs, or globally of a system’s overall functioning (e.g. Adadi & Berrada, 2018, Linardatos et al., 2021, Angelov et al., 2021). An important philosophical contribution to the field has been to highlight that explanations are useful to the extent that they make AI systems or their output understandable to relevant stakeholders in the context in question (Langer et al., 2021, Nyrup & Robinson, 2022, Páez, 2019, Fleisher, 2022). We shouldn’t expect that a ‘one size fits all’ explanation works for all uses of AI systems. Rather, the context in which a system is employed has an impact on what kinds of explanations and explainability methods will be useful. One crucial element of the context is the intended recipient of the explanation—an explanation succeeds in making an AI system explainable given that the recipient understands the system, or understands why it gave a certain output (Beisbart & Räz, 2022).<sup>1</sup> The person’s understanding will then contribute to the fulfillment of certain desiderata that are relevant in the context. For instance, it may enable an end user to (reasonably) trust the system, to bear responsibility for her AI-supported decision, or to detect whether the system’s outputs are due to algorithmic bias (e.g. Lazar, 2024, Purves & Davis, 2022, Baum et al., 2022, Schmidt, 2022).

This line of thought puts into focus the question under what conditions an agent understands something that’s explained to her –which is also my focus here. In particular, I will investigate how understanding depends on what is at stake in a particular context. Let me motivate this thought. It is often presumed that whether we need explainability at all, or how detailed or accurate explanations have to be, depends on whether we are facing a high-stakes or a low-stakes situation (House of Lords, 2018, Adadi & Berrada, 2018, Yuan et al., 2023, Munch et al., 2024, or the AI Act<sup>2</sup>). For instance, where an AI system determines a listener’s music playlist, very limited and superficial explanations of the music picks seem good enough, if any are needed at all; however, in case an AI system calculates the recidivism risk score for a convict, which then influences the severity of the convict’s sentence, a good explanation will have to be quite accurate and more detailed. Since the point of XAI is to provide understanding, the following claim is plausible: Whether an explanation suffices to ensure understanding depends on how much is at stake in a concrete situation. In other words, understanding depends on the stakes.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">1 Chapter [7](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_7) by Páez and Chap. [10](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_10) by Sullivan and Kasirzadeh in this volume discuss the importance of understanding of AI systems.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">2 See [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/headlines/society/20230601STO93804/eu-ai-act-first-regulation-on-artificial-intelligence](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/headlines/society/20230601STO93804/eu-ai-act-first-regulation-on-artificial-intelligence).</span></small>

This claim makes good pragmatic sense: Where AI systems support or take over potentially life-changing decisions, it is important that we can be sure they work flawlessly and that we grasp how they work or how their outputs come about. However, it would be a waste of resources to technically ensure understanding of these matters in situations where AI systems make or support clearly harmless decisions. In a more philosophical vein, the above claim is highly intuitive, and I will support the intuition with a pair of cases in the following section. I will further use the pair of cases to spell out how exactly the stakes affect understanding, specifically understanding why. To do so, I will connect discussions of the concept of understanding (Baumberger et al., 2017) with debates on pragmatic encroachment (Gao, forthcoming) and inductive risk (Hempel, 1965, Douglas, 2000). My discussion will thereby fill two scientific lacunae: First, little research so far has been done on whether pragmatic factors or non-epistemic values affect understanding (though see Phillips, 2020, Kelp, 2015, and Wilkenfeld, 2013), in addition to knowledge or the rationality of accepting or rejecting scientific hypotheses. Second, while the notion of inductive risk has been applied in several papers to the issue of design of AI algorithms and models (e.g. Johnson, 2023, Biddle, 2022, Karaca, 2021), little attention has been paid to whether the concepts of inductive risk or pragmatic encroachment can be employed to illuminate how practical stakes affect the understanding that is supposed to be generated by explainable AI (though see Sullivan, 2022a, 2022b).

Much will be said about the nature of understanding below. Let me immediately introduce one central conceptual distinction regarding understanding that will be crucial to my argument. Sometimes, ‘understanding’ picks out an onoff phenomenon, a mental state one either has or doesn’t have. Other times, we treat understanding as graded—a subject can have more or less of it (see Pedersen Phillips, 2020, 142; Bachmann, 2020). Kelp (2016) develops a graded notion of understanding that takes maximal understanding as its base point and defines degrees of understanding by their distance from the maximum. One aspect underlying this gradation is the depth of understanding; following Kelp (2015, 3812), depth concerns how many connections the subject can trace within the understood subject matter. Simultaneously, Kelp (2015, 3813) defends a contextrelative notion of outright understanding. A subject has outright understanding when her graded understanding meets a certain, contextually determined threshold. Which degree of graded understanding suffices for outright understanding depends on the practical task at hand. For instance, a ten year old has a lower degree of understanding of evolutionary theory than an adult with a PhD in biology. Nonetheless, when the ten year old gets an A in his fifth grade biology test about evolutionary theory, we can truly say of him that he understands (period) evolutionary theory. By contrast, when a search committee discusses whom to hire for a university professorship in biology, the child’s degree of understanding is not good enough to ascribe to him outright understanding of evolutionary theory (Kelp, 2016, 254). These cases indicate that a graded concept and an outright concept of understanding should both be acknowledged.

In my view, when it comes to the stakes bearing on whether an XAI method suffices to provide understanding in a context, it is outright understanding that is at issue. Here is how we should conceive the matter: A level of graded understanding that suffices for outright understanding given low stakes may not be good enough to ensure that a subject outright understands why an output was given when the stakes are high.

The aim of this chapter is to provide a pragmatic encroachment/inductive risk based account of how the stakes affect the outright understanding of the recipients of XAI explanations.<sup>3</sup> I will apply these notions to the understanding of individuals in XAI contexts in order to explain how an individual’s understanding, when the individual is confronted with an explanation of an AI system’s output, can be affected by how much is at stake. In one direction, that notions of pragmatic encroachment and inductive risk can be fruitfully applied in these contexts lends further support to the claim that pragmatic encroachment and inductive risk are genuine phenomena; in the other direction, that conceptual tools like pragmatic encroachment and inductive risk, which have been developed for other contexts, are a match here as well, lends additional plausibility to the claim that what’s at stake in XAI contexts indeed affects (outright) understanding.<sup>4</sup>

The plan for this chapter is the following: In Sect. 11.2, I introduce a pair of low stakes/high stakes cases and tease out the intuition that understanding why an AI system provided a certain output depends not just on the given explanation, but also on how much is at stake. To lay the foundation for my account of how the stakes affect understanding, I next provide a brief overview over necessary conditions of understanding why, taken from the recent philosophical debate (Sect. 11.3). I then turn to two ways in which the stakes make a difference to whether an agent understands why an output was provided: The stakes affect how good the subject’s evidence has to be for understanding (Sect. 11.4) and they affect how well the subject’s beliefs about why the system provided its output have to cohere internally or with her background beliefs for understanding (Sect. 11.5). Section 11.6 concludes the chapter.

## 11.2 Two Cases of XAI

Here is a pair of cases. In each of them, the subject wants to understand why an AI system provides a certain output. Imagine that the system in question has a reliable, built-in function for generating an explanation of a particular output upon demand, that the subject in both cases requests and receives such an explanation, and that the explanation is correct. Further imagine that the subject in both cases has little to no prior background knowledge of how AI systems work, or of how her particular system works.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">3 In the following, all unspecified uses of ‘understand’ will be about outright understanding.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">4 Beyond this, the purpose of this chapter is not to give a principled defense of pragmatic encroachment or inductive risk on the one hand, or of effects of the stakes on whether an explanation suffices for understanding in XAI contexts. It is to propose an account of how exactly the stakes may affect understanding, granted that they do so.</span></small>

Anger Management (low stakes): Luana is a member of a prison parole board who has to decide whether a Black prisoner, Connor, will be offered state-funded anger management training with his parole. She is supported by COMPAS in her decision-making (Northpointe, 2015, Angwin et al., 2016). COMPAS assigns a maximum recidivism risk score of 10 to Connor. Upon reviewing the case files, Luana estimated Connor’s recidivism risk as rather low, and she wants to understand why COMPAS assigns such a negative prognosis for him. She receives the explanation: “COMPAS assigned a risk score of 10 to Connor because convicts with music interests similar to Connor’s often committed further crimes within two years.”

Sentencing (high stakes): Juana is a judge who has to decide on the sentence length for a Black convict, Connor, and is supported by COMPAS in her decision-making. COMPAS assigns a maximum recidivism risk score of 10 to Connor. Upon reviewing the case files, Juana estimated Connor’s recidivism risk as rather low, and she wants to understand why COMPAS assigns such a negative prognosis. She receives the explanation: “COMPAS assigned a risk score of 10 to Connor because convicts with music interests similar to Connor’s often committed further crimes within two years.”<sup>5</sup>

In Anger Management, it seems intuitive that Luana understands why COMPAS provides the negative assessment of Connor’s recidivism risk, whereas in Sentencing, Juana does not understand. (Recall that my claims are about outright understanding.) For instance, it would be absolutely reasonable for Luana to think: “Weird, but ok – apparently many others who share Connor’s music taste recidivated, and that’s why COMPAS gives him the high risk score, so I get it.” If a friend were to challenge Luana, saying, “You don’t understand why COMPAS outputted the high risk score”, she would rightly feel that she was slighted qua epistemic subject. By contrast, it would be perfectly reasonable for Juana to think: “Why would COMPAS give Connor such a high risk score because of his music interests? I still don’t understand why it gave this prognosis!” At the same time, it would be unfitting for her to think: “Weird, but ok – apparently many convicts with music interests like Connor’s have recidivated, and that’s why COMPAS outputted the high risk score, so I get it.” If a friend were to challenge Juana’s understanding of why COMPAS provided this output, it would be appropriate for her to concede that she is unsure of what’s going on here, and doesn’t understand why COMPAS provided the high recidivism risk score for Connor. My suggestion is that subjects in high-stakes cases need deeper (graded) understanding to achieve outright understanding—not just understanding why the output was given, but also understanding why the system would give this output for this reason. This follows Kelp’s aforementioned suggestion that depth of understanding correlates with how well-connected the beliefs pertinent to one’s understanding are.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">5 These are moral cases. If readers prefer, they can, in the following, replace my cases by cases where the subject’s self-interest is at stake: Bachelor student Philip starts to write a philosophy essay and uses ChatGPT to find a topic. The system recommends to discuss why Hume was not a skeptic about induction. Philip was taught that Hume is an uncompromising skeptic, and so wonders why this suggestion was provided. He receives the following explanation: “ChatGPT recommends to discuss why Hume was not a skeptic about induction because Hume abandoned the Title Principle after the Treatise.” Philip only has beginner’s level knowledge about Hume and the Enquiry, and knows little else about him. Low stakes: The essay is only for practice and it wouldn’t matter if Philip were to start from a misguided presupposition (viz. that Hume was not a skeptic). High stakes: The essay will be Philip’s final paper for a course for which he needs a very good grade. He has only 2 days left to write it and would be unable to adjust his topic if he were to rely on a mistaken presupposition.</span></small>

Let me elaborate on these cases before placing them in the context of the pragmatic encroachment debate. They depart from reality in several respects: First, COMPAS doesn’t actually make available automated explanations of its outputs. However, there are other digital tools that automatically provide explanations— for instance, Google search allows users to get an explanation of why specific search results are presented, so such a service could plausibly be made available for COMPAS as well. There is also so far no consensus on how to evaluate the reliability of an explainability method, though proposals are discussed in the literature (e.g. Nauta et al., 2023, Nielsen et al., 2022).

Second, the explanation provided brings up a feature that is not actually available to the system—the questionnaire on which COMPAS relies as input has no entry for music interests.<sup>6</sup> I use this concrete example explanation because it doesn’t make any sense (to the subjects or, presumably, to my readers): It is not immediately clear why music interests should predict recidivism.<sup>7</sup> At the same time, the explanation appeals to a real correlation that an AI system might use for its predictions. Music interests predict race. For instance, rap music has a greater fan base among Black listeners. Assume in the following that the system’s output is due to a racial bias in both cases, and that COMPAS uses music interest as a proxy attribute for race (Marshall & Naumann, 2018, Tschantz, 2022; regarding algorithmic bias, see Fazelpour & Danks, 2021).

The described cases parallel the so-called ‘bank cases’ from the debate over pragmatic encroachment on knowledge (see e.g. Stanley, 2005, Fantl & McGrath, 2002, Schroeder, 2012). A subject is considering whether to deposit her check in the bank immediately despite the long lines in front of the bank. She has solid, but not perfect, evidence that the bank will be open tomorrow, on Saturday. In the low stakes version of the case, it is of no importance whether the money is deposited quickly or not; intuitively, the subject knows that the bank will be open tomorrow. In the high stakes version of the case, it is of great importance that the money is deposited before Sunday, since a large mortgage payment will be taken out of the subject’s bank account then. In this version of the case, the subject intuitively doesn’t know that the bank will be open tomorrow, exactly because the stakes are high—if the subject falsely believes that the bank will be open tomorrow and acts on this belief, this will have extremely negative practical consequences for her. Crucial characteristics of these cases are that, first, they are epistemically identical—the subject has the same evidence, the same intellectual capacities and background knowledge—and, second, the only pertinent difference is how much is at stake in each case.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">6 See [https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/2702103-Sample-Risk-Assessment-COMPAS-CORE](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/2702103-Sample-Risk-Assessment-COMPAS-CORE).</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">7 That said, if readers prefer a more realistic explanation, they can imagine that COMPAS gives the explanation: “COMPAS assigned a risk score of 10 because convicts with the same ZIP code as Connor often committed further crimes within two years.” Keep in mind that the subjects are unable to make sense of the explanation, as they lack the background knowledge to connect it to the given output.</span></small>

Anger Management and Sentencing share these characteristics. The explanation providing function of COMPAS is equally reliable in both cases—say that, in 90% of cases, the generated explanations highlight central factors bearing on COMPAS’s outputs. So the explanations provided are equally good evidence that COMPAS ascribed Connor a high risk score because of his musical interests. The explanation is true in both cases, and makes no sense from the point of view of its recipient— music interest seems completely irrelevant to recidivism probabilities. Finally, Luana and Juana lack relevant background knowledge and have equal intellectual capacities.

The cases differ with respect to the stakes, with respect to how much practically hangs on the subject getting the explanation right. Anger Management is a low-stakes scenario. If Luana were to accept the explanation and take herself to understand why COMPAS provided such a high recidivism score, but the explanation were incorrect or misleading, for instance because it leaves out relevant explanatory factors, this would have no negative practical consequences. The worst that could happen is that Luana offers Connor an unnecessary anger management course. By contrast, Sentencing is a high-stakes scenario, and a lot hangs on Juana getting the explanation right. If Juana were to accept the provided explanation and take herself to understand why COMPAS assesses Connor as high risk, even though the explanation was misleading—in the given scenario, it misleads by omitting the fact that algorithmic bias was a crucial factor—this would have very bad consequences. For if she were thus to get wrong core factors that really stood behind the system’s output, she would very likely discriminate against Connor by giving him a severe sentence because of algorithmic bias.<sup>8,9</sup>

Notice the difference between how pragmatic factors affect outright understanding in these cases and pragmatic encroachment on knowledge: There, the pragmatic encroaches on knowledge just in case the subject’s having a false belief and acting on it would lead to very bad consequences (see Schmidt, 2025). For understanding, the issue is: If the subject got the actual explanation of the system’s output wrong and acted on this basis, would that lead to very bad consequences? ‘Getting the explanation wrong’ covers scenarios in which the explanation accepted by the subject is false, but also scenarios in which it merely leaves out central contributing factors, so that the subject is misled about what really explains why the output was given. These points will become relevant below.<sup>10</sup>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">8 Following Altman (2020), I take discrimination to “impose a relative disadvantage on persons based on their membership in a salient social group”.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">9 Does this mean that my point is really whether subjects in high stakes situations are justified to act on the outputs of AI systems, given certain explanations (not whether they understand)? This is not so. My interest is in an epistemic status, understanding, and how it is affected by the stakes. Nonetheless, there is an effect on action, but this can be spelled out by appeal to understandingaction principles that parallel the knowledge-action principles discussed in the debate on pragmatic encroachment. For instance, Fantl and McGrath (2002) argue that one knows or is justified to believe that p only if it is rational for one to act as if p. I submit that, similarly, if the subject doesn’t understand why p, it may not be rational for her to act on the basis of p.</span></small>

To sum up, in Anger Management and Sentencing, the subjects are epistemic equals as far as the quality of their evidence, their intellectual capacities, or their relevant background knowledge go. But they intuitively differ with respect to their understanding of why the relevant output was given: While Luana understands why COMPAS assigned a high recidivism score to Connor, Juana does not. Since the striking difference between the cases is how much is at stake, it seems that the stakes affect understanding as much as they affect knowledge. To make this claim plausible and to see how exactly the pragmatic encroaches on understanding, we first need to take a closer look at understanding.<sup>11</sup>

## 11.3 Understanding: The Concept

The mental state of understanding—whether graded or outright—is currently much discussed in the philosophy of science and epistemology (see Baumberger et al., 2017, Grimm, 2021, Hannon, 2021 for recent overviews). One topic of debate is the nature of understanding (in both senses). Similarly to the long-running discussion on the correct analysis of knowledge, there are efforts to provide the conditions under which a subject understands. My aim in this section is to bring out the conditions of understanding that, on my proposal, are affected by the stakes. I will present some core elements of the debate over the nature of understanding, and particularly focus on four widely accepted necessary conditions on understanding. As before, my presentation focuses on outright understanding.

Let me start with a further important distinction, that between objectual and explanatory understanding (e.g. Baumberger et al., 2017, 5). A person has objectual understanding when she understands an overall subject matter or a broader domain, as when she understands machine learning or genetics. We say the person has explanatory understanding, or understanding why, when she understands why something happened or is the case, for instance, when she understands why inflation went up in 2022 or why the dinosaurs became extinct. Objectual understanding is plausibly relevant to XAI in situations where we want understanding of how an AI system works overall. My interest here is in understanding why a system gave a certain output, which I take to be an instance of explanatory understanding.<sup>12</sup> This is what I will focus on here.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">10 Similarly, see Biddle and Kukla’s (2017) push for broadening our conception of inductive risk to one of epistemic risk, which goes beyond risks from acting on false belief.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">11 I have introduced my proposal via a pair of cases that supposedly elicit a certain intuition, but intuitions tend not to be shared by everyone. In acknowledgement of this, readers can think of this chapter as starting from the observation that many contributors to the field of XAI hold that the stakes make a difference to whether explainability is needed; and of its aim as providing a theory of how the stakes can affect the need for explanation by way of a stakes-sensitive account of understanding. The cases then only serve an illustrative purpose.</span></small>

So what are the necessary conditions on understanding? As with conditions on knowledge, there is disagreement about the details, but many views converge on four conditions that a subject has to meet to understand: (1) belief/acceptance, (2) grasp, (3) truth/factivity, and (4) justification (see e.g. Baumberger et al., 2017, Pritchard, 2010, Chap. [4](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_4), Hills, 2015, Malfatti, 2023). Note the parallels with the traditional analysis of knowledge as justified true belief; a difference is that for knowledge that $p ,$ the necessary conditions apply only to a single proposition $p .$ By contrast, for understanding why $p$ is the case, propositions beyond $p$ are relevant, viz. those propositions q, r, s that constitute the explanans of why $p ,$ as well as the proposition that q, r, s explain why $p .$ With this in mind, let’s turn to the four necessary conditions on understanding.

S understands why $p$ is the case only if

(1) S believes or accepts that $p$ and that q, r, s (and maybe also believes or accepts that q, r, s explain why $p )$ ,

For instance, I understand why the dinosaurs became extinct 66 million years ago only if I believe that the dinosaurs became extinct then, and I additionally believe propositions such as: that an asteroid hit Earth, that this caused huge amounts of dust to enter the atmosphere, leading to temperature drops, which led to mass extinction, and that in this way the asteroid impact explains why the dinosaurs went extinct.

Some philosophers relax the belief condition and instead endorse an acceptance condition on understanding, so that S has to merely accept the relevant propositions as premises from which to draw further inferences, or on which to act. Unlike belief, acceptance is an attitude that a person can correctly have towards propositions that approximate the truth, but are not literally true (Elgin, 2017, Chap. [2](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_2); Malfatti, 2023, Chap. [8](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_8)). To illustrate, the dinosaurs didn’t go extinct exactly 66 million years ago, and not all of them did—the birds survived. And the explanation sketched above oversimplifies, since many species went extinct due to tsunamis, earthquakes, and wildfires caused by the asteroid impact. I wish to remain neutral between belief and acceptance, here; for ease of exposition, I will speak only of belief in the following.

(2) S grasps the interconnections between $p$ and the propositions q, r, s, which explain it,

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">12 Though see Páez (2019, 454) for the view that the relevant understanding is objectual, though localized. In the following, unqualified instances of ‘understanding’ will refer to outright explanatory understanding.</span></small>

Understanding is more than just knowing or believing individual pieces of information, it involves seeing how these connect or fit together. The notion of grasp is supposed to capture this. In the example, I understand why the dinosaurs became extinct only if I grasp how their extinction relates, e.g., to the asteroid’s impact on Earth, to the dust in the atmosphere, or to the temperature dropping, and how these explanatory factors in turn hang together. More specifically, I have to see what explanatory or counterfactual relationships exist between the dinosaurs’ extinction, the asteroid impact, and so on (Riggs, 2003). Grasp is often spelled out by way of relevant abilities the subject has to have, such as being able to explain how the extinction happened, or to say what would have happened in certain counterfactual situations, e.g. if the asteroid had bypassed Earth (Hills, 2015).

(3) At least central propositions among p, q, r, s (and the proposition that q, r, s explain why p) are true, or approximately true,

I cannot understand why the dinosaurs became extinct if this isn’t even approximately true, or if the explanation I believe isn’t even in the neighborhood of the truth. Whether the exact truth is needed or something more approximate is sufficient is contentious. Positions range from the view that all the mentioned propositions need to be true (Kelp, 2015), to the view that central propositions have to be true, while peripheral propositions may be false (Kvanvig, 2003), to the view that the relevant propositions need be merely approximately true (Elgin, 2007). I remain neutral between these positions.

(4) S’s beliefs that p, q, r, s (and that q, r, s explain why p) are epistemically justified: they are (a) supported by sufficient evidence and they (b) cohere among each other and with S’s background beliefs.

If a subject randomly accepts certain propositions (whether on the explanandum or on the explanans side), although it’s utterly nebulous to her why they should be true, she doesn’t thereby gain understanding (see Pritchard, 2010, 76, referring to Zagzebski, 2001). Instead, her beliefs must be epistemically justified to constitute understanding. In my view, this has two aspects. On the one hand, the relevant propositions have to be sufficiently supported by the subject’s epistemic reasons or evidence; on the other hand, they have to cohere sufficiently well, by being consistent or standing in explanatory or probabilistic relations with each other (Kvanvig, 2003, Elgin, 2007, 35) and fitting in well with the other beliefs of the subject (Malfatti, 2023, 38, Elgin, 2017).<sup>13</sup> For instance, my understanding of why the dinosaurs became extinct presupposes that I don’t just randomly guess that an asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago, but that I have evidence that this is so, e.g. that I read this in a reliable science book. Furthermore, there have to be interconnections between the relevant propositions (which I grasp, see (2)). If I justifiably believe several true propositions in addition to my belief that the dinosaurs became extinct, but these are completely unrelated to each other or to the dinosaurs’ extinction, this doesn’t amount to understanding. Imagine that, beyond these beliefs about dinosaurs, the asteroid, and so on, I am a dyed-in-the-wool creationist who believes that God created the world, including ready-made dinosaur fossils, 6000 years ago. Given the lack of fit (or rather, the contradictions) between my beliefs about the dinosaur extinction and my background beliefs, I don’t really understand how the dinosaurs became extinct.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">13 As this indicates, coherence is of central importance for understanding; to my mind, understanding differs from knowledge in this regard, which requires no coherence.</span></small>

Some philosophers object to a justification condition on understanding and defend the claim that we can understand why something is the case even where the beliefs involved in our understanding are supported only by defeated evidence (Hills, 2015). In Malfatti’s (2023, 189) example, if a medical doctor hears a patient’s report of his condition and infers that he suffers from anemia, and then receives the misleading evidence that the patient is a compulsive liar, her evidence (the patient’s report) is defeated. But, this line of thought has it, her understanding of why the patient exhibits certain symptoms is not thereby undermined.

Discussing this general point here would lead me too far afield. However, I find the claim implausible at least in XAI contexts, even for low stakes scenarios. Imagine that the advertisements in your Facebook stream seem to pick up on the fact that you just booked a vacation, and that you do not want this. In the Facebook settings, you look up which of your personal information Facebook advertisements use and see that they do not rely on your recent purchases. You thereby take yourself to understand something about how your Facebook advertisements are generated, and trust Facebook advertisements not to use information about recent purchases. Now imagine that from a reliable source, you receive the (albeit misleading!) evidence that Facebook’s statements about which information it uses to personalize advertisements are highly unreliable. This defeats your evidence that Facebook doesn’t use information about your vacation for its advertisements. So, your belief that the ads don’t respond to your booked vacation is no longer epistemically justified. I submit that simultaneously (and contrary to Malfatti), you lose your understanding of how Facebook came to display the ads in question to you. It would be perfectly reasonable for you to think: “I thought I understood which factors Facebook uses to determine which advertisements to display – but now I’m confused. I don’t understand why it shows me these specific ads!”

My claim is supported by the fact that now you rightly no longer trust Facebook’s algorithm not to rely on your recent purchases. Put more generally, understanding can be instrumental to reasonable trust in AI contexts (e.g. Ribeiro et al., 2016, EU High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019, 13, Schmidt, 2022). Given this, the fact that your trust is lost indicates that your understanding is lost also. More generally, the call for XAI is not a call for what one might call idle understanding, but for understanding that enables stakeholders to do things relevant in the context (Langer et al., 2021); but purported understanding based on defeated evidence is insulated from (reasonable) action. At least in XAI contexts, defeaters thus undermine the subject’s understanding together with her evidence, and (4) stands as a necessary condition for understanding.

How does all this connect to the claim, introduced in Sect. 11.2, that the stakes affect whether a subject understands? I will next propose that the stakes affect understanding by making a difference to whether the subject’s beliefs are epistemically justified in XAI contexts. The idea to be developed is this: The more is at stake, the stricter the justification condition—both in terms of whether the evidence is strong enough to suffice for justification, and in terms of whether the believed propositions cohere well enough to render the beliefs justified.

## 11.4 How the Stakes Affect Understanding (I): Strength of Evidence

Understanding (in XAI contexts) requires epistemic justification of the relevant beliefs, and justification requires sufficient evidence or reasons, just as in the case of knowledge. Correspondingly, one way for the stakes to make a difference to a subject’s understanding is by making a difference to whether her evidence or epistemic reasons suffice for justification, i.e., via ‘standard’ pragmatic encroachment.<sup>14</sup>

To illustrate, imagine (contrary to the original scenarios) that the explanation that the subjects are given for why COMPAS assigned Connor the high risk score is that individuals with a similar criminal history have often reoffended. Say that Luana/Juana knows that algorithmic bias is a real problem of some AI systems, possibly including COMPAS (Angwin et al., 2016, Chouldechova, 2017). Finally, imagine that the explanation is correct, and that COMPAS really is sensitive to features of Connor’s criminal history shared by convicts who frequently recidivated, and that this explains the system’s prognosis.

Luana is in a low-stakes scenario; if she simply adopted the explanation and acted on it, even if the explanation were false, nothing bad would happen in consequence. She might offer Connor an optional anger management course, but that’s all. Accordingly, her belief—that COMPAS assigned Connor the maximum recidivism risk score because people with a similar criminal history often recidivated—is justified by the explanation she receives from COMPAS (indeed, it amounts to knowledge). Luana understands why the high recidivism risk score was outputted.

By contrast, Juana is in a high-stakes situation: If—counterfactually—an algorithmic bias against Black people really explained the system’s prognosis (so the automatically generated explanation of the prognosis was false), this might lead to very bad moral consequences. For if Juana took the provided explanation at face value, formed the false belief that COMPAS provided the high risk score because of Connor’s criminal history, and gave him a severe sentence because of COMPAS’s high risk score, she would discriminate against him. Being imprisoned unnecessarily would be terrible for Connor, and the important moral and legal value of fair treatment in criminal proceedings would be violated.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">14 A related issue is whether the justificatory power of an AI system’s outputs may be undermined by its opacity. See Chap. [6](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_6) by Zednik and Verreault-Julien in this volume.</span></small>

In light of this, Juana’s belief that COMPAS provided the high risk score because of Connor’s criminal history is not justified (and it is not knowledge). True, the fact that a reliable explanatory mechanism gave the explanation—that Connor was assigned a maximum risk score because individuals with a similar criminal history have often reoffended—indicates that Connor’s criminal history explains COMPAS’s high risk score; it is good evidence that COMPAS provided the high risk score because of Connor’s criminal history. This evidence justifies belief in this explanation to a degree. However, because so much is at stake, this evidence does not suffice to justify Juana’s corresponding belief, all things considered.<sup>15</sup> Think about it this way: Given that Juana is aware of the real-world problem of algorithmic bias, and given that (as in the original Sentencing) her own perusal of Connor’s files led her to asses him as low risk, is it epistemically rational for her to simply accept the explanation provided by COMPAS? I think not; rather, it would be rational for her to remain in doubt as to the real explanation of the high risk score. As I have phrased it elsewhere (Schmidt, 2025), where a lot hinges on an agent’s getting a belief right, she needs to be especially diligent in weighing her reasons in forming the belief, which is to say that it takes more for her epistemic reasons to believe to suffice for all things considered justified belief.<sup>16</sup> In the current context, this means that Juana needs to be especially sensitive to possible limitations of her evidence, such as the possibility that the explanation she received might be incorrect or misleading. She should therefore accord the testimony provided by COMPAS’s explanatory mechanism less weight than she would if nothing much was at stake. Given that her evidence is thus weakened, it is insufficient to justify belief; and so her understanding of why COMPAS provided its output is undermined.<sup>17</sup>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">15 Two elucidations: (1) I here conceive of evidence as considerations that probabilify the target proposition. So, the fact that a reliable explanatory mechanism states that the risk score was given because of criminal history is evidence that, indeed, the risk score was given because of criminal history. The fact that an explanation is given here serves as evidence that a certain causal relation holds. (2) I rely on the distinction between a graded notion and an all things considered notion of justification that parallels the graded/outright distinction regarding understanding: A proposition can be more or less justified for a believer, where this does not fix whether this justification suffices to make belief the correct attitude, all things considered. Think of all things considered justification as knowledge-level justification—the kind of justification that is a necessary condition for knowledge (Schroeder, 2012).</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">16 My full account of pragmatic encroachment in Schmidt (2025) spells this thought out by appeal to attenuating conditions that weaken the pertinent reasons to believe. It further appeals to how much weight a perfectly virtuous reasoner would accord her reasons, and uses this to explain why the subject’s reasons are weakened. There is no need to take these claims on board to accept my proposal here.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">17 Another respect in which the evidence provided by COMPAS may be insufficient is that it is bare statistical evidence, where it is important to make judicial decisions on the basis of individualized evidence (Schmidt et al., 2023, Sullivan, 2022a, 314).</span></small>

The same point can be made with the help of the notion of inductive risk from the philosophy of science (Hempel, 1965, Douglas, 2000, Steel, 2010):<sup>18</sup> There is always some probability of error in accepting or rejecting a scientific hypothesis on the basis of empirical evidence. Errors of two kinds are possible: First, false positive error—the hypothesis that a certain phenomenon occurs is accepted, although it does not occur; second, false negative error—the hypothesis that a phenomenon occurs is rejected, but it does occur. The risk that one of these two errors will occur is called inductive risk. According to Hempel (1965), scientists cannot avoid this risk; the only latitude they have concerns whether to err on the false positive side or on the false negative side. In other words, there is a tradeoff—scientists can only minimize the risk of false-negative errors at the cost of an increased risk of false-positive results, and vice versa. They must thus independently determine how much evidence is needed before the hypothesis can be accepted. To do so, they need to look to non-epistemic values. It is what is of practical or moral value to us that determines which type of error we should rather risk—missing out on true hypotheses or accepting false hypotheses (see Douglas, 2000, 561/562).

Applied to Sentencing, this means that, since false positive errors (mistakenly accepting an automatically generated, seemingly unbiased explanation of why COMPAS deemed Connor high risk) raise the risk of violating important moral values, such as fair treatment in criminal procedures, the risk of false positive error should be minimized. Juana shouldn’t accept the explanation on the given evidence, but needs better evidence to do so. In other words, the belief that Connor was accorded a maximum risk score by COMPAS because of his criminal history is not justified for her. Since justification is a necessary condition for understanding, she therefore does not understand why COMPAS assessed Connor’s recidivism risk so negatively. By contrast, in Anger Management, no practical or moral values are violated if Luana believes COMPAS’s explanation of why it provided the high risk score, i.e. if she makes a false positive error. There is no need to minimize risking such errors, and so she is justified to believe the explanation, and thereby (outright) understands why COMPAS provided this output.

Inductive risk is used by opponents of the so-called ‘value-free ideal of science to argue that not only what is of epistemic value is directly relevant to science, but that matters of practical, moral, or political value affect which theories scientists correctly accept (e.g. Longino, 1990, Rudner, 1953). Again, the idea is that in many cases, practical or moral concerns set the standards within which scientists justifiably accept hypotheses, choose models, and so on. In recent years, several philosophers have argued that, similarly, the design of AI systems is not, and cannot be, value-free. The correct development of a system—e.g. how the model is designed, which data are chosen, or how they are labeled—is partly determined by what is practically or morally at stake (Sullivan, 2022a, Sullivan, 2022b, Karaca, 2021, Johnson, 2023, Biddle, 2022, Ratti & Graves, 2022). Sullivan (2022a,

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">18 See Miller (2014), Fantl and McGrath (2011) for the relation between pragmatic encroachment and inductive risk.</span></small>

2022b) extends this analysis to how practical or moral values impact individuals understanding of AI systems. In line with this, my proposal is that there is no suitable value-free account of when explanations suffice for understanding why certain AI outputs were given; any such account must be sensitive to the practical or moral values at stake in the context.

However, standard pragmatic encroachment and inductive risk, affecting the sufficiency of a subject’s evidence, don’t fully capture how the stakes impact understanding. I now turn to a second way in which the pragmatic encroaches on understanding why. I propose that pragmatic factors also impact epistemic justification (as a necessary condition on understanding) via its coherence component.

## 11.5 How the Stakes Affect Understanding (II): Coherence

My account as developed so far does not concern any aspects specific to understanding, but proposes that practical or moral values affect understanding exactly in the same way as they affect knowledge: by bearing on how much evidence is needed for all things considered justification. So the account so far may be rather unsurprising. For instance, philosophers who take understanding to be a kind of knowledge will have expected exactly this. However, there is an additional way in which the pragmatic encroaches on understanding which goes beyond this standard story. My proposal is that understanding is harder to acquire in high-stakes contexts because of higher demands on the coherence of the provided explanation with the explanandum as well as with the subject’s background beliefs, which again makes it harder to meet the justification condition.

To illustrate this additional way in which practical or moral matters affect whether a subject understands, let me contrast again (the original versions of) Anger Management and Sentencing. Recall that the explanation given for COMPAS’s negative assessment for Connor—“individuals with similar music interests as Connor often reoffended”—coheres little with Luana’s/Juana’s background beliefs, or with what each subject is trying to understand. As far as either of them knows, there is no explanatory or probabilistic relationship between a convict’s or prisoner’s musical interests and risk of recidivism generally speaking, and a fortiori none specifically between Connor’s music preferences and his (alleged) high recidivism risk. On the positive side, at least there is no inconsistency between explanans, explanandum, and background beliefs, and the subject may think that technical devices sometimes do things for odd reasons.

First, let’s ask whether in Anger Management, Luana is justified to believe that COMPAS assigns Connor the maximal risk score because people with similar music interests have often recidivated. As argued above, there is nothing at stake in Luana’s believing the explanans, and in her believing that the fact that others with similar music interests often recidivated explains why COMPAS assigns the high risk score. If she were to believe it, and it were misleading or false, there would be no bad consequences—as before, the worst that could happen is that Connor would receive an offer for an optional anger management course. In line with the intuitive judgment I outlined above in Sect. 11.2, that the explanation does provide Luana with understanding why COMPAS assigned Connor the high recidivism risk score, my proposal predicts that her belief is justified and so meets this necessary condition for understanding. In a low-stakes scenario little coherence suffices for justification.

In contrast to Anger Management, in Sentencing a lot is at stake: If Juana were to accept the explanation and take herself to understand why COMPAS assigned Connor a maximum risk score, but the explanation was misleading (by leaving out the important factors that music interest are used by COMPAS as a proxy attribute for race and that the system has a bias against Black people), then Juana’s sentencing decision would likely discriminate against Connor. Since a lot is at stake, there are more severe demands on the coherence of the propositions relevant to the subject’s understanding, internally and with Juana’s background beliefs. The little coherence of the explanation provided by COMPAS with Juana’s other beliefs and with what she is trying to understand does not suffice for justification. Since justification is necessary for understanding, and in line with the intuitive judgment teased out in Sect. 11.2, she does not understand why COMPAS assesses Connor so negatively.

The situation for Juana is different if the explanation provided coheres better. Imagine that Juana is not as uninformed as in the original version of the scenario, but that she has the following background knowledge: She is aware that music interests correlate with race in the United States and that some AI systems are affected by algorithmic bias and use proxy attributes for race. Further, imagine that the explanation is correct and that COMPAS gives its output in response to a proxy attribute for race due to algorithmic bias. If so, the explanation is highly coherent for her—she can infer that COMPAS is probably using music interest as a proxy attribute for race and is biased against Connor as a Black convict, and that COMPAS gives Connor a maximum risk score because of algorithmic bias. In this case, the coherence is high enough to ensure justification and to allow Juana to understand despite the high stakes.

My proposal is distinct from, but relates in interesting ways to that of Sullivan (2022a). Emily Sullivan applies the concept of pragmatic encroachment to high stakes XAI contexts, but appeals to my condition (2) on understanding—to grasp—and in particular to the abilities constitutive of grasping. She claims that “full-fledged understanding . . . depends on the threshold of the number of what-if questions in the set of all possible what-if[-things-had-been-different] questions on a given topic in a particular context that is necessary to attribute understanding” (p. 316). The core of Sullivan’s proposal is that, depending on how much is at stake, a subject has to be able to answer fewer or more questions about what would happen in counterfactual situations, to count as having outright understanding. Such abilities show the quality of the subject’s grasp of the relations between the relevant propositions.

Although Sullivan appeals to a different condition on understanding, her view picks up on related features of the subject and her situation: To have counterfactual reasoning abilities (i.e. abilities to answer relevant what-if questions) is, at bottom, to see how the different elements of the explanation, the state of affairs to be explained, and surrounding matters cohere. For example, in Anger Management, Luana can give only very limited answers to questions like, “What risk score would COMPAS have assigned to Connor if he had different musical interests?” This corresponds to the limited coherence of the explanation provided by COMPAS with her background beliefs and with the fact in need of explanation, that COMPAS assigned Connor the maximum risk score. To provide some contrast, re-focus on the scenario in Sect. 11.4, in which COMPAS explains the high risk score by appeal to Connor’s criminal history. This explanation coheres extremely well with Luana’s background beliefs about how people’s criminal history and their future recidivism risk relate. And correspondingly, Luana can provide more detailed answers to the question, “What risk score would COMPAS have assigned to Connor if he had a different criminal history?”

Still, my proposal and Sullivan’s are not identical. In my high-stakes scenario, it’s the missing coherence between the given propositions that calls into question the subject’s understanding, not that she fails to grasp existing coherence relations or to answer what-if questions on the basis of grasping them. Both necessary conditions are distinct, as there might be cases where subjects have beliefs that cohere in the right way, but fail on the grasp/abilities dimension. I am happy to allow that both the grasp condition and the justification condition are stakes-sensitive. Sullivan’s and my proposals can thus be seen as complementary.

The following picture of pragmatic encroachment specifically on understanding in XAI contexts has emerged: Say that a subject’s belief that a certain factor explains an AI system’s output coheres only weakly with her beliefs about this output or with her background beliefs. Given low stakes, this can nonetheless be good enough for justification on the coherence dimension, so that the justification condition on understanding may be met. By contrast, when much is at stake, this raises the requirements for how well the relevant beliefs have to cohere, so that it is harder for the subject’s beliefs to be justified. And accordingly, in cases with weak coherence, the relevant beliefs will typically not be justified, which is to say that the subject does not understand why the AI system gave the output it did.

## 11.6 Concluding Remarks

I have started from the assumption, widely accepted by theorists working in the field of XAI, that there are higher demands on explainability in contexts in which important decisions are made or supported by AI systems. This raised the question how exactly the stakes in a context might affect whether an explanation is successful, which is to say, how they affect whether a subject receiving the explanation in the context understands what is explained. To answer this question, I focused on explanations of why certain outputs were provided, and looked to philosophical debates on pragmatic encroachment and inductive risk.

According to my proposal, it is the epistemic justification condition on outright understanding that is sensitive to what is at stake in a situation and which thus leads to the stakes-sensitivity of understanding—when the stakes are higher, there are more stringent requirements on all things considered justification and thus on understanding. I developed this idea, first, by appeal to the claim that in highstakes contexts, the subject must have better evidence in order to have justification, and second, by appeal to the claim that in such contexts, there must be greater coherence between the propositions involved in the believed explanation, and greater coherence of these with the subject’s background beliefs, for her beliefs to be justified.<sup>19</sup>

Let me conclude with practical implications of my proposal. In real-world highstakes situations in which AI systems are used, it is important to ensure not only that relevant stakeholders receive explanations of the systems’ outputs, but also that they sufficiently understand these outputs (we are now focusing on a graded concept of understanding). For this, it must first be ensured that the technical systems providing such explanations are highly reliable, so that the recipients of the explanations can accept the given explanations on the basis of sufficient evidence.<sup>20</sup> Moreover, it is important that the provided explanations cohere well with the web of the recipients’ background beliefs. This can (second implication) be facilitated by designing explanatory tools to provide explanations that match their recipients level of expertise and intellectual capacities. Such coherence can (third implication) be facilitated by improving recipients’ background knowledge, for instance, by educating subjects who will be faced with high-stakes AI situations with regard to the functioning of such systems or with regard to relevant domain knowledge. In these three ways, stakeholders’ understanding of why an AI system came to a certain decision or gave a certain recommendation can be improved in practice.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">19 Another possible account of the stakes-sensitivity of understanding appeals to graded understanding. On this account, the subject needs a greater degree of graded understanding when stakes are high. This idea is certainly worth exploring. Since I cannot discuss this in detail, let me at least briefly give my motivations for focusing on outright understanding instead: (1) This focus allows us to treat pragmatic encroachment on knowledge and understanding in parallel. (2) It transparently offers a very clear treatment of the stakes affecting the epistemic states of the subject; by contrast, proponents of the ‘graded’ proposal needs to tell us in what sense subjects need a higher degree of understanding in high-stakes situations. Is this an instrumental, purely practical or an epistemic demand? I don’t want to deny that such a proposal could be developed in one or another way; though I am doubtful that it would be able to uphold the—to my mind rather attractive—claim that the stakes impact understanding itself.</span></small>
