**Part V**

**Scientific Models and Representation**

# Chapter 12 Representation Learning Without Representationalism

# A Non-representational Account of Deep Learning Models in Scientific Practice

**Phillip Hintikka Kieval**

**Abstract** Both machine learning research and philosophy of model-based science appeal to representations. Given this shared emphasis, it seems natural to conclude that we should understand the epistemic worth of deep learning models in science in terms of their capacity to represent the world. I argue that this is a mistake. I distinguish the prevailing notion of representation used in machine learning research from the concept of scientific representation that figures in the philosophy of model-based science. I argue that the former cannot do the work of the latter in model-based inferences. I then defend an artifactualist approach to machine learning models in science, which aims to understand their epistemic worth in terms of the material practices of constructing and applying them. Machine learning models are instruments that we use to facilitate our epistemic activities in science. They do so without scientific representation.

**Keywords** Deep learning · Models in science · Scientific representation · Representationalism · Artifactualism

## 12.1 Introduction

Many philosophers of science agree that the defining characteristic of scientific models lies in their capacity to represent (Frigg & Nguyen, 2017; Frigg & Hartmann, 2020; Giere, 2004, 2010; Morgan & Morrison, 1999; Parker, 2020; Suárez, 2004; van Fraassen, 2008; Weisberg, 2013). Models’ epistemic value rests on our ability to use them to reason about aspects of the world, and this is possible because models represent their targets. As Frigg and Nguyen (2017) put it, “models must be representations: they can instruct us about the nature of reality only if they represent the selected parts or aspects of the world we investigate” (Frigg & Nguyen, 2017, p. 49).

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">P. H. Kieval (🖂) Department of History and Philosophy of Science, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK e-mail: [pzhk2@cam.ac.uk](mailto:pzhk2@cam.ac.uk)</span></small>

Discussions of machine learning place similar emphasis on representations. Machine learning is a set of algorithmic methods for learning representations of data. Deep neural networks, for instance, involve passing signals through a network of simple computational nodes. Each node transforms a representation of input data and passes it along to the next layer in the network. By composing these simple transformations at subsequent layers, the model learns increasingly abstract representations of the data. This allows deep learning methods to learn and exploit complex patterns in large datasets.

For this reason, researchers sometimes refer to deep learning and similar methods as representation learning. As LeCun et al. (2015) write,

Representation learning is a set of methods that allows a machine to be fed with raw data and to automatically discover the representations needed for detection or classification. Deep-learning methods are representation-learning methods with multiple levels of representation, obtained by composing simple but non-linear modules that each transform the representation at one level (starting with the raw input) into a representation at a higher, slightly more abstract level (LeCun et al., 2015, p. 436).

Given this shared emphasis on representation, it seems natural to conclude that we should assess the epistemic worth of deep learning models in science in terms of their capacity to represent the world. This approach seems to reflect the reality of much of the extant philosophy of science for machine learning. Emily Sullivan’s (2022) illuminating discussion of “link uncertainty,” for example, centers around the degree to which empirical evidence supports a link between a model and its target. More recently, Tamir and Shech (2023) take an explicitly representationalist approach to machine learning models in applying what they call the “C-schema” to understand the connection between models and their targets. They propose that we should understand machine learning models as targeting the relationship between features represented by data. Conversely, Boge (2022) claims that deep learning models do not contain structure that can be mapped to features of their target system. He thus takes up a representationalist perspective to argue that deep neural networks fail to explain their targets.

Though they diverge in their exact diagnosis of deep learning models in science, these authors seem to share a broad commitment to understanding their epistemic value in terms of their capacity to represent the world. This makes sense in light of the history of philosophy of science, which has continually centered representation as a characteristic feature of scientific models. I argue, however, that this is a mistake when it comes to deep learning. We should distinguish the prevailing notion of representation used in machine learning research from the concept of scientific representation that figures in the philosophy of model-based science. Scientific representations must be usable by researchers to make inferences (Contessa, 2007; Giere, 2004, 2010; Suárez, 2004, 2010). The intended use of a model specifies how it represents. The shared practices of modelling communities fix standard conventions for reading a model. These conventions clarify how we can use the model to reason about its target (Suárez, 2004; Weisberg, 2013, p. 39).

But no such conventions exist in the case of deep learning. In most cases in science, there just isn’t a sensible way of interpreting the parameters of a deep learning model in a way that would enable a competent user to make inferences about a target. Learned representations, in contrast with scientific representations, are used by the machine itself. Human investigators cannot use them to make model inferences. Thinking about deep learning through a representationalist lens is thus bound to generate confusion. Yet, I think there are good reasons to think of these systems as models, given their extensive use in contemporary science. We, therefore, need to explore alternative avenues for making sense of their epistemic utility.

I argue that artifactualism—an approach that understands scientific models as tools that mediate our epistemic activities (see especially Knuuttila, 2011; Morgan & Morrison, 1999; Sanches de Oliveira, 2022)—can help to bridge this gap. According to artifactualism, preoccupation with representation doesn’t do justice to the diverse roles of models in science. The view, instead, aims to understand models’ epistemic utility in terms of the material practices of constructing and applying them. Yet, artifactualists tend to be somewhat circumspect about the exact nature of the epistemic benefits of their view. I thus make the case that adopting an artifactualist approach helps us to recognize the epistemic and practical value of skill in scientific modelling. I examine the use of deep learning in scientific practice through such a lens. The design and construction of deep learning models involves an iterative process that depends on a combination of skill and tacit knowledge about how to get the most out of these systems. Developing such a skill scaffolds genuine understanding about the relationship between our means and our epistemic ends. Deep learning models are instruments that we use to facilitate epistemic activities like prediction, exploration, and manipulation. They do so without scientific representation.

My argument goes like this: I begin by introducing the role of representation in model-based science. Next, I consider the concept of representation used in machine learning research and distinguish it from scientific representation. I then argue that the former cannot do the work of the latter in model-based inferences. Finally, I present some considerations in favor of an artifactual account of deep learning models in scientific practice cashed out in terms of the epistemic benefits of skilled engagement with epistemic tools.

## 12.2 Scientific Models and Representation

Scientists use models to learn about the world, to predict and explain what’s going on around us. We construct models of everything from atomic particles to economic systems using diverse methods and materials. There are many reasons for doing so. Often the targets of our investigations are too complex to study directly. We thus need to simplify them to make inquiry possible. It might be appropriate, for instance, to consider an abstract model that includes only the causal factors we think are essential. At other times, we may introduce false assumptions that help us understand the structure underlying a phenomenon (cf. Elgin, 2004; Potochnik, 2017; Weisberg, 2007).

Despite these distortions, models contribute to the epistemic success of science. Many philosophers agree that models help scientists achieve their aims by representing the targets of inquiry (Frigg & Nguyen, 2017; Frigg & Hartmann, 2020; Giere, 2004, 2010; Morgan & Morrison, 1999; Parker, 2020; Suárez, 2004; Weisberg, 2013). This is appealing because it provides a ready answer to how we can reason with models to learn about the world. Modelling involves representing a select aspect of the world. This aspect is the model’s target. We can thus think of a model as the source of a representation that is directed at a target (Suárez, 2010).

And yet, defining representation is a matter of controversy (for a thorough review, see Frigg & Nguyen, 2017). Representation alone comes cheap, but models need to do more than just denote what they stand for. Callender and Cohen stress that anything can represent anything else by stipulative fiat (Callender & Cohen, 2006, p. 73). I can stipulate that the coffee mug on my desk represents alpha Centauri, but that alone doesn’t mean that I can use my mug to infer anything about stellar parallax. Any adequate account of model representation needs to tell us how those representations enable surrogate reasoning. That is, models represent in ways that license inferences about their targets. I will call a representation that satisfies this desideratum a scientific representation.<sup>1</sup> Their inferential power sets scientific representations apart from brute signs, but philosopher disagree about how models meet this demand.

We can characterize theories of scientific representation as either substantive or deflationary (Suárez, 2010). Substantive accounts take the relationship between a model and its target to be a matter of fact; they aim to specify a robust feature or relation that holds between models and their targets. Two time honored examples include similarity and isomorphism. Similarity maintains that a model represents its target just in case that model is similar to its target in some relevant respect. Isomorphism, on the other hand, is a well defined mathematical relation between extensional structures. Setting formal sophistication aside, isomorphism holds that a model represents its target when there is a one-to-one mapping between elements in the model’s structure and elements in the target’s structure. Both of these substantive accounts aim to ground the capacity for surrogate reasoning in an objective relation that holds between models and their targets.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">1 My use thus departs from the most general sense of the term understood as any representation produced by scientific inquiry. This more general notion includes instrument readings, visualizations of data, photographs and digital images, and so on. It is impossible to draw a sharp line between models and these other kinds of representation, given that many of these other forms appear to be “model-laden” (Bokulich, 2020; Chang, 2004, p. 188; Leonelli, 2019; Tal, 2017). A full account of the relation between narrow, model-centric scientific representations and the more general notion is beyond the scope of this chapter.</span></small>

Deflationary accounts, on the other hand, deny any such robust, factual relationship obtains between models and their targets. These accounts, instead, tie representation to its use in modelling practices. Mauricio Suárez (2004, 2015) inferentialist account, for instance, spells this out in terms of the capacity of a model to direct competent and informed users to consider a target and draw out specific inferences. Inferentialism nevertheless maintains an objective component. This is because only some kinds of structures will let informed agents draw good inferences about their targets. Suárez writes that it’s a model’s “internal structure that allows informed agents to correctly draw inferences” (Suárez, 2004, p. 774). For the Lotka-Volterra model to count as a scientific representation of predation ecologists need to be able to use it. Ecologists can, in fact, use oscillations in the model to represent the relationship between changes in predator and prey populations. This helps them understand, for example, how an environment stays below its carrying capacity. Without this inferential capacity, the model would be a vacuous mathematical structure. Our ability to make sound inferences constrains what structures will be admissible in a particular modelling context.

Many philosophers now appreciate that scientific modelling is an activity practiced by agents with particular research agendas and goals (Giere, 2004, 2010; Godfrey-Smith, 2006; Knuuttila, 2005, 2011; Parker, 2020; Suárez, 2004; Weisberg, 2013). They thus stress the importance of human judgement and competence in the successful use of models to represent the world. Learning with models comes down to our ability to interpret their structure in ways that enable us to infer things about their targets. More and more, both substantive and deflationary views share this attention to scientists’ ability to use models in practice.

Along these lines, recent substantive accounts allow human agents to fill in the details of scientific representation (Giere, 2004, 2010; Godfrey-Smith, 2006; van Fraassen, 2008; Weisberg, 2013). Michael Weisberg, for example, says that “models consist of an interpreted structure that can be used to represent a real or imagined phenomenon” (Weisberg, 2013, 15 emphasis original). For Weisberg, this involves agents adopting particular construals of a model, which set up relations of denotation between models and their targets (2013, p. 39). A crucial part of a construal is what Weisberg calls the assignment. Assignments determine the relationship between parts of the model’s structure and the parts of their target system. Assignments are thus “explicit specifications of how parts of real or imagined target systems are to be mapped onto the parts of the model” (Weisberg, 2013, p. 39). Assignments, as such, are often implicit in the practices and conventions for reading out model descriptions adopted by specific epistemic communities. They serve as a kind of record of the coordinating actions of modelling communities. Assignments thus resemble Suárez (2004) characterization of the practical maintenance of what he calls representational force—the capacity of a model to lead informed users to consider its target.

Of course, there are important differences between all of these accounts. Yet, they agree that the successful use of a model depends on our ability to interpret that model’s structure in a way that licenses correct inferences. Scientific representation requires that agents intend to use a model for a particular purpose. Communities of modellers may codify, implicitly or explicitly, conventions for reading out that model’s structure. This structure must be such that a competent and informed inquirer could use it to infer something about the target. If we can’t use a model, then it’s not a scientific representation.

## 12.3 Learning Representations of Data

Machine learning as a discipline aims to engineer systems that learn from data. We can take “learning” here to mean improving performance on the basis of observed data. Evaluating performance depends, in turn, on specifying a measure of success—maximizing, for example, predictive accuracy on unobserved data. Modellers expose their model to data and then optimize some measure of performance over that data.

Machine learning involves many different methods, including decision tree methods such as random forests, Bayesian non-parametric techniques like Gaussian processes, and artificial neural networks. All of these involve procedures for learning a plausible model that fits observed data. We can characterize this model as a function expressed in terms of a set of parameters whose values are initially unknown. This model is both a description of observed data and a hypothesis about the underlying phenomena that produced said data. That is, the model provides a hypothetical description of the data generating process that aims to cohere with background knowledge and facilitate reliable extrapolations. Learning, then, is a procedure for finding the parameter values that maximize the likelihood of our data, often while balancing the need to generalize to unseen data. In most real-world cases, we can’t solve for these parameters analytically. Machine learning algorithms thus use numerical methods to estimate these unknown parameter values.

The last decade bore witness to remarkable advances in machine learning driven by a set of neural network methods called deep learning (LeCun et al., 2015; Buckner, 2019). All neural networks consist in an array of simple computational nodes. So-called deep neural networks feed input values through multiple layers of nodes, which are connected together by weights that determine the strength of signal passed from one layer to the next. Each node takes the signal from the preceding layer and transforms it according to various functions. By composing these simple transformations, a deep neural network can learn complex features of observed data from low-level information. An image classifier, for instance, can learn to identify objects like cars, people, or animals from the pixel values of a digital image.

Deep neural networks (hereafter, DNNs) learn by adjusting their weights in response to data. Depending on the specific network architecture and modelling context, modellers may assign random values to these weights prior to training, or they may opt for a more sophisticated initialization scheme. In either case, the network’s initial performance may be no better than random guessing. As we expose the network to data, however, a learning algorithm determines how the network will adjust. Such an algorithm tells the network when it’s made an error and by how much. The network then learns from its mistake by altering the strength of connections between nodes that were most responsible for the error.

When a network experiences labeled data, we call this process “supervised learning” because the learning algorithm acts like a tutor watching over the network and pointing out when it has gone wrong. The network thus gets to compare its outputs with the label assigned to its target and corrects accordingly. Many scientific contexts call for supervised learning. It works well in any situation where we want to predict the value of a target variable from a set of known features. When the target takes on a discrete set of possible values, we call the task classification. If we want instead to predict a continuous, real value, then we call the task a regression.

Sometimes, however, we don’t have access to good labelled data or our aims diverge from straightforward prediction. In such cases, we might train a model to learn features of the dataset without explicit guidance. This is called “unsupervised learning”.<sup>2</sup> Unsupervised models experience an entire dataset and learn useful properties of its structure. This often means learning the entire probability distribution that generated our data. Useful applications include density estimation, learning to generate samples from a learned distribution, de-noising data, clustering and outlier detection, and reducing the dimensionality of complex datasets so that we can visualize them (cf. Goodfellow et al., 2016; Raghu & Schmidt, 2020).

DL promises to accelerate scientific progress by automatically extracting subtle patterns in large datasets and exploiting those patterns to make novel predictions. One recent lesson data scientists have learned from these models is that flexible methods of learning from large quantities of data tend to produce the best predictions when dealing with very complex phenomena (Ghahramani, 2015). Such flexibility means modellers make minimal assumptions about their targets. Rather than relying on domain-specific theoretical assumptions to tightly constrain the space of possible functions a model could learn, we engineer domain-general models that learn interesting features of the data on their own.

Machine learning researchers often couch this in terms of learning a representation of data (Bengio et al., 2013; Goodfellow et al., 2016, ch. 1; LeCun et al., 2015). We can understand what this means by contrasting DL with simpler statistical methods. In classical statistics and simple machine learning, modellers impose significant structure on their model before fitting it to data. They gather and prepare a dataset and then invoke prior hypotheses about the features of the phenomena that generated their data. Modellers use these hypotheses as the basis for a representation of their data. This representation takes the shape of a probability model whose parameters correspond to features of the data. Fitting this model to the data involves maximum likelihood estimation, an analytic method of finding the parameter values that maximize the probability of a dataset.<sup>3</sup> These parameter values are the so-called “best estimator” of the dataset given a class of models with a certain structure. After fitting the model, modellers can evaluate it by plotting the residuals, or the difference between our model’s predictions and what they actually observe in the data. The aim here is to identify any systematic pattern that modellers can use to improve the model.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">2 The distinction between supervised and unsupervised learning is not a formal one and often the lines become fuzzy, as in the cases of, for example, semi-supervised and self-supervised learning.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">3 Since an exact solution to the likelihood function is often intractable, modellers typically use an approximation like the method of least squares estimation instead. Least squares estimation,</span></small>

Let’s consider a simple example of classical statistical modelling with supervised learning. Suppose I want to model how the average monthly temperature in Cambridge has changed over time so that I can predict average temperatures over the next few years. I can take some data of temperature readings over time and design a model to represent features of that data. Fortunately, the UK Met Office makes some historic data from a weather station in Cambridge publicly accessible.<sup>4</sup> I can take this data and design a probability model to represent changes in temperature as a function of time. I can then use supervised learning to find the parameter values of my model that constitute the best estimator of my labeled temperature dataset. Now, I know that annual temperatures are cyclical. So I can describe my model in terms of a simple periodic function like this

$$
\mathrm{Temp} \approx \alpha + \beta \sin (2 \pi \mathfrak {t} + \theta) + N (0, \sigma^ {2})
$$

where t is the date in years, $\alpha , \beta ,$ and $\theta$ are unknown parameters that fix the shape of our periodic model, and $N ( 0 , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ is a Gaussian noise term that represents the idea that our data is a noisy realization of the target phenomenon.<sup>5</sup> When I fit my model, a simple algorithm finds the values of these predetermined parameters that are the best estimator of my data. Figure 12.1 shows the fitted model.

Right off the bat, I have a pretty strong sense that this toy model isn’t very good. That’s because I’m aware of warming trends that are not captured by my initial representation. To get a grip on how this omission affects my model I can compute and plot the residuals, as shown in Fig. 12.2.

There’s a certain immediacy to this plot. A secular trend that shows temperature steadily increasing jumps right out at me. To confirm, I might fit a linear regression to this residual plot. I would then modify my original model to include an additional parameter representing this linear warming trend.

Real cases in data science will be a good deal messier than this example. We may not know what features to represent in our model and diagnosing weaknesses might turn out to be an arduous process. But the point I’ve tried to show is that in simple supervised learning, as in classical statistical inference, we begin with a representation that we want to fit to our data. Domain-specific theoretical knowledge about the target systems motivates our choice of representation. Training the model is about learning a good mapping between this representation and our dataset. Such a representation is intelligible in light of the substantive modelling assumptions that we’ve imposed on our data. Intelligibility enables us to iteratively manipulate our model in response to its performance and use it to make inferences (de Regt, 2017). We can see how well it does and make theoretically informed changes to how our model represents different features of the target system. Moreover, we can use the representation to make inferences because the parameters were hand-chosen to account for these features.

In deep learning, things look much different. We build a deep learning model (henceforth, DL model) that learns not only a good mapping but also the representation itself (Goodfellow et al., 2016, p. 4). This is the notion of representation invoked in talk of “representation learning” (Bengio et al., 2013; Goodfellow et al., 2016, p. 5; LeCun et al., 2015, p. 436). Representation learning is much more flexible than methods that impose considerable parametric modelling assumptions. This is because learning a representation in this sense requires little domain knowledge about the target system. Overparameterized models that exploit learned representations, moreover, tend to outperform models with representations designed by hand without the need for significant hypotheses about what to expect from our data.

This works out because DNNs are so-called “universal function approximators” (Hornik et al., 1989). That is, we have a theoretical guarantee that any feedforward neural network with three or more layers “can approximate virtually any function of interest to any desired degree of accuracy, provided sufficiently many hidden units are available” (Hornik et al., 1989, p. 360). This means that, if we suppose that we can describe our data in terms of a complex function mapping inputs to outputs, a neural network with enough nodes can approximate that function arbitrarily well.<sup>6</sup> Basically, we can think of the network as function $y \: = \: f _ { \theta } ( x )$ where θ is a set of parameters. θ includes a set of weight matrices joining nodes between each layer of the network. Supervised learning here involves estimating the set of weight values that allows the network to best approximate the functional relationship between a vector of predictor features, x, and the target variable(s), y. A trained model thus learns how to represent functional relationships in the data in terms of a set of parameters. But unlike classical methods, we don’t choose those parameters on the basis of features of the target system. We instead choose a network architecture on the basis of the general kind of task we want to solve. Architectural choices amount to domain-general inductive biases that constrain the actual set of functions the network can learn.

More flexible learning works so well because training leads a network to learn representations of data that have properties that make the relevant task easier. Statistical modelling and machine learning often draws on a geometric metaphor here. We can conceive of each data sample as a point in a multidimensional space whose axes are constituted by the qualitative features of the dataset. Representation learning involves finding a set of transformations of this “feature space” that reduces the complexity of the task. In a classification task, for example, the final layer of a network will be a linear classifier. Learning a good representation for this task might mean learning a representation of the inputs that makes them linearly separable in feature space at the penultimate layer. This basically means that we can draw a straight line that separates inputs into mutually exclusive categories. Such separability will then make classification simple.

This stresses, however, an important theoretical detail of representation learning that machine learning researchers often fail to make explicit. Learned representations are provided to later stages of processing within the network itself. In a feedforward classifier, the network learns a representation that makes input features linearly separable. This representation is used by the network’s output layer, which typically computes something like a softmax regression on this representation. Learned representations are thus representations for the network. The high-dimensional nature of feature space precludes our ability to visualize or even imagine the structural properties of a learned representation. A neural network, and not a human inquirer, is the user of learned representations.

We should take care to attend to this distinction, else we are liable to equivocate. In cases of simple statistical learning like the example above, modellers handpick a representation in the form of a probability model. The model then finds a mapping between this representation and a dataset by learning the parameter values that make the model a good fit for the data given the chosen representation. Consider another example of this kind. Chhatwal et al. (2009) built a statistical model to estimate breast cancer risk. The modelers mapped a range of diagnostic criteria to discrete variables and performed a logistic regression on these features to predict the presence of breast cancer. They assigned each diagnostic feature to a predictor variable weighted by an unknown parameter. The model then learns how to weight these features to maximize accuracy. Models like this one are straightforward to evaluate through cross-validation. We can even perform tests to evaluate how significant specific features are as breast cancer predictors. It’s clear how clinicians and researchers can use the model to make inferences about what diagnostic features are reliable indicators of cancer risk.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">6 Of course, this does not come without limitations (see e.g. Wolpert, 1996). Building models, which learn from finite data, that we can rely on to generalize well is far from trivial.</span></small>

Contrast this with a DL model designed to predict the presence of cancer. Esteva et al. (2017) designed a DL model to detect the presence of melanomas and carcinomas from pictures of skin lesions. Unlike the logistic regression example, this model does not have a built-in representation of clinical features that might predict cancer risk. In a regression, the modellers give the model information about the patient in the form of independent variables. These variables function as explicit representations of those clinically relevant features. The DL model receives only a large set of digital images of skin lesions with corresponding labels. The model learns to represent features of skin lesions that predict the presence of different kinds of skin cancer directly from these images. Such representations turn out to be complex patterns of weighted activity distributed throughout the network that facilitate classification at the output layer. A good representation is thus “one that is useful to a supervised predictor” (Bengio et al., 2013, p. 1798). It’s difficult to see, on the other hand, how clinicians or researchers could use these learned representations as scientific representations.

Unless human inquirers can use learned representations to make inferences about a target, they just won’t qualify as scientific representations. In the section that follows, I argue that learned representations can’t satisfy this use requirement. In fact, there is no good way of construing a DL model or its parameters as a scientific representation.

## 12.4 Learned Representations Are Not Scientific Representations

DL models cannot function as scientific representations. This section lays out the case for this claim in more detail. I consider first whether we can use learned representations in model-based inferences. I show that, even if we can provide a characterization of learned representations, they won’t help us make inferences about their targets. We should, therefore, de-center representation in our epistemology of DL models in scientific practice.

It will help to first have an idea of how DL models learn useful representations. Let’s continue on with the example of deep, feedforward classifiers. The most successful kind of modern classifier network is called a deep convolutional neural network, or ConvNet (LeCun et al., 1990, 1998, 2015). ConvNets underlie significant breakthroughs in multiple areas of artificial intelligence research made over the last decade. They set the state-of-the-art in object recognition (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) and facial recognition (Taigman et al., 2014) technologies. ConvNets even played a role in the success of AlphaGo, the first artificial intelligence system to defeat a human world champion in the game of Go (Silver et al., 2016). They also find useful applications in science (Raghu & Schmidt, 2020). Modelers can appropriate the same strategy used in image recognition to learn predictive features from scientific data.

ConvNets take innovations made by Fukushima and Miyake (1982) and add end to-end supervised learning, which was made possible for DNNs by the application of the backpropagation algorithm for training multi-layer neural networks (Rumelhart et al., 1986). The characteristic depth of these networks allows them to learn representations of increasingly abstract, or conceptually framed, features at successive stages of processing (Bengio et al., 2013; Buckner, 2018). As Bengio et al. (2013) put it, DL models “learn to identify and disentangle the underlying explanatory factors hidden in the observed milieu of low-level sensory data.” ConvNets involve a sequence of stacked layers that combine two types of computational operations: linear convolutional filtering and non-linear pooling. I’ll elaborate briefly on both.

Convolution is a linear algebraic operation whose properties make ConvNets very effective for processing input data that has a grid-like structure (see e.g. Goodfellow et al., 2016, pp. 321–330 for a more precise overview of the technical details). Image processing, for instance, takes digital images as input. A 2-D grid of pixels comprises each image. Pixels are the smallest unit of usable information in a digital image. Each pixel is a vector of red, green, and blue color intensity values at a given location in an image. Convolutional nodes—often called kernels or filters— operate on a rectangular spatial region of the whole grid. They transform the pixel values at a small chunk of the image in a way that maximizes some values while minimizing others. In image recognition and classification tasks, this has the effect of emphasizing salient features present in a given region of the image. A verticaledge kernel, for instance, uses convolution to maximize pixel values that fall along vertical edges, while minimizing adjacent ones. Each kernel will then pass its output to a rectified linear unit (ReLU), which activates if the signal from the preceding kernel exceeds a given threshold. This ReLU node acts like a kind of “detector,” since it sends signal forward through the network only if the preceding kernel detects a certain feature such as a vertical edge. The combination of convolutional filters with ReLUs results in a set of low-level feature detectors that operate on different spatial regions of the input.

Recognizing and classifying objects, however, requires more than just detecting low-level features like vertical edges. We need to be able to detect edges in different orientations and assemble them into composite features like curves and shapes. Networks achieve this through a kind of downsampling. Feature detectors pass their output to a non-linear pooling function. Pooling replaces the output of a detector at a location with a summary of nearby outputs. Max pooling, for example, selects the greatest output within a given rectangular region. Pooling introduces a degree of invariance. This means that the output of a layer becomes more or less insensitive to small translations in the input. This kind of invariance is useful if we want to detect the presence of a feature but don’t care exactly where it appeared or how it was oriented. We can thus move from vertical edge detection to detecting edges in general. Invariance is especially important for tasks like object recognition, since we want to accurately identify objects in the face of irrelevant “nuisance variation” like changes in pose, angle, or lighting conditions (Buckner, 2018).

Each layer in a ConvNet implements this sequence of processing. Their joint operations equip ConvNets with the capacity for a kind of hierarchical abstraction, which Buckner (2018) calls transformational abstraction. From a grid of pixel values, the combined effort of convolutional filtering and max pooling allow the network to learn a representation of low-level, visual features of a digital image like edges. By passing this representation through subsequent layers, the network can assemble these low-level features into a representation of increasingly abstract features. Processing thus involves an iterative transformation of available information into a representation that preserves and emphasizes features that are relevant for a given task. Training a ConvNet, then, means finding the right set of weights between layers such that the network can find a multi-level configuration of feature representations that enables the network to perform its task well while also avoiding overfitting idiosyncratic features of its training set. The network needs to find a set of transformations that strike a good balance between context sensitivity and invariance.

Given this characterization, it’s hard to see how scientists could fruitfully use learned representations in the course of model-based inferences. Learned representations amount to a learned set of transformations over the feature space of sampled data that emphasizes task-relevant features. Inspecting learned representations can thus at best reveal how specific transformations of input data enable more efficient estimations of the target variable.

To see this, let’s consider a recent scientific application of deep learning. The accelerating loss of Arctic sea ice threatens dire consequences for both local ecosystems and global climate conditions. Accurate deterministic models of sea ice concentration exist, but their performance breaks down at even moderate timescales of a few months due to various stochastic elements. To enhance our predictive capabilities, Andersson et al. (2021) developed a probabilistic DL model for sea ice forecasting they call IceNet. IceNet is a stack of twenty-five ConvNets. Each constituent in this ensemble is a U-Net, a specific type of encoder-decoder ConvNet architecture originally developed for medical imaging segmentation (Ronneberger et al., 2015). A U-Net takes grid-like data structures—like digital images—as input and produces a new image as output. Each U-Net consists in the standard, contracting feature-extraction pathway described above, but subsequent layers augment this architecture with a symmetrical, expanding pathway that replaces pooling operations with upsampling to generate precise, localized outputs. A U-Net thus takes an image and extracts predictive features from contiguous regions of the image, then uses those extracted features to output a reconstructed image that facilitates some pre-specified goal, such as producing a precise segmentation map of the original image (Ronneberger et al., 2015). Andersson et al. (2021) trained IceNet to predict seasonal changes in Arctic sea ice concentration (SIC) from a combination of satellite imaging,<sup>7</sup> fifty monthly averaged climate variables, and synthetic climate model data. IceNet outputs SIC forecast maps for the following six months wherein each grid cell within the map is labelled with one of three SIC classes (less than or equal to 15% SIC, greater than 15% but less than 80% SIC, or greater than or equal to 80% SIC). Moreover, it assigns a discrete probability distribution for each labelled cell.<sup>8</sup>

What would it look like to apply a representational account of model-based inference to IceNet? One way would be to treat them analogously to simpler parametric statistical models. On this approach, we would treat a neural network like any other probability model by investigating how the learned parameter values of an estimator represent the complex relationship between predictor features and target variables. We might thus try to consider how the internal structure of the model relates to its capacity to accurately forecast SIC. After all, there is one sense in which the IceNet’s internal structure is fully transparent. All DL models are—in a restricted sense—mathematically tractable (Creel, 2020; Leslie, 2019; Lipton, 2018; Zerilli, 2022). No matter how complex, “an algorithmic model is a closed system of effectively computable operations where rules and transformations are mechanically applied to inputs to determine outputs.” (Leslie, 2019, p. 41). It’s thus, in principle, possible to manually inspect the complete structure of a DL model. Perhaps, then, we can use IceNet’s structure to understand how it represents its target phenomenon.

But such naive optimism would soon dissipate once we consider what interpreting the internal structure of IceNet would require. In his recent discussion of ML opacity, Zerilli (2022) distinguishes between several ways that a model can be more or less transparent.<sup>9</sup> Following Lipton (2018), he identifies fathomability with the degree to which someone could immediately grasp the relationship between features in the model and its predictions. Hence, for a model to count as fathomable, “a human should be able to take the input data together with the parameters of the model and in reasonable time step through every calculation required to produce a prediction” (Lipton, 2018, pp. 38–39). The high dimensionality and extreme nonlinearities characteristic of deep learning thus present paradigmatic barriers to fathomability. IceNet—a relatively compact DL model by today’s standards— contains roughly forty-four million trainable weights (Andersson et al., 2021, p. 9). Clearly, the sheer number of parameters rules out the possibility of contemplating the structure of the model all at once. In other words, the brute size of DL models makes them unfathomable (Lipton, 2018; Zerilli, 2022).

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">432 432</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">7 Satellite observations of microwave brightness get converted into a  ×  grid estimating SIC based on the fractional area covered in sea ice at each grid cell of the image.</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">8 The latter two classes are summed to obtain P(SIC > 15).</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">9 See also Creel (2020) for a similar discussion on the varieties of transparency in computational systems.</span></small>

Yet, it’s not the case that intelligibility requires the ability to visualize—mentally or otherwise—a model (cf. de Regt, 2017, Ch. 7). A lack of fathomability thus marks a practical—rather than in principle—obstacle to intelligibility (on essential versus non-essetial epistemic opacity, see also Humphreys, 2004, 2009). For example, linear statistical models can also become so complex as to be practically unfathomable. Yet, such models remain intelligible as scientific representations in the sense that each parameter is assigned a clear, semantically interpretable role within the overall functioning of the model. This is, at least in part, because linear models typically involve plugging predictor variables into a chosen linear link function, which then maps features of the target system to a linear probability model. Linearity here means that every term in the model is either a constant or a feature variable weighted by a tune-able parameter. Preserving linearity is crucial for intelligibility, as it functions as a proxy for conditional monotonicity.<sup>10</sup> That is, conditional on all other explanatory variables, a change in the value of one independent variable begets a predictable, corresponding change in the dependent variable. Without conditional monotonicity, our intuitions about the relationship between features of a target phenomenon tend to fail. Linearity also guarantees that we can apply validation techniques like sensitivity analysis, which allows modellers to determine the degree to which uncertainty in the various parameters of the model accounts for uncertainty in the model’s outputs. Such techniques provide a degree of information about patterns of counterfactual dependency between the structure of the model and their target, which is crucial for their explanatory power (cf. Bokulich, 2011; Woodward, 2003). Linearity thus ensures that statistical models remain somewhat intelligible even when they are very complex.

This reveals that DL models are unintelligible in a much deeper sense, one that goes beyond their unfathomable number of parameters. DNNs contain extreme nonlinearities due to the many stacking layers of functions embedded within functions. These many nonlinear, higher-order interactions make it practically impossible to disentangle how a model relates features of the target to produce its predictions. DL models thus lack what Creel (2020) calls “functional transparency,” which involves our ability to distinguish the high-level, logical rules involved in the transformation of inputs into outputs. Moreover, a complete mathematical articulation of a trained DNN admits no intelligible semantic interpretation. In other words, there is no way to meaningfully interpret the parameters of the model in terms of the qualitative features of its target system. This is because there is no presumed connection between the model structure and the target system. In scientific practice, the number of neural network parameters often far outstrips the number of quality dimensions found in the data they are modelling. IceNet’s parameters, for instance, outnumber its target features by a ratio of close to one million-to-one. These parameters correspond to autonomously learned weights that govern the transformation of signal between layers, but those transformations need not have any intrinsic connection to the target phenomenon. Hence, although DL models are, strictly speaking, parametric, they share much in common with nonparametric statistical models in the sense that modellers choose them for the richness of their mathematical structure rather than for any relevance to their target (Desai et al., 2022; Napoletani et al., 2011, 2021; Pietsch, 2015).<sup>11</sup> We, therefore, cannot use the mathematical structure of a trained DL model as an informative representation of the target system.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">10 This, however, is not a guarantee. Achen (2005) argues that a serious problem with large regression models—especially in the social sciences—lies in their tendency to sneak in unnoticed nonlinearities, which would undermine the reliability of any conclusions drawn from such analyses.</span></small>

## 12.5 Post Hoc Interpretability Methods and Scientific Representations

An alternative possibility remains for someone who wants to preserve a representational account of DL models in science. If we can assess how a model has learned to represent data via a series of transformations between its hidden layers, then we may be able to evaluate what information the network has learned to preserve. If we can identify the informational content within substructures associated with these transformations, then we might be able to use the model’s learned representations to understand how the relative importance of different features present in our data leads to better estimations of the target (cf. Boge, 2022; Tamir & Shech, 2023).

In principle, inspecting the activity of hidden layer units might thus shed light on the informative relationship between features in the sample data and the target phenomenon. But in practice, this runs into deep methodological and philosophical difficulties with identifying the content of learned representations (see Chap. 13 by Freiesleben in this volume). As I argued above, characteristic features of deep learning—domain-generality, extreme nonlinearity, and overparameterization— mean that it is impossible to associate particular parameters with qualitative features of a model’s target. This applies also to learned representations, since many qualitative features the model learns to represent are not explicitly provided to the network. Instead, the model learns informative patterns directly from the “low-level” sensory data. IceNet, for instance, learns predictive features directly from satellite imaging without having those features explicitly encoded as an input variable. We hope that the model will learn transformations of the data that preserve and exploit genuinely explanatory features of the target phenomenon, but there is no guarantee that this will be the case.

What’s more, learned representations are often inscrutable because information is distributed throughout the nodes in a network such that it cannot be broken down into semantically interpretable units. There is a wealth of research on interpretable machine learning and so-called “explainable AI” (XAI) that aims to ameliorate this problem by understanding how information travels through hidden layer representations (see parts 3 and 4 of this volume for valuable discussion). Some of this work aims to “disentangle” DNNs in ways that make information flow interpretable (Chen et al., 2018, 2021; Olah et al., 2020). Disentanglement is a constraint on nodes in a network such that they acquire “disentangled representations” (Chen et al., 2021). Disentangled representations carry interpretable semantic information about explanatory features of sample data. In a fully disentangled network we would be able to inspect the activity of individual nodes and understand how they represent interpretable features of data. But disentanglement is a difficult, open problem in machine learning research. Given the current state-of-the-art, demanding fully disentangled networks is impossible without loss of performance, which undermines the motivations for using DNNs in the first place.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">11 A wealth of recent, theoretical work aims to draw explicit connections between neural networks and nonparametric models (for example, see Dutordoir et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2021; Jacot et al., 2018).</span></small>

Additive explanations offer a more promising alternative for the representationalist. Additive explanations refer to a set of XAI tools developed to explain how opaque models produce their outputs. Additive explanations work by deploying a simpler model that explains an opaque model’s outputs as a linear function of a set of feature variables (Lundberg & Lee, 2017; Ribeiro et al., 2016). The idea here is that if we can reliably explain the predictions of DL models in terms of these additive feature attributions, then we can understand deep learning systems as representing the relative salience of features in a dataset. To return to the IceNet example, an additive explanation would produce a linear model of IceNet’s predictions that would tell us which features in the input data were the most salient factors in its making those particular predictions.

But this view remains untenable for two reasons. On the one hand, additive explanations are not reliable. Prominent methods, such as SHAP (Lundberg & Lee, 2017), LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016), and breakDown (Staniak & Biecek, 2019) produce explanations of DL models that are not robust, are highly uncertain, have low-fidelity with respect to the original model, and often produce mutually inconsistent explanations (Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola, 2018; Gosiewska & Biecek, 2019). These results have led some authors to caution against relying on additive explanation methods (Rudin, 2019; Lakkaraju & Bastani, 2020). On the other hand, philosophers of science broadly recognize that non-factive explanations can contribute to the epistemic success of science. While this may be so, it cannot rescue the representationalist view of DL models. This is because additive explanations simply target the wrong phenomenon. Additive explanations are model-centric: their target of understanding is the original model, not the world. They are models of models. Such explanations may thus help us gain modest understanding of how a DL model works, but they will not thereby furnish explanations of phenomena in the world. Additive explanations, as such, fall on the wrong side of Lawler and Sullivan’s (2021) distinction between model explanations and model-induced explanations. For techniques like SHAP or LIME, the content of the model is itself an explanation (of the original DL model). But what we want is to use the original model to induce understanding of some target phenomenon.<sup>12</sup>

A final way of considering DL models representationally involves treating them as abstract models of biological neural circuits or the algorithms they compute. We can associate this perspective with the arrival of so-called “neuroconnectionism” on the scene of cognitive computational neuroscience (cf. Cichy & Kaiser, 2019; Doerig et al., 2023; Kieval, 2022; Lindsay, 2021; Stinson, 2020; Yamins & DiCarlo, 2016). This view has recently come under fire from critics who argue that methodological flaws in how neuroscientists assess hierarchical correspondence between DNNs and brains undermines their status as successful models (Bowers et al., 2023; Schaeffer et al., 2022; Sexton & Love, 2022). But these arguments trade on a substantive notion of model correspondence (e.g. in terms of isomorphism) that many representationalist would contest. Neuroconnectionism may thus be a genuine exception to our inability to make representational use of DL models. This leaves the domain of application of DL models severely restricted if we maintain a representationalist perspective. In general, this approach to DL modelling diverges substantially along multiple axes from their broader use within data science. I think it is, therefore, productive to open up non-representational avenues for understanding DL models in science. As I show in the next section, such a view can also further illuminate the use of DL models in neuroscience and even assuage some of the worries raised by critics of neuroconnectionism. I think we thus have good theoretical reasons to extend my account to all uses of DL models in science.

## 12.6 Understanding DL Modelling as a Skill

I have argued that representationalism is not the way to go when it comes to DL models in science. There just doesn’t seem to be any plausible way to use them as scientific representations in most cases. It’s thus incumbent upon us to reach for other conceptual tools. I take the first steps towards doing so here.

First, however, I need to face up to a potential objection. Namely, why think DL models are models at all? Perhaps the way that computer scientists use the term ‘model’ is just a bit of misleading, idiosyncratic lingo. If scientific models are models in virtue of their capacity to represent the world in a particular way, and DL models fail to represent in this way, then maybe they just don’t play the role of scientific models. This position is not unheard of in the philosophical literature (Napoletani et al., 2011), for instance, take pains to avoid calling neural networks models, instead referring to them as “techniques.” Picking up on this subtlety, Paul Humphreys calls them “non-linear prediction and classification techniques” (Humphreys, 2013, p. 580).

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">12 Sullivan (2023) herself makes a similar point in a recent exchange with Tamir and Shech (2023).</span></small>

This worry is hard to shake. Philosophers of science are not obliged to always take scientists’ descriptions of their practice literally. We needn’t insist that DNNs are models just because practitioners use the word ‘model’ to describe them. I do think, however, that philosophers of science should take scientific practice seriously. We should look to modelling practices to understand scientific models. Likewise, we should appreciate how scientists use DL systems to adjudicate their status as scientific models. Attending to model use in scientific practice reveals a great diversity of objects and methods suited for different epistemic aims. It’s not clear that we should always consider representing the primary goal of these activities. This calls for broadening the scope of our philosophical analyses of models in science.

Understanding the epistemic significance of DL models in science requires attending to what scientists do with them. Proponents of representationalism, as I see it, are too preoccupied with a conception of scientific knowledge in terms of the accumulation of facts. They locate the epistemic value of models exclusively in their ability to generate new propositional knowledge about aspects of the world. As Frigg and Nguyen (2017, p. 49) put it, “a model can instruct us about the nature of its subject matter if it represents the selected part or aspect of the world that we investigate.” The word ‘instruct’ suggests a picture of the scientist as a passive pupil in whom the model deposits information about its subject. But models are objects embedded in a complex web of activities. When it comes to philosophical analyses of DL models, I want to stress the importance of modelling rather than that of models. Recent accounts of models as epistemic artifacts can help to reorient the conversation around modelling activities. I emphasize that DL modelling demands a peculiar set of skills. When combined with specific domain knowledge, these skills help us achieve our epistemic goals. I will argue that a distinctive sort of scientific knowledge consists in the manifestation of DL modelling skills in scientific practice.

Artifactualism provides an account of models that de-centers representation. The basic proposal laid out by Tarja Knuuttila (2005, 2011, 2021a, 2021b) treats models as “epistemic artifacts” that we use in a plethora of ways to gain knowledge. The artifactual approach emphasizes two key elements of modelling: multifunctionality and materiality. By stressing models’ multifunctionality, artifactualism “suggests that the links between models and reality are more complex than appears when we focus only on representation” (Knuuttila, 2005, p. 1267). By emphasizing materiality, artifactualism also brings much needed attention to how a medium enforces constraints and enables affordances. Knuuttila draws on insights from Morgan and Morrison (1999), who stress that models can take on “a life of their own” as material mediators between theory and observation (Morgan & Morrison, 1999, p. 18). As material artifacts whose construction proceeds quasi-independently, models have “distinctive ways of functioning. They are not open to all possible interpretations and uses, which simplifies or modifies the cognitive task scientists face in their work” (Knuuttila, 2005, p. 1267).

Artifactualism stresses the usability of models as goal-oriented, epistemic tools. We construct models via diverse material means and use them for some intended purpose. One such purpose can be to represent a target system. In short, some models are tools built for representing the world, but some are made for other purposes such as extending our predictive powers. Hence, artifactualism is consistent with a representational perspective on some models but is broader in scope since it does not require representation as the purpose of all model construction. Artifactualism thus denies representation pride of place in our theory of scientific models. So understood, representation is neither necessary nor sufficient for a tool to count as a model (Sanches de Oliveira, 2022). Following Sanches de Oliveira (2022), I suggest that we can get at the core of this dispute over representationalism in the following way. First, the ontology of models is function dependent. In a slogan, models are what they do. Representationalism insists that what models do is represent the world. Artifactualism suggests instead that models facilitate our epistemic activities or ends through their diverse, material affordances.

Artifactualism better accounts for DL models in scientific practice, especially their emphasis on useful predictions. This comes out most clearly through Knuuttila’s brief description of the results-orientedness of modelling activities (Knuuttila, 2011, p. 268). On this point, she echoes Paul Humphreys (2004), who stresses the “enormous importance of a relatively small number of computational templates” (Humphreys, 2004, p. 68). Such templates get uptake throughout the sciences due to their ease of use and tendency to produce dependable results. As Knuuttila explains,

. . the starting point is often the output and effects that models are supposed to produce. Instead of directly trying to represent some selected aspects of a given target system—as is conventionally assumed—modellers often proceed in a roundabout way, seeking to build hypothetical systems in the light of the anticipated results or of certain general features of the phenomena they are supposed to exhibit (Knuuttila, 2011, p. 268).

The practices of DL modelling reflect just this kind of opportunistic appropriation of computational templates. IceNet, for instance, seizes on a successful model architecture originally designed for medical imaging to handle climate data. We have dynamical models that adequately represent seasonal patterns of Arctic sea ice concentration, but these turn out to be inadequate for our non-representational purposes. Hence, Andersson et al. (2021) adapted existing U-Net architectures to meet the needs that a representational model could not. IceNet is just one of many readily available cases of such opportunism. These kinds of model transfers and extensions to new domains are only possible due to the generality of deep learning architectures; DL models are not crafted to represent a particular target, but we can appropriate them to learn useful properties of data in any domain. As Knuuttila puts it “the overall usability of computational templates is based on their generality and the observed similarity between different phenomena” (Knuuttila, 2011, p. 268). But doing this well requires a degree of joint understanding of how different DL model architectures behave, the kinds of data structures on which they are effective, and how to recognize that a particular problem can be operationalized in a way such that a DL template can be suitably applied. I argue that, for this reason, we should resist thinking of DL modelling activities in terms of what Alisa Bokulich (2011) calls “phenomenological” models, which involve an ad hoc fitting of a model to data that merely “saves the phenomena” (Bogen & Woodward, 1988). In what follows, I develop a sketch of how DL models—construed as domain-general epistemic tools—can scaffold understanding through the manifestation of the skills required to construct and apply them.

Skill provides a natural way to conceptualize this epistemic scaffolding. Ellen Fridland (2020, 2021) has developed an account of skilled action in terms of strategic control structures that proves illuminating. On her account, skills are “functions from intentions to controlled, successful actions, where the functional transformations from intention to action are implemented by control structures that have been developed through practice” (Fridland, 2020, p. 247). For Fridland, strategic control involves the successful execution of intentions, which are themselves control structures acquired through practice that both automatize the motor components of skilled action and organize our practical plans. These structures sit at the intermediary between agent-level, abstract representations and low-level sensorimotor processes, and they are instrumentally rational states (Fridland, 2020, p. 250). Moreover, attention and motor control guide the successful instantiation of these control structures in skilled actions.

Acquiring skills often involves apprenticeships and begins with the imitation of more skilled practitioners. Fridland (2013) argues persuasively that through imitation, we take up an intrinsic interest in the means of an observed intentional action. Through this “means-centric orientation” (Fridland, 2013, p. 205) we acquire a stance that’s required for us to refine our skills in such a way that facilitates genuine understanding of what we are doing. New knowledge manifests through the understanding of how our means relate with their consequences. As Michael Polanyi put it, learning to use a tool or a probe involves “the transformation of the tool or probe into a sentient extension of our body” (Polanyi, 1966, p. 17). In doing so, we gain the capacity to fully integrate its affordances into our own cognition. Truly understanding a model thus comes about only by treating it as an extension of ourselves. Only then do we cease to merely copy the activities of others and instead integrate the model as a subsidiary means to our own epistemic ends.

We can apply this picture of skill to DL modelling activities. Constructing a working DL model requires skillful manipulation of multiple interconnected elements. Having identified an appropriate problem, we can conceive of the model construction process in terms of three interrelated sets of decision procedures. First, we have choices related to data, like sampling, labeling and curating observations into datasets, pre-processing, and visualization. Next, we must make various choices about the structure of our model itself. This involves decisions about the architecture of the model, whether to appropriate and modify existing computational templates, how to tune hyperparameters, what kind of learning paradigm to use, how to structure the task goals, how to regularize and optimize for performance, and how to diagnose and correct systematic errors or biases. Finally, we implement various kinds of validation strategies like testing the model’s performance on held out data. What’s more, this entire process is highly iterative in the sense that we may use the outcome of decisions at any one stage to further modify our choices at other stages. Recognizing and diagnosing failures and iterating on the model is thus essential to effective model construction, but also an exceptionally complex matter. Doing so well requires understanding how interactions at each choice point affect the overall performance of the model. The skills required for DL modelling must be learned through practice via engagement with various model architectures across a range of contexts. This engagement may start out as a brute imitation of more skilled modelers, but with an intrinsic interest in understanding how skilled modelers achieve their ends. Over time this develops into a genuine, intelligent skill through which a modeler can recognize subtle ways that model structure relates to performance on real world phenomena.

Using a model to learn about the world depends on our ability to construct a model that is adequate for our purposes. We need to understand how to relate the model to our epistemic aims. Using DL models in science requires knowing how to train a DNN, which means possessing modeling skills. Unlike many classic examples of theoretical models, however, DL modelling skills do not depend on significant, domain-specific knowledge about the target system. DL modelling requires understanding how to flexibly modify and apply domain-general computational architectures to suitable data structures. Skilled modelers can build a DL model that will work well on a given data structure whilst knowing very little about the content of that data. Take, for instance, the toy example from Sect. 12.4, predicting future weather patterns in Cambridge from historic weather data. Suppose that I had access to the .CSV file containing the very same historic weather data, but I had no knowledge of what that data was about except that one column is a target label that I want to predict. If I was tasked with predicting future values of that target, I could build a simple, feedforward neural network that would perform better than the toy model described in Sect. 12.4. And I could do this without even knowing what I am predicting. This is the sense of domain-generality that sets DL modelling skills apart from other kinds of modelling skills in science.

The domain-generality of deep learning means that the process of learning DL modelling skills makes the models themselves into the object of inquiry. The means of inquiry become an end in themselves. But we really want to understand how to use DL models to learn about the world. This requires moving away from a means-centric orientation, which requires fully integrating modelling skills into the broader aims of our inquiry. Once integrated, the object of inquiry shifts. In this context, DL models become tools that researchers build and evaluate in terms of their capacity to generate understanding of an aspect of the world. Modelling skills thus become an important tacit dimension of scientific knowledge production, facilitating more effective inquiry by directing our attention towards aspects of a problem. DL modelling skill thus reflects a deep and genuine form of understanding that underpins successful scientific inquiry.

Generating new scientific knowledge with DL models, however, requires integrating domain-general modelling skills with domain-specific, theoretical knowledge. Successful DL modelling in science requires more than just knowing how to get a model to perform well on validation data. It also requires knowing how to use a model to pursue a particular epistemic aim. This requires the ability to apply one’s modelling skills in pursuit of a well-posed scientific problem. Doing so involves what Henk de Regt (2017) calls pragmatic understanding. De Regt clarifies this sense of understanding in terms of intelligibility, which he describes as the cluster of qualities that facilitate the use of a theory (cf. de Regt, 2017, p. 40). De Regt’s notion of intelligibility emphasizes that pragmatic understanding promotes the fruitfulness of our epistemic activities. Scientific progress requires fruitfulness, because the ability to apply a concept or theory is necessary for generating predictions, crafting experiments, and producing new explanations (cf. Stuart, 2016, p. 31). Pragmatic understanding is what makes our epistemic activities go well in scientific practice. We need intelligible theories to make good use of DL models in science; drawing out inferences about the world using a DL model requires a confluence of modelling skills and domain knowledge. This requires pragmatic understanding, the ability to use theoretical knowledge to construct a model that is adequate for purpose. Pragmatic understanding enables the transition from learning a good estimator of patterns in data to model-based inferences about the world.

## 12.7 Conclusion

This chapter began by distinguishing representations in machine learning from the notion of representation that figures prominently in the philosophy of model-based science. I argued that the former cannot do the epistemic work required of the latter. Hence, I suggest that the represenationalist idiom is liable to produce a stagnant philosophy of machine learning in science. I suggest instead that artifactualism, couched in account of skilled practice, is a more promising starting point.

It takes a plethora of skills to build models that work well. These skills are not mysterious or illusory. They are implementations of strategic control structures acquired through practice. Skills involve flexible scripts of action. Modelling skills scaffold genuine understanding because we need to be able to grasp the complex relations between our means and methods and our desired epistemic ends. When we marry DL modelling skills with pragmatic understanding, DL models become fruitful tools of inquiry. This initial sketch makes some progress towards a richer account of what artifactualists mean when they talk of modelling as a material engagement with epistemic tools. We can apply this picture to better grasp the contribution of deep learning to genuine, world-directed understanding.
