# Chapter 14 Defining Formal Validity Criteria for Machine Learning Models

**Chiara Manganini and Giuseppe Primiero**

**Abstract** In the context of deterministic scientific simulations, formal validity requirements have typically been defined to help us reason about the relationship between the mathematical model underlying the target system and the computational model used to simulate it. With machine learning simulations entering the picture, we argue that these formal requirements need to be reviewed, as the objects to which they apply have significantly changed. This is due to several reasons: the target system is no longer an available system object of investigation; the probabilistic mathematical model is abstracted from the target system through the mediation of the computational model, which however remains largely opaque to us due to its high complexity. For these reasons, we formulate weaker, probabilistic versions of the traditional relations of Simulation, Bisimulation, and Approximate Simulation. Accordingly, we define three corresponding validity criteria that capture a range of cases, from the strongest to the weakest, depending on the extent to which the machine learning model can be assumed to correctly represent its target system.

**Keywords** Non-deterministic computation · Probabilistic simulation · Validity Model · Markov semantics · Process algebra

## 14.1 Introduction

The introduction of computational systems in the practice of science has had a major significance for the related philosophical reflection. In particular, the use of computational modeling and simulation software has called for the definition of specific methodological principles to establish what is a valid scientific result obtained through algorithmic processes. The problem of validity as a property of a scientific result obtained by computational methods could be formulated as follows:

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">C. Manganini (🖂) · G. Primiero Logic, Uncertainty, Computation and Information Lab and PhilTech Research Center, Department of Philosophy, University of Milan, Milan, Italy e-mail: [chiara.manganini@unimi.it](mailto:chiara.manganini@unimi.it); [giuseppe.primiero@unimi.it](mailto:giuseppe.primiero@unimi.it)</span></small>

**Problem 1** (Computational Model Validity). What are the conditions for accepting as valid the results of a computational model, and how do we express them formally?

In this broad context, the integration of machine learning (ML) methods in computer simulations has represented another turning point. Widely discussed in the context of “traditional”—i.e., non-ML—simulations (Humphreys, 2004; Durán, 2018; Durán & Formanek, 2018; Alvarado, 2023), two problematic aspects characterize most ML systems, and hence most ML simulations:

1. Opacity, due to their high structural complexity,

2. Non-determinism, resulting from their instantiation of learning methods to spot statistical patterns in the data.

The problem of validity for ML simulations can therefore be reformulated as follows:

**Problem 2** (Opaque and Non-Deterministic Computational Model Validity). What are the conditions for accepting the results of an opaque and non-deterministic computational model, and how do we express them formally?

Despite the abundance of technical and philosophical analyses of ML opacity (Guidotti et al., 2018; Boge, 2021; Facchini & Termine, 2022) and ML non-determinism (Summers & Dinneen, 2021; Cooper et al., 2022; Creel & Hellman, 2022), a full-blown theoretical examination of Problem 2 is still at early stages at the moment. With the present contribution, we wish to help to address it.

In order to do so, we start from an overview of the philosophical debate on deterministic simulations in Sect. 14.2. We then turn to non-deterministic ones, first in general terms (Sect. 14.3) and then focusing on four specific aspects constituting relevant departures from the deterministic scenario (Sect. 14.4). We then advance our proposal for a formal approach to Problem 2 that essentially consists in extending one already formulated for the deterministic case in (Primiero, 2019) to non-deterministic simulations. This idea is offered in Sect. 14.5, where we justify the choice of the relevant formal structures, without providing any full-blown formalization yet, which will be addressed in further work. Finally, in Sect. 14.6, we formulate some related questions on the notion of validity emerging from the use of non-deterministic, opaque computational models. Section 14.7 concludes the work with an overview of the future steps of this research.

## 14.2 The Story So Far: On the Validity Criteria for Deterministic Computations

The conceptual study on what kind of validity conditions can be established for results obtained from implemented computational systems, such as simulation software, is a complex issue. It is strongly intertwined with the question of whether such criteria can be formulated in a formal setting. The origin of this debate is notoriously traced back to Humphreys:

Inasmuch as the simulation has abstracted from the material content of the system being simulated, has employed various simplifications in the model, and uses only the mathematical form, it obviously and trivially differs from the ‘real thing’, but in this respect, there is no difference between simulations and any other kind of mathematical model, and it is primarily when computer simulations are used in place of empirical experiments that this element of falsity is important. But if the underlying mathematical model can be realistically construed (i.e. it is not a mere heuristic device) and is well-confirmed, then the simulation will be as ‘realistic’ as any theoretical representation is. (Humphreys, 1990, pp. 501–502)

From the assumed epistemological identity of the validity of computer simulations and their use in place of empirical experiments, the question arises of how to formulate their validity conditions. In particular, it becomes pressing to establish whether a formal treatment of such criteria is possible. Here the debate has diverged, with different positions being formulated in the literature. On the one hand, it has been argued that such a question cannot be answered in absolute terms, and that the very conditions of knowledge of the target system determine the appropriate methodology to formulate what validity means:

For the data to hit the target, the experiment, simulation, or “simulating experiment” must mirror the target in a number of relevant aspects. Whether the mirroring should be purely formal or material in character, depends on the kind of question we are asking, and on the amount and quality of background knowledge we have accumulated regarding the target system itself. (Guala, 2002, p. 15)

On the other hand, detractors of formal methods—including Humphreys himself— have argued against the usefulness of formalization, seen as imposing a further departure from the observed system, to be added to the abstractions and idealizations already implied by equation-based models:

[ . . . ] no comprehensive model at the level of the total system exists. Computationally irreducible processes thus occur in systems in which the most efficient procedure for calculating the future states of the system is to let the system itself evolve. [F]ormalization takes one away from what is important about the form of the equations, and hence is at best unnecessary; at worst it distorts the important formal features. [ . . . ] logic is not well suited to deal with every goal of science, or even particularly well with any one of them. (Humphreys, 2004, pp. 149–153)

Nonetheless, provided that computational models have proven time and again their extraordinary capacity for accurately predicting the behavior of real systems, their reliability inevitably requires formal criteria to assess their correctness:

If computer simulations are reliable processes that render correct results, then we need a way to characterize what a ‘correct’ result would be. [ . . . ] Verifications and validations are two fundamental pillars for asserting the reliability of computer simulations [ . . . ] [R]esearchers are on good grounds for claiming that their computer simulations are reliable processes, and thus that they are justified in believing that the results of the simulation are correct. [ . . . ] [R]eliability of computer simulations support the claim that researchers are able to claim for explanation, prediction, and [ . . . ] for understanding of the results. [ . . . ] Although neither software nor hardware can be fully verified or validated, researchers are still developing methods that reduce the occurrence of errors and increases the credibility of the simulation. (Durán, 2018, pp. 91–96)

As stressed also by Humphreys (2019) with the notion “construction assumptions” for formal templates, the role of formal methods is crucial to establish what kind of idealizations and approximations are appropriate in knowledge construction. Determining such assumptions for computational methods is essential to distinguish which validity criteria hold. It is, in fact, necessary if we want to know under which conditions the results of such models can be deemed valid.

One attempt to ground such formal validity conditions is the notion of isomorphism, well-known in the philosophical debate on what enables a scientific model to represent the target system (van Fraassen, 1980; Brading & Landry, 2006). The isomorphic view anchors scientific representation in the existence of a formally definable one-to-one, bijective correspondence between the set of states representing the dynamic evolution of the target and the one representing the dynamic evolution of the computation. Notoriously, it has been argued that such a conception is somewhat too strong, as it requires perfect matching between the target’s and the model’s structures. Moreover, it imposes properties like reflexivity and symmetry that seem undesirable for qualifying the representation relation (see, for example, the directionality requirement by Frigg & Nguyen, 2017, p. 55). To respond to these shortcomings, weaker variants of target-model correspondence have been proposed, like partial isomorphism and homomorphism.

In what follows, we are interested in developing an approach inspired by the isomorphic view and its weaker versions. In particular, we borrow the concept of simulation relations from the process algebra literature, where they have been used to define different identity conditions for software systems (Angius & Primiero, 2018). Moreover, in (Primiero, 2019) these relations have been applied to the problem of validity of computer simulations, to formalize the correspondence between the deterministic model of a target system and the deterministic computational model of a simulation software that should predict or describe it.<sup>1</sup> Such an application defines the underlying formal mappings between:

1. An observed target system;

2. An abstract mathematical construct that describes the dynamic transformations of the target system and the relationships between its scientifically relevant variables;

3. A computational model, i.e., an algorithmic structure that translates the mathematical model into discrete and approximate solutions that computers can process;

4. A physical computational system executing the computational model.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">1 This formal strategy relies on an idealization process which assumes the ability to construct models for both the target and the computational systems. Especially for the former, such an idealization is not trivial and it may have to take into account certain limitations, such as partial observability (see Sect. 14.5).</span></small>

Essentially, the basic idea behind the present contribution is that of translating the above entities and the relations among them into proper formal counterparts known from process algebra. In particular, we will primarily focus on (1–3) and their relations, leaving aside the questions relative to (4) and its relations with the other three entities (in other words, we will assume the physical implementation of the simulation software to be correct, which is of course a crucial requirement for the validity of the simulation results).

Without entering into the formal treatment yet, suffice to say that simulation relations can be used to define formal criteria for simulation validity as they allow us to express whether and how the target system and the computational model match in their dynamic evolution (i.e., in terms of their initial states and transitions). The ultimate goal is to verify property satisfaction, thereby checking whether a condition holding for one structure (something the target system satisfies) also holds for the other (i.e., the computational model). In regard to this, three fundamental types of simulation relations can be described as follows:

• In a Simulation Relation, the computational model displays only behaviors of the target system;

• In a Bisimulation Relation, the computational model displays all and only the behaviors of the target system;

• In an Approximate Simulation Relation, the computational model displays some but not only behaviors of the target system.

Hence, a Simulation Relation holds between a computational model and the target system whenever the former mimics all stepwise behaviors of the latter, but not vice versa. A Bisimulation Relation holds if the above relation is shown to hold in both directions, i.e., when the two systems exhibit identical stepwise behavior. The Approximate Simulation Relation expresses incompleteness and divergence of the computational model with respect to the target, as some computational behaviors have no counterpart in it. By means of these relations, one can for instance guarantee properties of the target system by verifying their presence in some or all behaviors of a sufficiently precise simulative computational structure. Moreover, the relations of Simulation and Bisimulation have been used to define the notions of exact and inexact copies of computational artifacts (Angius & Primiero, 2018), while a notion of Approximate Simulation Relation is introduced to define approximate copies. The corresponding safety and liveness checking algorithm over approximate copies is defined in (Angius & Primiero, 2023).

At this point, one might wonder whether this framework is applicable to the case of ML simulations where, as we said, the deterministic assumption fails because of their inherent stochastic nature. In the next section, we extend the investigation in this direction.

## 14.3 The New Scenario: Entering Non-Deterministic Computations

Machine learning systems have almost entirely changed any discussion on algorithms. Although deterministic computations still represent a crucial and overwhelming technological component of our daily lives, as well as the object of recent philosophical investigation (Angius et al., 2021), the new generation of AI systems is increasingly employed in scientific and industrial contexts alike. From the point of view of the present investigation, we are interested in assessing which formal criteria can be formulated to establish whether the result of an ML simulation (for example, to generate input data in driving scenarios or product lines in simulated factories) can be considered valid. To better understand what kind of validity is adequate for ML simulations, let us first clarify their underlying ontology and how it differs from that of traditional simulations.

We begin by considering a general statement applicable to any simulation, whether traditional or ML-based: the target system is what ultimately grounds the notion of validity for all simulation results. Not only in the sense that the resulting predictions are a posteriori evaluated against observations of the target system itself (to statistically validate the model), but also in the sense that the target system plays a pivotal role in the actual process of simulation construction. The dual role played by the target system could be seen as roughly tracing the distinction between, respectively, the context of justification and the context of discovery (Reichenbach, 1938): on the one hand, based on the target system we justify whether the simulation is valid; on the other hand, we find such a simulation model by looking at the target.

Against this general characteristic of simulations, we notice that ML simulations constitute a departure from traditional ones in regard to the actual process through which the computational model is constructed from observations. In the traditional simulation scenario, the mathematical model given by an already established mathematical description of the target phenomenon—for instance, a set of differential equations—is top-down translated into the computational model by a manual process:

It is well documented, for example, that the mathematical operations that form the basis of computer simulations of dynamic systems are quite different from those found in the theoretical stages of inquiry. [ . . . ] The way a computer simulation solves an equation is by providing approximate values to discretised parameters that roughly correspond to the results one gets from a continuous equation. While the results can be similar or approximate to an almost negligible degree, the fact remains that both the results and the methods by which they are arrived at are distinct from a continuous equation. Often the translation of mathematical models into code for a computer to run includes many idiosyncratic engineering practices that are far removed from the sound theoretical principles in virtue of which the initial model was constructed. (Alvarado, 2022, p. 1190)

On the other hand, in the ML case, something different happens. Through the training process, the mathematical function is automatically extracted from a sample of data—the training set—that is considered to be representative enough of the target system. This process is, instead, bottom-up, in the sense that the mathematical model is obtained from the computational one, rather than the other way around. As a result of this bottom-up process, ML systems inherently exhibit two fundamental characteristics: non-determinism and opacity.

Regarding the former, in fact, the result of the learning process is a computational model implementing the learned function $\hat { f }$ which constitutes the mathematical model of the ML-based simulation. This describes a probability distribution that associates each input with its outcome probabilities. Therefore, the input-output relation is non-deterministic to the extent that it is stochastic, i.e., can be reasoned upon using probabilities.

As for the opacity, we can see the training phase as a process that makes it possible for the designer of the computational model to formulate a specification (i.e., the set of functional requirements) of its functioning without explicitly expressing it. The training data set in fact provides a partial specification of the required behavior, thus partly replacing the designer’s intentions and requirements.<sup>2</sup> A first, crucial aspect of the ML opacity is that the outcome of the training process is not already the probabilistic function $\hat { f } ,$ but the computational model that implements it—i.e., the list of parameters of a neural network. This means that a work of abstraction is further required to extract the mathematical model out of the computational one, as the former is not immediately accessible to us. However, even when the mathematical model is successfully reconstructed from the algorithm, this may not be a guarantee of epistemic transparency, due to its inherent complexity. A second and significant obstacle to transparency is hence represented by the huge number of variables $X _ { 1 } , \ldots ,   X _ { n }$ of $\hat { f } ,$ that makes its decomposition into simpler joint distributions P(X<sub>i</sub>) with $1 \leq i \leq n$ a very complex epistemic task (see Facchini $\&$ Termine, 2022).

The computational model is in turn implemented into a physical artifact which materially executes the computational processes fixed by the formal dynamic descriptors. The result returned by such a physical computational execution constitutes the final experimental result of the entire ML simulation. Standard software testing techniques can be used to verify its correctness and validate it. For the verification of machine learning models, both the training engine and the trained model can be tested through standard software techniques, while the validation of the trained model is usually carried out by means of well-known performance metrics, such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. Note, however, that here we are not interested in asking which among these statistical measures is best suited to evaluate the fitness of a machine learning system for a given prediction task. Rather, what we are seeking to do is to establish a formal counterpart to such statistical criteria of validity. This goal is not entirely new. Indeed, formal approaches to the verification of ML systems are slowly emerging within the literature. Starting from the work by Seshia et al. (2018), computer scientists have increasingly focused on the formal verification of deep neural networks, in order to check some properties of interest—such as safety, liveness, and robustness. Within the philosophical literature, noteworthy contributions include the work by Angius and Plebe (2023). In a similar spirit to ours, the authors investigate what are the appropriate validity criteria for Deep Learning (DL) systems. Interestingly, they claim that the most appropriate notion of correctness for such systems is that of experimental validity, as defined in (Primiero, 2019). An experimentally valid simulation is one in which:

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">2 Under this perspective, machine learning could be thought of as a new, automatic process of “requirement engineering”, in the sense of the term discussed by Jackson (1995), aimed at producing “learned” specifications (Banks & Ashmore, 2019; Vogelsang & Borg, 2019).</span></small>

• The mathematical model is fit for purpose, i.e. it is able to represent some of the requested variables and inferential properties of the target system;

• The derived computational model is isomorphic or partially isomorphic to the mathematical one and usable, i.e., it allows to accomplish the desired experimental analysis.<sup>3</sup>

Here, we want to expand the intuition further. We agree with Angius and Plebe in considering the notion of experimental validity as the most appropriate to account for the evaluation of machine learning models. Nevertheless, reasoning transparently and deterministically about the identity of their behaviors—as we saw in the previous section, by means of deterministic simulation relations—seems impracticable for the reasons that will be illustrated in the next section.

## 14.4 Novel Aspects of Simulation Relations for Non-Deterministic Computations

We now turn to four aspects of ML simulations marking a significant difference with respect to traditional ones. These aspects, we argue, make simulation relations defined in Sect. 14.2 inapplicable to the ML context.

To begin with, it is extremely hard to establish what is the relevant or appropriate target system for an ML simulation. In other words: defining correctness is a hard task for computational systems of this sort. In traditional simulations, one usually starts with the object to be modeled (a physical, social, or engineering system), and only then designs the relevant computational model to simulate and study it. On the other hand, when a machine learning system is at work, one may only extract intended or desirable behaviors for a correct prediction, while establishing whether false negatives and false positives occur—and their frequency—is a different matter and so is determining whether unintended results are produced. For instance, in the case of a self-driving autonomous system trained on real data, surely there is an informal intention, possibly expressed by the relevant rules of road navigation in urban and non-urban environments, to avoid collisions and in general to drive safely. This certainly can be taken to constitute “the norm” that the trained model should respect. The formal specification of such rules and habits, against which the model trained on the data should be evaluated, is a different matter. Verifying that the algorithm is correct would require such a formal specification and that it does satisfy it for all potential cases and nothing else, which is a matter of testing against numerous, if not infinite, cases of use.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">3 Note that these notions are to be considered weak as opposed to robustness of a model, where the model is able to include all variables of interest and all the inferential properties of the simulated empirical system.</span></small>

Second, which learned model is working as a computational model is not necessarily known beforehand. While in standard deterministic software systems the definition of the mathematical function is sufficient to establish the behavior of the system for any given input, in the case of machine learning systems the mathematical function is largely determined by the training data. Change the data, change the learned function. Hence, only by knowing in detail both the function and the training data, one can be at least sufficiently aware of what type of computations one can expect to occur once a new input data is provided.

Third, even when the computational model is known, an accurate definition of its behavior with respect to the intended mathematical function—the desired behavior—is not always possible. To this aim, one would need to be able to perform statistical inferences on its behavior on the given test set, to establish whether there are input/output relations that falsify the intended functional behavior represented by the mathematical function of learning. Unfortunately, performing such inferences is often impossible, due to the inaccessibility of the structure of the model and its complexity.

Finally, the computational model itself cannot be directly evaluated as to whether it is appropriate to the task at hand. To do so, one would need to have full access to its structure, namely, parameters which are automatically set, and hyper-parameters which are tuned either manually or automatically. Full understanding of these coefficients is extremely hard in practice, and often totally missing for the end user. Even more crucially, even assuming its availability, it is unclear whether this knowledge would make the validation of the model any easier, since we might be unable to establish cognitively meaningful simulation relations between the model structure and the target system, as discussed in Chap. [12](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_12) by Kieval (2025).

All the above makes it very hard to establish what is a valid result for such a system. One would need to know that the test set agrees with the training set and that the distribution stability is satisfied to prevent loss of prediction accuracy or distribution shift. One would also need to have both structural and inferential knowledge of the computational model, while the former is hard and the latter very hard, especially without any formal modeling. The result of these considerations is double. On the one hand, it seems that the very essence of the formal model on which simulation relations are defined, i.e., the requirement of representing states of both the target system and of the computational model, the ability to establish valid evolutions of both structures, and the strategy to compare them to identify whether their behaviors are totally or partially identical, is bound to fail because of the opaque and non-deterministic nature of the new computational model at stake.

On the other hand, though, it is evident that without such a formal analysis, the evaluation of such systems based on their accuracy can only rely on non-structural, almost epi-phenomenal reasons, thereby making the claim of validity for their use in scientific contexts void. What is needed, therefore, is a formal model which may accommodate the uncertainty of both the structure and the behavior of machine learning systems.

To take stock, when it comes to ML simulations, it becomes impossible to assume a well-defined and sufficiently fine-grained representation of the computational model to check its structural identity with the target system; this calls for some new formal validity principles, as those that will be introduced in what follows.

## 14.5 Extending Validity Criteria to ML Simulations

A well-studied and natural way to represent the uncertain behaviors of machine learning systems is provided by probabilistic extensions of state transition systems—such as Markov Chains, Markov Decision Processes, or Probabilistic Process Algebra (Jonsson et al., 2001; López & Núñez, 2004)—and their associated simulation relations (Baier et al., 2000; Baier et al., 2006). An equivalent approach consists in devising an appropriate inferential system (see, e.g., D’Asaro et al., 2025; Genco & Primiero, 2023). Either way, a common strategy underlies these formalizations:

• Assign probability distributions to training and test data as frequencies in the population to represent possible data for the trained model and possible test inputs;

• Assign to each feature the probability to hold for the current data point;

Compute, by an appropriate probabilistic consequence (or inference) relation, the probability that any set of assignments of features leads to an assignment of the target feature (as an equivalence class).

An attribution of features to a data point for classification or prediction represents a state of the model (or a derivable formula); an evaluation of a new feature is an action that allows one to move from state to state (or a rule to proceed in the deduction); and the end state is one where the target feature is reached (or deduced) with a certain probability. Doing so for the target system and for the computational model respectively allows one to ask how much the two resulting abstract structures are similar to each other, or else how much the model of the ML classifier represents the model of the target system. To do so, one may refer to simulation relations for probabilistic systems to evaluate the adherence between the ML computational model and the target system, based on the given probability assignments.

In the literature, it is usual to distinguish between strong and weak simulation relations to distinguish cases where a simulation relation<sup>4</sup> holds between two systems whose states are completely observable, from those cases where the systems are only partially observable (Baier et al., 2006). ML models clearly refer to the latter case. Hence, we can define three weak counterparts of the simulation relations previously introduced, to express partial identity of the computational ML model and the probabilistic representation of the target system:

• In a Weak Simulation Relation, the non-deterministic computational model displays only behaviors with at least the same probability as in the target model;

• In a Weak Bisimulation Relation, the non-deterministic computational model displays only behaviors with the same probability as in the target model;

In a Weak Approximate Simulation Relation, the non-deterministic computational model displays not only behaviors with the same probability as in the target model.

Some observations are necessary concerning these variants of the simulation relation. The relation of Weak Simulation admits the case of underfitting: the ML system does not predict beyond the scope of the target system, while it may assign to certain predictions a higher probability than the corresponding value in the target system. In contrast to this, Weak Bisimulation expresses in formal terms a perfect fitting of the computational model with respect to the target system: what the model predicts is as in the system. This relation can only be instantiated by a perfect classifier: despite not knowing all the probabilities for the intermediate evaluations, the observed results do not show any false positives or false negatives. Finally, the Weak Approximate Simulation Relation renders the notion of overfitting: the model may make predictions which are in the scope of the target system, but it may also predict features of variables which the target system does not admit. In this sense, the computational model may create predictions which do not reflect the complexity of the model, and therefore the classification may show high bias.

The formal translation of these relations is left for another occasion. Instead, we now focus on how these relations, and the notion of validity they induce, allow us to answer crucial questions on the correctness of results produced by computational systems based on machine learning algorithms.

## 14.6 Validity Principles

When using systems based on machine learning algorithms, the question of their validity reduces to understanding how much can be known about the correctness of their results with respect to the intended or actual behavior of the target system. Such functional knowledge would be inferable under the assumption of structural knowledge of the computational system under observation. Unfortunately, as highlighted above, such structural knowledge is almost always not available for ML algorithms, except for trivial cases. A possible strategy to attack such a problem, under the assumption of the ability to determine simulation relations for probabilistic systems as formulated above, is to establish what type of knowledge we can infer from the fact that such a relation holds. To further explain this aspect, we will formulate some questions related to the structural knowledge of the computational system under analysis and show which answers can be provided in terms of simulation relations.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">4 This applies to Simulation and Bisimulation. The notion of Approximate Simulation Relation introduced in (Angius & Primiero, 2018) misses such a distinction in the literature. The definition of a Weak Approximate Simulation Relation in this section is meant to precisely fill this gap.</span></small>

The first pair of questions concern the relation between the characteristics of a seemingly correct prediction/classification and the inferable knowledge on its underlying causal structure and its verifiability:

**Question 1** Can we establish why a certain ML classification/prediction is correct? **Question 2** Can we verify that an ML system classifies/predicts correctly for the same reasons we would use to explain the real-world phenomena?

To answer these questions, let us reconsider the criteria associated with ML-based simulations. The assertion that a non-deterministic model of the ML system validly represents the target system would require, at the very least, that the former displays only behaviors expected or assumed to hold for the latter. Failing this, one would have evidence that the structure of the computational model exceeds in some way that of the target system. Such validity of the structure should, in principle, be of a causal nature.5 Arguably, of the three simulation relations defined in the previous Section, only the Weak Bisimulation captures a necessary (although not sufficient) criterion for establishing causal correctness between the ML model and the target system. Hence, a machine learning model can be assumed to be causally correct for a given target system only if a weak bisimulation relation holds between them. Accordingly, a machine learning artifact is causally correct only if it implements without errors a causally correct computational model.

Unfortunately, this is a necessary but not sufficient condition, as a much stronger criterion would need to be formulated. Interventionism or causal manipulation is currently considered the most adequate one, as it requires to qualify which variables are significant by observing structural variations induced by changing their values (Woodward, 2000). This approach is largely used in ML practice through perturbation techniques, consisting in switching some features’ values from current to alternative ones (Liu & Lorini, 2023).<sup>6</sup> The following principle summarizes the above:<sup>7</sup>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">5 There is a long-standing debate on the causal validity in models and the associated problems. See, for instance (McKim & Turner, 1997; Beckers et al., 2023). For a recent overview of the notion of causality in machine learning see (Termine & Primiero, 2024).</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">6 For a non-causal interpretation of ML systems and their explanations see Chap. [8](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_8) by Buijsman (2025).</span></small>

**Principle 1** (Justifiably Valid Model). A machine learning based computational model is justifiably valid for a given target system only if at least a weak bisimulation relation holds between them, i.e.:

• The test data satisfy all and only probabilistic assignments of the training data, and

The assignments of the machine learning model to data points in the test data match only the features in the target system.

Note that the formulation of the first point in the above definition assumes that no distribution shift occurs between training and test data.

The second pair of questions concern the possibility that a correct model for some target system is wrongly extended to be used for a different target, or what in the literature is known as the Out-of-Distribution problem. So, assuming that an implemented system matches the real-world phenomenon’s causal structure, how do we know the underlying test set is representative of the real-world phenomena? And moreover: if the classification is not too limited by the training set, is its distribution stable with respect to the currently given test set? In other words:

**Question 3** What are the limits of the training set for the validity of the ML classification/prediction?

**Question 4** What are the limits of the test set for the validity of the ML classification/prediction?

In this case, the necessary condition for the simulation relation is that the computational model displays behaviors that have at least the same probabilities as in the target system, or that the machine learning system does not underestimate the predictions which are realistically assigned by the target. This brings us to a weak notion of validity:

**Principle 2** (Weakly Valid Model). A machine learning based computational model is weakly valid for a given target system only if at most a weak probabilistic simulation relation holds between them, i.e.:

• The test data satisfy probabilistic assignments with at least the same values as in the training data, and

• The assignments of the computational model for features to points in the test data are at least the same as in the target system.

Also in this case, the condition is necessary but not sufficient. This means that a guarantee that the current model is applied with a valid training set and to a valid test set would again require a stronger condition, reducing in the first place to (but not just) the notion of justifiably valid model.

Consider that verifying Weak Bisimulation (which implies perfect fitting) is hard: this is not just 100% accuracy, but a full-blown probabilistic structural identity on data sets and step-by-step probabilistic evaluations. On the other hand, weak simulation (admitting underfitting) implies the ability of the machine learning model to correctly classify/predict multiple data sets, a phenomenon hardly known in reality. This suggests that justifiable validity and weak validity for machine learning based computational models may be difficult to obtain.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">7 For significant contributions to the role of justification in ML, see Chap. [4](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_4) by Durán, (2025), Chap. [5](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_5) by Alvarado, (2025), and Chap. [6](http://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03083-2_6) by Zednik and Verreault-Julien (2025).</span></small>

The last and weakest degree of validity is the one expressed by the relation of approximate weak simulation:

**Principle 3** (Almost Valid Model). A machine learning based computational model is almost valid for a given target system only if at most an approximate probabilistic simulation relation holds between them, i.e.:

• The test data satisfy probabilistic assignments with at least the same values as the training data, but not only, and

The assignments of the computational model for features to points in the test data are at least the same as in the target system, but not only.

In other words, we are considering a computational model which might be expressing underfitting evaluation for the variables of interest, while this does not exclude that it assigns values to non-relevant features. The corresponding ontological notion is what has been called a usable computational artifact in (Primiero, 2019, p. 266), that is, a computational system which allows for a consistent and fit-for-purpose experimental analysis of the conceptual space determined by the variables of interest, although it does not exclude assignment of probabilities outside of the scope of the target system. Note that usability is here intended in a deprecative sense, since an artifact can be usable, yet without ensuring the validity of its result. In fact, the relation of approximate simulation is the most realistic case, as it admits both overfitting and underfitting: this implies asking for which features the computational model is too strong, and for which is too weak, for which features the model might be positively and negatively biased. In this sense, verification of approximate simulation might be a crucial step for improving the fairness of machine learning models.

## 14.7 Conclusions

In this work, we have approached the problem of formulating validity criteria for ML-based computational models. We argued that such a task requires formal modeling: the validity problem consists in assessing correctness criteria, and hence it assumes the necessity of essentially formal verification techniques. It was then pointed out that a currently available strategy—based on defining simulation relations between the structure of the computational model and that of the target system—is challenged by two characteristics of ML methods: opacity and non-determinism. To address this limitation, we have proposed that weak simulation relations based on the definition of probabilistic models are appropriate to the definition of validity conditions for the computational models of interest. The result of such an approach suggests that formal validity criteria can be formulated for a nuanced range of cases, going from the strongest to the weakest, according to how much a computational model can be assumed to correctly represent a given target system.

We have furthermore formulated a notion of justifiable validity expressing necessary (but not sufficient) conditions for a computational model capable of fully expressing the range of results assumed to be correct for the target system. The notion of weak validity offers necessary (but not sufficient) conditions for a computational model capable of being at least as correct as the intended results of the target model but possibly admitting overfitting. Finally, the criteria for an almost valid model spell out the necessary (but, again, not sufficient) conditions for a computational model capable of at least being as correct as the intended results of the target model but possibly admitting high bias. The formalization of the associated simulation relations and the formulation of appropriate verification algorithms are the next steps in this research.
