# Chapter 16 Values, Inductive Risk, and Societal-Epistemic Coupledness in Machine Learning Models

**Milou Jansen and Koray Karaca**

**Abstract** We offer a novel perspective on how to manage inductive risk in the context of machine learning (ML) models used for societal purposes. Since ML models can produce erroneous results to varying extents, whether to accept a given ML model requires taking account of the inductive risk associated with its use. Deciding which levels and types of inductive risks are acceptable in the application contexts is a value-laden activity. While ML models are increasingly used for societal purposes, their epistemic features are more strongly connected with their societal purposes and underlying value judgments. We suggest that the epistemic and societal value judgments should be understood as coupled in the sense of mutually influencing each other, rather than as two separate kinds of factors, in the construction and assessment of societal ML models. We provide a coupled societalepistemic analysis of the inductive risk in the context of societal ML models. Based on a case study concerning the societal use of an ML model by the City of Amsterdam, we suggest that finding the right balance of acceptable inductive risk is a collective quest, in the sense that this risk is prioritized and interpreted differently by the relevant stakeholders of the model.

**Keywords** Machine learning · Error · Inductive risk · Social and epistemic values · Social-epistemic coupledness · Value-ladenness

## 16.1 Introduction

Governmental institutions are increasingly relying on machine learning (ML) models to optimize societal decision-making processes in the name of the public good (Veale & Brass, 2019). These models are implemented in a wide range of public domains for various optimization purposes, such as to optimize routes of garbage trucks and predict and distribute pedestrian and vehicle traffic intensity. The deployment of ML models in public domains indicates that the social and the technical are increasingly intertwined. What should be taken as optimal in those domains differs widely, and it is determined not only through technical and epistemic considerations but also through social considerations. For what is technically optimal may not always be normatively defensible in societally relevant terms, and the optimal performance of an ML model is ultimately bounded by its fit with society. Therefore, ML models and the practices surrounding their construction and deployment should not be understood as neutral, but rather laden to varying extents with both epistemic and societal value judgments. This not only raises the question of what kind of knowledge base we assign to these tools, but also what kind of values are embedded in them (Dotan & Milli, 2020; Karaca, 2021; Ratti & Graves, 2021). This in turn illustrates that modeling practices involve diverse choices resulting from human value judgments (Douglas, 2000; Winsberg, 2012; Diekmann & Peterson, 2013).

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">M. Jansen (🖂) Amsterdam, Netherlands</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">K. Karaca University of Twente, Enschede, Netherlands</span></small>

In this chapter, we will argue that epistemic and societal value judgments should not be seen as separate, but rather as coupled throughout the ML modelling practice, including not only their construction but also their validation. To this end, we will develop an analysis as a heuristic tool to jointly analyze the epistemic and societal dimensions of the ML modelling practice. Throughout this chapter, we use societal values to refer to considerations—including ethical, political, and pragmatic ones— that shape judgments about the social consequences of ML models. We avoid the term social values to maintain conceptual clarity and to highlight how societal framing reveals the coupling between a model’s epistemic features and the specific features of its use context. Our analysis shares similarities with those developed in similar techno-science studies to characterize couplings of different kinds, e.g. between descriptive and evaluative, between facts and values, and between different philosophies. In recent years, it has been shown that the coupling approach has contributed to a better understanding of the interplay between the epistemic and ethical dimensions of knowledge-production practices in complex and social contexts (Katikireddi & Valles, 2015; Tuana, 2013; Valles et al., 2019; Russo et al., 2023), while the question of how the values embedded in these bridging concepts should be managed remains as a challenge (Alexandrova, 2015). In this chapter, we will also address this challenge by making use of the concept of inductive risk that has been fruitful in dealing with the management of value trade-offs (Elliott & Richards, 2017).

The plan of the present chapter is roughly as follows. In Sect. 16.2, we provide a characterization of the concept of inductive risk that is applicable to the context of ML modelling. In Sect. 16.3, we discuss the involvement of epistemic and societal values in ML modelling. Sections 16.4 and 16.5 are devoted to what we shall call the coupled societal-epistemic analysis of inductive risk, which is subsequently illustrated through a case study discussed in Sects. 16.6 and 16.7. In Sect. 16.8, we provide concluding remarks concerning the societal uses of ML models.

## 16.2 Error and Inductive Risk in ML Modeling

ML refers to mathematically modelling the mapping relationship that exists between a set of inputs $X = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } )$ and a corresponding set of outputs $Y = ( y _ { 1 } ,   \ldots , y _ { m } )$ with respect to a specified task, such as a classification task (Alpaydin, 2010). For instance, in the case of binary (two-class) classification which is widely used in societal applications, the inputs are assigned to the set of outputs consisting of two distinct classes denoted by a binary tuple $( y _ { 1 } , y _ { 2 } )$ . ML is based on the assumption that there exists a target function $f : X \to Y$ that correctly maps all the given inputs to the corresponding outputs for a given task. ML is used to find the function $g$ that provides an optimal approximation to the unknown function $f .$ The function $g$ is a parametric function of the input variables and it is referred to as the ML model that optimally represents the foregoing mapping relationship. In the case of supervised learning, which we shall consider in this chapter, the training data contains examples of inputs together with the corresponding outputs.<sup>1</sup>

The essential elements of supervised ML include a training data set, learning algorithm, hypothesis set (H), and loss (error) function together with an optimization procedure. H contains the candidate functions, namely the functions chosen by a ML modeler to be suitable to represent the mapping relationship under consideration. The learning algorithm is used to find the most optimal set of parameters that will constitute the function $g$ as an ML model. This is achieved through a training process that is basically an optimization process aiming at minimizing the loss (or cost) function that specifies the total cost incurred due to error. Here, error denotes the extent of the difference between the outputs drawn from the training data and the outputs provided by the function $g .$ The chosen learning algorithm is implemented according to an optimization procedure in such a way that instances drawn from the training data, such as $( x ^ { 1 } , y ^ { 1 } ) , ( x ^ { 2 } , y ^ { 2 } ) , \; \ldots ( x ^ { n } , y ^ { n } )$ , are introduced to the learning algorithm until the latter finds the set of optimal parameters (of the function $g )$ that minimizes the total loss. As a result of this optimization process, the parameters of the function g are fixed by the learning algorithm, thus fixing this function as the ML model of the sought mapping relationship. The ML optimization process underlies the inductive character of ML model construction, in that it consists in generalizing from the input-output relations in the training data (found by the learning algorithm) to a model (namely an ML model) that can be used to determine the input-output relations in previously unseen data sets, which have the same characteristics as the training data.

Loss function is used to quantify the loss incurred due to incorrect predictions (such as misclassifications) made during the training process. What is called training error is defined to be the sum of losses over the individual input-output instances classified during the training. For example, in binary classification tasks, classification classes are usually marked as positive and negative. While true positives and negatives are correct outcomes, false positives and negatives are erroneous outcomes. Since training error is concerned with the construction of an ML model, it can be regarded as an indication of the error-proneness of an ML model based on its performance on the training data. In this sense, the extent of training error can be taken to indicate the extent of inductive risk built into the model during its construction. Here, inductive risk can be understood as arising from the possibility that the outcomes of the model could turn out to be erroneous to varying extents due to the inductive character of ML model construction (Douglas, 2000). This means that minimization of training error during ML optimization serves to minimize the inductive risk built into an ML model (Karaca, 2021).

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">1 See Alpaydin, 2010 for other types of ML.</span></small>

## 16.3 Value-Ladenness in ML Modelling

Accepting a particular model also means accepting its potentially erroneous outcomes and thus facing the potential consequences of those errors. Securing an optimal balance in the performance of a model is an important aspect of model construction. In this quest, modelers are expected to take account of not only epistemic values but also ethical and other societal values in their practice concerning modelling (Winsberg, 2012; Karaca, 2021; Schmidt, 2025; Ratti, 2025). This is mainly because it is not possible for them to provide the relevant stakeholders with value-free information regarding the constructed models and let them deal with the social implications of these models (Parker & Winsberg, 2018). As a result, ML modelers are forced to move beyond the value-free ideal of knowledge production when engaging in model practices. What constitutes objectivity, according to the value-free ideal of knowledge discovery, is the active exclusion of social values from the inferential aspects of science (Reiss & Sprenger, 2020). This means that only epistemic values should be allowed when making inferences about which models to accept. In this regard, Martin Carrier (2013) suggested that epistemic values play both what he calls significance and confirmation roles in the process of knowledge production. In this section, we will suggest that this two-fold role equally holds for social values in the practice of societally relevant modelling.

Even in the idea of a value-free knowledge pursuit, societal values are accepted to play a role in the external significance requirements of modelling. First, both epistemic and societal values play important roles in the selection of modeling problems to pursue (Longino, 1990). The extent to which a societal goal is accurately reflected in a model depends on the influence of relevant societal values (Diekmann & Peterson, 2013). Therefore, some models are influenced, and ought to be influenced, by social values. Second, the way in which the knowledge is put to use in society requires the consideration of societal values. Third, both epistemic and societal values place direct limitations on methodological options. Societal ML models are implemented as solutions to directly address and analyze societal problems. This involves choices about how to define and frame a problem and thereby its solution.

As the previous section has shown, optimization is key to ML modeling. Optimization is generally regarded as something instrumentally valuable rather than inherently valuable. This means that optimization is not valuable in itself, but rather is valued for what it brings about. It is in this sense that modelers share an overall perspective on design as an exercise in optimization (Franssen et al., 2023). The technical requirements for most modelling problems do not explicitly prescribe what should be optimized. In the context of societal ML modelling, social and epistemic judgments are thus needed to justify the optimal performance of ML models (Basu, 2020; Dobbe et al., 2020; Wong, 2020). What to optimize for is a directly valueladen question when taking account of significance requirements. Social influences on goal and problem framing of a public issue have bearing on the assumptions underlying an ML model and directly influence the representation of public issues. While technical requirements on ML models cannot always be endorsed because of epistemic and social motivations (Ratti & Graves, 2021), these requirements do impact the outcomes of ML models and this way they have epistemic and social repercussions.

Confirmative requirements help in assessing how well a model can be confirmed by the evidence available given its underlying assumptions and uncertainties. In the light of error and associated inductive risk, there are several types of uncertainty to consider here, namely data uncertainty, structural model uncertainty, and parameter uncertainty (Winsberg, 2012). The informational content of data is often regarded as fixed and context independent. However, this is an oversimplification of the data component in scientific inquiry, as even what is called raw data is already processed and gathered with a specific goal in mind (Leonelli, 2019). To truly understand the representational capacities of data, it is important to distinguish data about a phenomenon from the phenomenon itself (Woodward & Bogen, 1988). While data does not provide direct access to or the representation of the phenomena, it sets the evidential space within which phenomena are identified (Leonelli, 2019). In this sense, it is unknowable if all data points and features are included, which causes data uncertainty in the modelling process. Data uncertainty may lead to under or non-representation of issues, characteristics, events, or groups of people.

Each model brings different auxiliary assumptions on the underlying relationships of the data. These assumptions lay in structural model choices, resulting in structural model uncertainty. The same model structure will make different predictions for different values of the parameters. Parameters and thresholds bear assumptions on the weight and significance of different features and set the boundaries that balance the outcome of a model. It is often highly uncertain about what the best values for many of these parameters are, thus resulting in parameter uncertainty. Data uncertainty bears on both parameter uncertainty and structural uncertainty, in that it acts as input and thereby affecting our ability to judge the accuracy of our parameters and our model structures. ML models can be seen as optimal estimation models that are aimed to map accurate relations onto social phenomena under investigation. ML involves the ability to generalize from past experiences to deal with new situations related to those experiences. As a result, ML models require various assumptions, including idealizations and simplifications.

The assumptions made in ML modelling processes can cause value-laden structural and paratemer uncertainties that manifest as uncertainties in model predictions. As in the context of scientific models, the evidence never suffices to completely prove or disprove an ML model. As a result, what serves as sufficient evidence as well as what seems to be the best ML model in a given societal context becomes a matter of judgment related to the uncertainties in model predictions. This is why modelers aim to quantify this type of uncertainty, and this can be seen as an effort to quantify inductive risk (Karaca, 2021). In this regard, model choices reflect balances of inductive risk, and models are being optimized to particular purposes and thus to particular metrics of success (Winsberg, 2012).

## 16.4 Ethical-Epistemic Coupledness in Modelling

The framework for coupled ethical-epistemic analysis is conceptually developed by Nancy Tuana (2013) to advance interdisciplinary collaboration in scientific knowledge production. Interdisciplinary practices give space for reflection on both epistemic and social issues that are typically intertwined. She states that this type of analysis should lead to trustworthy scientific practice and thus better science. First, because it advances knowledge by building on current knowledge. Second, because it leads to scientific research that better benefits society. Most concretely, it broadens our understanding of the types of value decisions that are entrenched in research models and methods, offering resources for identifying the ethical implications of research decisions, and providing a lens for identifying the questions that are ignored, under-examined, and rendered invisible.

The focus here is not only on the ethical aspects of the scientific research process itself, but rather on the ethical issues external to the production of scientific research as well as on the ethical values embedded in the production of scientific knowledge (Tuana, 2013). A coupled ethical-epistemic analysis will provide a more interdisciplinary approach that links procedural ethics, but especially extrinsic and intrinsic ethical issues closer together with the epistemic issues under investigation. Katikireddi and Valles (2015) reformulated Tuana’s account through a set of questions concerning the choice of variables. They used this analysis to examine the interplay between the ethical and epistemic challenges related to the choice of variables in the practice of health public research. Valles et al. (2019) extended the scope of the foregoing framework’s applicability so as to include “research practices” through the following set of questions:

Q1. What are the research practices’ strengths and weaknesses for evidence gathering and analysis?

Q2. What are the research practices’ ethical strengths and weaknesses?

Q3. How will the research practices’ strengths and weaknesses for evidence gathering and analysis affect ethical issues?

Q4. How will the research practices’ ethical strengths and weaknesses affect evidence gathering and analysis? (Ibid., 270–271)

In this analysis, Q1 and Q2 respectively concern epistemic and ethical features, while Q3 and Q4 jointly concern the interplay between epistemic and ethical features, namely how epistemic features affect ethical features (Q3), and vice versa (Q4). The “epistemic” concerns the requirements set for the knowledge-production processes as well as the judgments made concerning the quality of the produced knowledge. The coupledness of the ethical and epistemic makes it possible to conceptualize the epistemic and ethical value influences on models and the insights they produce, as being connected, rather than as being two separate factors that independently shape the model’s capacity for knowledge production. They are linked and thus mutually shaping. Epistemic strengths and weaknesses give rise to ethical strengths and weaknesses and vice versa. Some of the dynamics therein are more conceptual than causal (Valles et al., 2019). Coupledness can then also be defined more philosophically, as it points out that in a conceptual sense, features of one type (epistemic or ethical) can be altered by features of the other type without being caused by them (Valles et al., 2019). In ML modelling, this primarily means combining the context of model use with the various aspects of modelling, including data-uncertainty, model performance, structural model uncertainty and parameter uncertainty, and thereby linking these aspects to the management of inductive risk.

## 16.5 Societal-Epistemic Coupled Analysis Applied to ML Modeling Practices

We will now turn to an elaboration of how the above coupledness framework can be specifically applied in the context of public ML modelling practices, while addressing concerns related to value-ladenness and management of inductive risk. A coupled ethical-epistemic analysis can be conducted in advance as well as in retrospective by answering the following questions as paraphrased based on Valles et al. (2019). To this end, we will first respectively look into the societal and epistemic dimensions of the ML modelling practices. Here again, we note that by societal we mean all kinds of social considerations including those that are ethical. In this context, model construction and model validation are two main epistemic activities whose strengths and weaknesses are to be assessed. Therefore, we shall adapt Q1 above by specifying “research practices” as “ML research practices” and accordingly by replacing “evidence gathering and analysis” with “model construction and model validation” as well as “ethical” with “societal.” Moreover, since we suggest that not only ethical but also societal strengths and weaknesses need to be considered, we shall modify Q1 and Q2 in such a way that they read as follows:

Q1. What are the ML research practices’ strengths and weaknesses concerning model construction and model validation?

Q2. What are the ML research practices’ societal strengths and weaknesses?

Accordingly, Q3 and Q4 read as follows:

Q3. How do the ML research practices’ strengths and weaknesses concerning model construction and model validation affect societal issues?

Q4. How do the ML research practices’ societal strengths and weaknesses affect model construction and model validation?

Concerning Q1, we suggest that the epistemological weaknesses and strengths of ML research practices lie in the extent to which the methodological choices concerning model construction and validation are justified. Like other types of scientific models, ML models are constructed and validated based on certain methodological choices, which are in turn justified on the basis of certain methodological assumptions made by the developers of these models and on the basis of the existing limitations of the chosen models. This means that ML research practices concerning model validation and construction are epistemically strong or weak to the extent that their underlying methodological choices are justified by the modelers. The previous discussion indicates that the modelers need to make certain methodological choices to specify the following elements of ML model construction: training data, hypothesis set, learning algorithm, loss (error) function, optimization procedure (including utilities assigned to different types of errors). Similarly, they also need to make certain methodological choices to specify the following elements of model validation: validation data and procedure, and performance metric to be used to measure the predictive performance of the model.

Concerning Q2 above, we suggest that ML research practices’ societal strengths and weaknesses are related to the social constraints imposed on ML models by the particular contexts in which these models are (to be) used. This means that the extent to which ML research practices are societally strong or weak depends on whether the constraints concerning the phases of model construction and validation are correctly identified by the modelers prior to these phases. Since Q2 is aimed to isolate social aspects from epistemic aspects, it is not directly concerned with the extent these methodological constraints are satisfied by the models. This issue will be addressed in what follows.

The coupledness of the epistemic and societal aspects of ML research practices can be analyzed by addressing Q3 and Q4 above. Q3 is concerned with how epistemically unjustified methodological choices concerning model construction and model validation can result in societal issues, such as unacceptably large errors in model predictions used in high-stake decision contexts, e.g. medical context, and biased or discriminatory decisions based on those predictions, e.g. credit applications. Q4 is concerned with the kinds of methodological constraints entailed by the social constraints imposed by the contexts in which ML models are to be used. The latter type of constraints need to be translated by the modelers into methodological constraints underlying ML models. These methodological constraints may concern the intended use of the model; the inclusion or exclusion of different types of data—such as datasets associated with underrepresented groups or personal characteristics; the choice of utilities assigned to false positives and false negatives for optimization purposes; and the selection of a metric for model validation.

Answering Q3 serves to identify the societal issues arising from unjustified methodological choices, while answering Q4 serves to identify the methodological constraints imposed by the contexts-of-use dependent social constraints. It is worth noting that answering Q3 and Q4 requires in the first place answering Q1 and Q2, as the foregoing methodological choices and constraints can be identified through answering the latter questions.

The foregoing societal-epistemic coupledness analysis can be used to carry out an inductive risk analysis. This analysis can be used by the relevant stakeholders of an ML model to effectively manage inductive risk associated with its practical applications, or to understand if the developers of the model have effectively managed the inductive risk built into the model during its construction.

Since ML models are typically used for societal applications, an inductive risk analysis in such contexts is concerned with the social consequences of the risk of erring in accepting and using these models for their intended uses (Rudner, 1953; Douglas, 2000). As has been argued above, their contexts of use impose social constraints on these models. There will be social consequences arising from the failure of the ML models to meet these methodological constraints. The extent of inductive risk will be mainly concerned with these social consequences in the sense that whether the ML models are to be accepted and uses for their intended purposes will depend on the extent to which these models satisfy the methodological constraints to be imposed by their social constraints. Therefore, the question that is relevant to determine the extent of inductive risk in a specific application of a ML model is the following:

To what extent do the methodological choices underlying ML model construction and validation satisfy the methodological constraints related to inductive risk?

Since the methodological constraints and choices are identified through the coupledness analysis outlined in Q1–Q4, this analysis provides the basis for answering the foregoing question.

The above question serves to determine the extent of inductive risk. Its management is a related but different question. Users can manage inductive risk through the value judgments they make (Rudner, 1953; Douglas, 2000). That is to say that given some form of evidence, they make certain methodological choices (including accepting or rejecting a given model) when they decide that they can (not) afford taking the inductive risk, i.e., the risk that the model’s predictions are false. This also indicates that management of inductive risk is mainly about assessing the severity of the inductive risk associated with the methodological choices. This assessment is always made (by users) with respect to both the epistemic and societal values that they hold. Therefore, the management of inductive risk requires in the first place determining those values and associated value judgments. This leads to the following question:

What epistemic and societal values, and associated value judgments, held by users underlie the methodological choices involved in ML model construction and validation?

The severity of the inductive risk would differ with respect to different values hold by users. This is mainly due to the fact that different values may clash with each other about the severity of the inductive risk. In other words, the severity of the inductive risk may weigh differently for different values. This means that an effective management of inductive risk requires users to understand how values clash in the assessment of its severity. Therefore, the following question needs to be answered:

What trade-offs exist among the different values relevant to methodological decisions in model construction and validation?

As pointed out above, users can manage inductive risk through value judgments they make. If different values (hold by users) are relevant to the methodological choices, then the following question needs to be answered to understand how the values of users bear upon the methodological choices:

What value judgments do users make to guide their methodological choices in accordance with value trade-offs?

## 16.6 Applying the Societal-Epistemic Coupledness Framework to ML in Practice

In Amsterdam, citizens can report issues that take place in the public space of the city. These issues are so called micro-events that concern a small geographical area and only affect a limited number of citizens. They are linked to nuisance in public space, e.g. a loose tile, a streetlight that is not working, a non-functioning container, bars making too much noise or a fallen tree on the street. These cases fall under the responsibility of different municipal departments. An ML classifier model is used to detect the class of a report and route it to the correct department (Sukel et al., 2019). The ML model fulfills a small but crucial role in the process from report submission to report closing. After a citizen report has been submitted, the classifier ML model automatically classifies the report, while sending it to the right department. The officers of the specific department follow up on the report. This model is implemented by the city-government of Amsterdam, and it thereby plays an important public role in facilitating the correct and timely response towards issues in public space.<sup>2</sup> As such, its epistemic qualities are intertwined with a multitude of societal considerations as we will argue in this section by performing a societalepistemic coupled analysis of this case.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">2 See the following URL through which the citizens can submit reports to be processed by the ML model in question: [https://algoritmes.overheid.nl/nl/algoritme/gm0363/21579514/meldingen-openbare-ruimt](https://algoritmes.overheid.nl/nl/algoritme/gm0363/21579514/meldingen-openbare-ruimt) The same model is currently used by other Dutch municipalities.</span></small>

## 16.6.1 Introducing the Case and Structuring the Coupledness Analysis

Societal-epistemic coupled analysis may give us a better grip on the impact of a model on its social context. A focus on societal or epistemic values alone cannot cover the inductive societal risks of ML models. Looking at how exactly both kinds of values are mutually influencing each other brings new tools to better understand the epistemic status attributed to these models in society. To this end, we will draw upon the analysis we presented earlier by revisiting each of its underlying questions in turn. It is worth noting that the discussion in what follows in part depends on personal communications with individuals who were involved in the design and management of the ML model in question.

Q1. What are the ML research practices’ strengths and weaknesses concerning model construction and model validation?

Since Q1 is concerned with both the phase of model construction and the phase of validation, we will address this question for each phase separately.

**Model Construction** The ML model in question is a textual classification model that was constructed (or trained) by using citizen reports as training data (Sukel et al., 2019, p. 1460). Over 500,000 citizen reports were divided in two parts, i.e. data for training and data for validation separately. The use of such a training data makes the performance of the model for a specific issue highly dependent on previous representation of that issue in the training data. This is justified by the expected similarity of context in which the reports were produced as well as how they will be produced in the future. The reporting behavior in previous years as well as the recurring issues in public space are expected to be relatively similar.

For the training (or optimization) of the ML model, what is called term frequency–inverse document frequency technique was used (Ibid., p. 1458). This technique determines weights for each word. These weights show how unique they are for the specific citizen report compared to the overall collection. It aims to define how important a keyword is for a specific class (or category). This makes it suitable for classes that have very specific words describing them, as is the case with citizen reports. A word like “the” will get a low weight, and a word as “garbage” will get a higher weight. In addition, a multi-class probabilistic classification model based on logistic regression is used to classify these reports. This means that this classification model is a classifier with multiple classes. During its implementation in 2019, the classifier consisted of 8 classes and more than 50 sub-classes.<sup>3</sup>

The model was trained such that it can perform as good as possible on each class. On the other hand, a difference exists in how well the classifier works for each class. Words—understood here to include phrases—which are less precise will be less accurate in their classification. The more unique the word, the better, since every class has specific wordings. ‘Speeding Boat’ for example, does not have many previous reports, but very precise wording. New or underrepresented events will perform less. For example, ‘processionary caterpillar in trees’ and ‘Covid19 houseparty’ are more difficult for the model to classify correctly, since not many previous examples have come across. The learning algorithm was tasked with finding the balance among which the overall accuracy across classes was the highest. This threshold was partly determined based on the notion that the threshold should enable the best possible average performance for each class. Probability proved optimal at a 40% threshold, meaning that there had to be at least 40% certainty on the assigned class being the correct class. If this percentage is less, the classification is being processed manually by employees of the Service Center.

**Model Validation** The model performs better on some classes than the others, because the words were represented more often in the training data or the wordings were very precise and therefore easy to be classified by the model. That is why an optimal balance between classes is important. Therefore, a balance of recall and precision is sought throughout all classes (Ibid., p. 1460). F1 score was used to evaluate the classification performance of the ML model, because the imbalance among the multiple classes had to be considered. F1 score is a metric (ranging between 0 and 1) that takes into account uneven class distributions and works well if false positives and false negatives do not have similar costs (Karaca, 2021). F1 score was calculated for every class as well as for the entire model performance (Sukel et al., 2019, Fig. 5).<sup>4</sup> F1 score of the entire model performance was found to be close to 0.7.

The issues related to the model’s performance per class are taken into consideration through manual corrections and periodically retraining of the model. Citizens have provided the past report on which the model was trained, but they do not provide perfect reports as input. They submit reports that are incomplete, have spelling mistakes, lack language skills or provide excessive information. In addition, this input is also not perfectly distributed among societal groups and neighborhoods. The number of citizens that are more or less likely to submit reports to the municipality differs across neighborhoods and socio-economic factors in society. It is important to take account of this lack of diversity. Not doing so would give rise to a problem of lack of representativeness of certain groups within the training data, but also in the validation data.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">3 See the URL: [https://medium.com/maarten-sukel/how-to-use-machine-learning-for-the-classification-of-citizen-service-requests-b71159a85f36](https://medium.com/maarten-sukel/how-to-use-machine-learning-for-the-classification-of-citizen-service-requests-b71159a85f36)</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">4 Precision is the ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to the total positives, this relates to a low false positive rate. It shows how many labelled reports are classified correctly. Recall is the ratio of all correctly predicted observations to the total of observation. It indicates how many reports belonging to a particular class were actually labelled correctly. F1 score is defined to be the harmonic mean of precision and recall.</span></small>

Q2. What are the ML research practices’ social strengths and weaknesses?

**User Context of the Model** At its core, the ML model is in place to ensure an optimal internal process for allocating reports to the right department. As such, the ML model seems to primarily facilitate the effective management of the public space, while also improving its livability. The main criteria for success here are improved service towards citizens, limiting follow-up time of reports and limiting the number of mistakes. All in all, the collaboration between departments had to be improved upon, resulting in a better service towards the city. The identified goals are social, as they the sense that they prioritize usefulness over knowledge discovery.

**Changing Priorities Over Time and Across Users** Civil servants came by with requests for the prioritization of specific keywords or classes related to their specific department. Ideally, finding the optimal balance between which words link to which classes is a task for the learning algorithm. Initially, the reporting system did not work well enough specifically for street lighting. Therefore, street-lighting reports had to be prioritized over other classes, in order to increase the feeling of safety in the city, which was a political choice. Reports concerning individuals do not occur often, so have less frequency, but are crucial to quickly follow up on. However, a report referring to confused, lost or harmed people must be classified correctly 100% of the time, in order to prevent dangerous situations for those involved.

**Ambiguity in Purpose** Citizen reports sometimes seem to function as indirect signals for civil servants across different domains. They help to identify urban issues and gain actionable intelligence about objects on the street (Sukel et al., 2020). The model implicitly seems to move from a classification tool to a signaling device. However, only a small number of citizens actually report issues in the public space. It should be safeguarded that the servicing of the entire city does not get customized solely to the needs of reporters. From a social perspective, this risks the exclusion of certain types of stakeholders and phenomena that are not included in the reports.

## Q3. How do the ML research practices’ strengths and weaknesses concerning model construction and model validation affect social issues?

There are several aspects that link to data, model and parameter uncertainties affecting social issues. Regarding the accuracy of classifications, there will always be some classes that perform slightly better than others. It was seen as the model’s task to find an optimal balance among accuracy of keywords and classes, by setting the parameters accordingly. A modeler can prioritize the overall performance of the model or manually guide its performance towards specific classes within the limits of this model. This is where room for choice arises and where requirements of confirmation are relevant. While the ML model’s calculations determined the balance among the classes, two were prioritized on normative grounds, as shall be discussed in Q4 below.

**Training-Data and Biased Performance** How well a specific class performs in terms of accuracy relies on the frequency of keywords in past reports, as was earlier explained. It is important to note here is that prior reports reflect a particular language and education-level. Foreign languages, lower language skills and individual levels of trust towards governments also cause limitations for equal representation. Moreover, some citizens seem more willing to submit a report to the municipality and submit requests sooner and more frequently. These characteristics can be traced back to over- and underrepresentation of certain groups within the training data.

**Use of Output in Public Context** The topics that find their way into statistical overviews often serve as indication for decision making across institutions and departments. The fact that reports concerning garbage on the street have decreased in a particular neighborhood does not necessarily mean that the amount of garbage on the street has actually decreased there. When fewer complaints come in, it could also mean that people are tired of complaining. No reports do not mean no issues. On the other hand, receiving more reports can also be a result of better service. When making a report is effective, people are likely to do it more. It is therefore important to consider reports as a question for help from citizens, not as an accurate representation of the factual state of events.

Q4. How do the ML research practices’ social strengths and weaknesses affect model construction and model validation?

In the context of the current ML model, because of an erroneous classification, a wrong department will receive the public issue report, resulting in a delay of the issue being resolved. As mentioned, one can prioritize the overall performance of the model or manually guide its performance towards specific classes. This system was fully reliant on the self-learning capabilities of the ML model. It is the model’s purpose to find an optimal balance among accuracy of keywords and classes. Two expectations were made based on social grounds, as shall be described.

**Zero Uncertainty Tolerance** The accuracy of reports involving people was prioritized over the overall performance of the model in order to ensure fast intervention. Reports concerning people do not occur often, so have less frequency, but are incredibly important. Reports referring to confused, lost or harmed people have to be classified with almost full accuracy in order to prevent dangerous situations for those involved. As mentioned, underrepresented events or new events (low frequency) have been harder to classify correctly. As a result, new trends might be missed in the beginning, resulting in a delayed action on new and upcoming public issues.

**Political Priority** Initially, the reporting system did not work well enough specifically for street lighting. Therefore, street lighting reports had to be prioritized over other classes, in order to increase the feeling of safety in the city. This was mentioned as a political priority that directly influenced the optimization priorities of model development, which may conflict with the developer’s aim to reach a statistical optimum. Likewise, civil servants requested the prioritization of specific keywords or classes relevant to their departments. Ideally however, finding the optimal balance between which words link to which classes is a task for the learning algorithm. This is why no other interventions were made based on employee preferences.

## 16.6.2 Inductive Risk and Societal-Epistemic Trade-offs

The purpose of the ML model is to find an optimal balance among the accuracy of keywords and classes, by setting the parameters accordingly. This is where room for choice arises and where requirements of confirmation are relevant. Uncertainties that arise here indicate inductive risks associated with a model, in that uncertainties give rise to potential errors (false positive and false negatives) that have potential consequences.

A trade-off necessarily occurs between the entire model performance and between every separate class, which provides the opportunity to judge and balance the societal consequences of these errors. The F1 score was used for this evaluation to take account of the imbalances among multiple classes.

What is seen as most important within the scope of cleaner and safer streets more specifically, may differ from time to time. Sub-priorities could relate to societal problems concerning trash, streetlights, or tourism. Stakeholders have different perspectives on what is useful. In this sense, the model has multiple meanings as a tool for optimization.

With an overall F1 score that is close to 0.7, the textual classifier ML model works well for most issue-reports. The classification and the performances concerning each class bear coupled social-epistemic implications because their focus determines which sub-topics receive signaling and how departments act based on these signals. In what follows, we shall identify the trade-offs that exist among the different values. This provides further insight into the value judgments that are made by users to determine their methodological choices in accordance with the value trade-offs.

**Overall Accuracy vs Care** Care is a social value and refers to valuing what is necessary for the health, welfare, maintenance, and protection of someone or something. In the use-context of the ML-model, care requires a high degree of accuracy for one specific class of reports, namely that any report containing the word “person” or “confused person” needed to be classified almost fully correctly in order to ensure fast intervention. Reports concerning people do not occur often, so have less frequency, but are crucial in terms of its social consequences concerning care. As a result, the accuracy of the model concerning reports involving confused persons was prioritized over other classes and thus over the overall accuracy of the model.<sup>5</sup> This means that while the model performs with great accuracy on one specific class, its overall accuracy for all other classes is sacrificed.

**Overall Accuracy vs Public Safety** Due to public safety, which is a social value, the class of broken streetlight is also prioritized in such a way that a predictive accuracy that is less than the overall predictive accuracy of the model is not accepted for this class. Initially, the reporting system did not work well enough specifically for street lighting. Therefore, street-lighting reports had to be prioritized, to increase the feeling of safety in the city. This was mentioned as a political priority that directly influenced the optimization priorities of model development, which may conflict with the developers’ aim to reach a statistical optimum.

**Overall Accuracy vs Organizational Preferences** In navigating the priorities between overall accuracy and organizational class preference, the main focus of the ML modelling process leaned towards optimizing the overall accuracy across classes, rather than facilitating specific optimizations regarding specific classes. Many specific requests or preferences were shared with the developing team. These requests came from a wide range of policy departments working with the ML-model. Given its operational context, the construction of the model underscored practical effectiveness as a priority. Many classes already existed for a long time within the process of the organization. However, this approach risks engendering a “class bias,” where labeling tendencies conform to established classes and objectives (Barocas & Selbst, 2018, p. 677–678), potentially compromising result accuracy. Classes (labels) for the ML model were constructed in dialogue with the departments of the municipality as the users of the model. A designated class manager oversees this iterative process, aligning classes with existing municipal processes and departments. Nevertheless, what remained decisive in the model development and evaluation process was the overall accuracy of the model across all classes. This in turn limited the possibility for interventions based on department or class specific preferences in general. Exceptions were made only for the classes of ‘confused people’ and ‘street lights.’ For all other classes, the optimization of the overall accuracy was prioritized over class specific accuracy optimizations.

The aforementioned trade-offs need to be managed in ways acceptable by the relevant stakeholders. The current model is accepted as sufficiently optimal by the municipality, since the harm of errors for reports on people has been mitigated and the bias towards certain neighborhoods can be limited by other process interventions. The first one being a human in the loop approach, by having a helpdesk team ready to tackle any wrongly classified report, also available by phone. The second one being to also drive independent service routes with municipal vehicles, and not only respond to areas with a high reporting rate. The third one being a ‘classmanager’ that represents different departments when they would manually improve something about a class. This manager speaks to the ML modelers to see what is possible. Finally and importantly, special attention has been paid to training the

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">5 This information is based on personal communications with the designers of the model.</span></small>

ML model on different specific language levels of citizens to reduce unintentional performance bias towards different language levels. The classification primarily bears on social-epistemic implications because their focus determines which subtopics receive signaling and how departments act based on these signals and who benefits from this service.

The above analysis demonstrates that various relevant trade-offs exist between epistemic and societal values in the context of the present case study. This indicates the societal-epistemic coupledness aspects of the inductive risk and its management in this context. Here, the societal and epistemic dimensions are coupled in the trade-off between statistical accuracy and care through the justification that reports concerning confused, lost, or harmed individuals must be classified correctly 100% of the time. Similarly, the trade-off between accuracy and public safety represents the societal-epistemic coupledness of the acceptability of certain inductive risks over others. The trade-off between accuracy and practical effectiveness, the latter being a societal value, directly effects the overall understanding of public issues that can be produced by the model. Importantly, which classes are added determines what you optimize in the city, which becomes coupled when you let the managerial structure of an organization determine the labels that you use to classify issues in public space. Finally, due to variations in language use, language skills, and reporting behavior, groups submitting deviating reports are likely to consist of people who can often be linked to similar neighborhoods or backgrounds. Over time, particular classes will continuously be processed slower or without corrections. They will eventually perform less. The opposite is true for classes that are processed faster over time. Therefore, inductive risks and the potential consequences of error are unequally distributed among those affected by the model.

## 16.7 Stakeholder Perspectives and the Management of Inductive Risk

Uncertainties, which are inherent to ML modelling, have different levels of acceptability, giving rise to the need for responsible management of inductive risk in ML modelling. The goals we assign to ML models are shaped by societal and political perspectives that carry both epistemic and societal value judgments. Epistemic values are central to the assessment of how much uncertainty we can afford to take. Societal values concern the acceptability of such uncertainty, and this is where inductive risk considerations arise. It requires reflection on the level of uncertainty acceptable to stakeholders, as well as on which kinds of errors they are willing to tolerate. Constant negotiations concerning what is optimal manifest on the level of model features as well as on model outcomes through confirmative requirements that are related to inductive risks and associated possible errors. False negatives and false positives are unequally distributed among social groups, meaning that these errors do not necessarily entail equal costs for all stakeholders. As the case study has shown, this results in inductive risks and their potential consequences varying across stakeholder groups.

Stakeholders can co-determine decisions concerning specific trade-offs in managing inductive risk. Negotiations may also take place through the articulation of significance requirements in the context of use. The epistemic status of ML models as knowledge producers in public decision-making processes should not be regarded as merely instrumental, nor as objective statistical tools for automation. Since ML models—and the knowledge they produce—are societally and epistemically coupled, the inductive risks associated with their use will be prioritized differently by different stakeholders. This raises the question of who has—or should have—the authority to make such decisions.

We suggest that the inclusion of relevant stakeholders is necessary to justify the use of ML models in public domains. This is because stakeholders may evaluate inductive risks differently, as their potential consequences can vary significantly across social groups.

This asks for normative and value-laden decisions, as there is no common measure for weighting inductive risks and potential consequences. The second reason is that the moral, political and epistemic standards we set for ML models as knowledge producing tools are related to the collective meaning we assign to such methods. The present case study has demonstrated that ML models serve to implicitly negotiate relations among different stakeholder groups. Likewise, the framing of the optimization goals for both models has been subject to multiple formulations. The goals and perspectives that underlay these models is not static. When straightforward answers on how to arrive at acceptable principles of conduct are lacking, we speak of normative indeterminacies (Dobbe et al., 2020). When city governments, as authorities and democratic institutions, use ML models to produce insights there is a need for democratic dissent mechanisms for such indeterminacies (Daniels & Sabin, 2008; Binns, 2018; Wong, 2020). As such, public participation could strengthen reliable and responsible tools for public knowledge-production and decision-making.

What serves as sufficiently optimal for the performance of an ML model should be determined on both epistemic and societal grounds. Depending on which stakeholders are concerned, a less accurate model may better align with societal needs. Value-laden choices navigate how one handles the uncertainty of a model, its potential errors, the desirability and severity of such errors and the acceptance of the available evidence. Model-choices reflect particular balances of inductive risk and models are being optimized for particular purposes towards particular metrics of success (Winsberg, 2012). This means that while possible errors are unavoidable, we can influence both the types of errors that are likely to occur and their extent through our modeling decisions. These decisions represent a negotiation of different priorities to arrive at the most optimal tool needed for a particular goal or quest. Judging a model’s optimality requires making it intelligible and acceptable to specific groups within particular contexts. There is not one stable, single, essential characteristic that brings a fixed predictable power or agency to these models. Rather, the focus should be on the set of relations that enable an

ML model to be brought into being (Neyland, 2016). The interpretations of a model will be different for different stakeholders across society (Seaver, 2017). This stems from varying interpretations of the data, the phenomena and the outcome among stakeholders (Erasmus et al., 2020). Therefore, ML models would need to fulfill diverse explanatory requirements, as different stakeholders are likely to pose different kinds of questions (Zednik, 2021).

## 16.8 Conclusions

In this chapter, we have shown that incorporating philosophy through the lens of coupled societal and epistemological questions cannot only deepen our understanding of the values embedded in ML models used in public decision-making, but also improve the management of inductive risks by involving diverse stakeholder perspectives. This approach will unveil the value and limits of ML modelling as a knowledge producing practice that is part of the public domain. The ML model in the presented case study is geared towards increased livability in Amsterdam’s urban environment. This model is concerned with the objects in public space, which only indirectly affect people’s lives in the city. The case study has shown that using ML models as tools for knowledge production and decision-making in governmental processes raises not only the question of what kind of knowledge base we embed in these tools in our cities, but also what kinds of moral norms or virtues should be programmed into them.

According to the concept of inductive risk, when accepting a ML model, its uncertainties, and thus its potential errors, are also indirectly accepted. These errors are likely to affect particular groups in the city differently. As such it will always be the same kinds of people, often linked to particular neighborhoods, who live through such systems without any problems, as in the presented case study. Simultaneously, it is the same kind of people that always fall in the potential errorzone of uncertainty, or that fail to comply with such a system. This is closely linked to coupled judgments of inductive risk. Specific potential errors may be judged as highly undesirable because of the social evaluation of their consequences. Rather than treating the epistemic model-performance and its social consequences as separate entities, the norms we hold for each of them should be seen as coupled. Our treatment of the case study, based on this analysis, demonstrates that like epistemic values, societal values play a key role in the production and evaluation of the model’s epistemic qualities and potential consequences. The coupled societalepistemic analysis presented in this chapter places societal values at the center of the evaluation of model performance and outcomes. It thus suggests that assessing optimal functioning of ML models requires epistemic and societal value judgments, as they are coupled and mutually influence each-other. This means that accepting ML model performance as sufficient means accepting their epistemic output and both direct and indirect societal consequences.

The societal-epistemic coupledness analysis shows that the knowledge generated by societal ML models is not neutral. Since moral norms are an essential part of a ML model’s appropriate epistemic functioning, what counts as usable knowledge for public decision-making becomes highly political. As a result, the insights to be produced by these models should not be understood and perceived as purely epistemic, but as coupled from the start. Going beyond the epistemic-societal divide will provide new tools to discuss the status we assign to ML models as knowledge producers in public decision-making processes. In such contexts, societal and epistemic aspects are deeply intertwined. For instance, the case study presented in this chapter shows a sensitivity to the consequences of the model’s potential errors, as the cost of error is not seen as neutral towards those affected. This suggests that involving citizens more in the goal and outcomes of ML models may reduce uncertainties concerning the moral and epistemic judgments of these modelpractices. Without such collective insights about public issues and phenomena in the real-world, these interpretations and interventions are highly rhetorical. Hence, the current analysis offers fertile ground for more democratically epistemic practices that promote transparency and strengthen the reliability of knowledge production.
