**Chapter 21**

# Artificial Intelligence in Climate Science: From Machine Learning to Neural Networks

![](images/page_470_image_2.jpg)

**Greg Lusk**

**Abstract** This chapter analyzes the extent to which the introduction of NNs into climate science might change its methodology and the way we understand climate science epistemology. It proceeds by examining areas of climate research already heavily influenced by artificial intelligence in the form of machine learning, and then considers areas of research where the introduction of neutral networks would be novel. The goal of this chapter is to bring out the structure of the extant debates in the philosophy of climate science and demonstrate how they might change with the introduction of neural nets. Overall, this chapter shows that if there is a revolution coming anytime soon, it is unlikely to take the form of a wholesale replacement of theory-based climate models by data-driven neural nets. Rather, the analysis here demonstrates that there is likely to be further hybridization of theory-driven models with data-driven NNs in a way that trades some intelligibility or representational accuracy for computational efficiency.

## 21.1 Introduction

Climate science has not been spared the enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) exhibited in public discourse since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022. In fact, some pronouncements indicate that the impact on climate science could be drastic. For example, Google’s ex-CEO Eric Schmidt has declared that “With the advent of AI, science is about to become much more exciting—and in some ways unrecognizable,” and specifically discusses AI’s impact on climate science, claiming “The hoped-for revolution in climate modeling” is already underway (Schmidt, 2023). While it is unclear who exactly was doing the hoping that Schmidt refers to, climate scientists have been examining the extent to which artificial intelligence could be used to further their scientific goals. If the tone of recent publications is indicative of the field (e.g. Chantry et al., 2021; Ebert-Uphoff & Hilburn, 2023), there is a high level of excitement that these methods of research can be fruitfully applied to problems in weather and climate research.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">G. Lusk (🖂) Department of Philosophy, Durham University, Durham, UK e-mail: [greg.lusk@durham.ac.uk](mailto:greg.lusk@durham.ac.uk)</span></small>

Whether this excitement will translate into a revolution is unclear, but there are reasons why such a claim looks hyperbolic. After all, since its early days, climate science has been inventive in the way it produces and manages data (Edwards, 2010), and in its modern form, embraces its own distinctive style of big data analysis (see Lloyd et al., 2022). Climate disciplines embraced machine learning (for example, kernel and ‘random forest’ techniques) beginning in the $1 9 9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { s }$ to help with classification tasks arising in the context of remote sensing and the assimilation of observations by numerical weather models. Since then, machine learning (ML) has become “a universal approach” in many areas of climate research (Reichstein et al., 2019, 196). So, if by “revolution” one means integrating AI in the guise of ML into everyday climate research and modeling, then this revolution is 20 or 30 years in the making.

But it is because climate research has long embraced AI in the form of machine learning that it is interesting in the present moment. The recent clamor over AI is not due to the kind of ML techniques that climate science has long employed, rather, the excitement is a product of the success that neural networks (NNs) have shown in accomplishing predictive tasks (see Buckner, 2019).<sup>1</sup> Such NNs have not been widely used in climate science, and thus it makes a good case to examine how NNs might alter research practices. And because climate science has long been a discipline that is comfortable with a broadly empirical-reliabilist epistemic stance, and has continually sought novel ways to leverage data-driven techniques to overcome theoretical and computational shortcomings, it seems ripe for utilizing these NNs.

This chapter analyzes the extent to which the introduction of NNs into climate science might change its methodology and the way we understand climate science epistemology. It proceeds by examining areas of climate research already heavily influenced by AI in the form of ML, and then considers areas of research where the introduction of NNs would be novel. In each area of research, I engage the relevant philosophical analyses of these practices and assess how NNs might impact scientific understanding, explanation, representational transparency, or other epistemically relevant properties. The goal of this chapter is to bring out the structure of the extant debates in the philosophy of climate science and demonstrate how they might change with the introduction of NNs. Overall, this chapter shows that if there is a revolution coming anytime soon, it is unlikely to take the form of a wholesale replacement of theory-based climate models by data-driven NNs. Rather, the analysis here demonstrates that there is likely to be further hybridization of theory-driven models with data-driven NNs in a way that trades some intelligibility or representational accuracy for computational efficiency.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">1 The terms “artificial Intelligence” (AI), “machine Learning” (ML) and “neural network“(NN) are often vague and used imprecisely in recent discourse. In this chapter, NN is the most specific category of the three and I use it to refer to all kinds of neural nets (e.g. convoluted, recurrent, perceptron). I use the term ML to refer to methods of learning that are not NNs, this includes decision trees and Bayesian statistical inference or optimization. I use AI as the broadest category to cover ML, NNs, and other instances of automated pattern recognition when used for inference.</span></small>

## 21.2 Climate Observations and Pseudo-Observations

When it comes to climate science, models get all the attention. However, climate science relies on a whole host of observations, and turning these observations into usable information is one potential area in where NNs might be helpful. The observations that climate science relies upon are diverse. Observations can be gathered from ground-based stations that provide information about temperature or precipitation, but information can also be acquired from ships, ocean buoys, aircraft, and earth-orbiting satellites.<sup>2</sup> Scientists can also learn about conditions of the past from so-called “proxy” sources, like ice cores, tree rings, and pollen found in sediments.

Though there is a wide variety of data available, making that data useful can be difficult. After all, there are certain characteristics that the data have that are not aligned with the information researchers often want to know. For example, researchers are interested in quantities that represent certain regions of the globe, or the entire globe itself, often over long periods of time. Observations, however, are local, only representing one spatial area at one particular point in time. Thus, one may have significant gaps in their data; there may be geographic areas where observations are simply lacking. Furthermore, observations are often made with different instruments with different characteristics that go in and out of service on different lifecycles and have different error profiles. To see the difficulty that climate scientists often face, and how they can leverage AI to overcome it, it is worth examining two methods of obtaining observations in climate science where philosophers have shown particular interest: remote sensing and reanalysis using data assimilation.

## 21.2.1 Observations: Remote Sensing

Oftentimes, scientists are interested in observing areas of the planet that are not easy to access, for example, areas near the poles or areas over remote ocean. To observe these areas over extended periods of time, climate researchers employ various remote sensing devices. These devices can be ground based—positioned in the arctic for example—or placed on satellites, and monitor the atmosphere on a consistent and (if possible) continuous basis.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">2 See Parker (2025) for a more detailed overview.</span></small>

However, remote sensing is itself a complex procedure, one that has already taken advantage of AI. Take, for example, the detection of atmospheric trace gases— which include greenhouse gases and water vapor—in an area. It is often difficult to obtain trace gas measurements through relatively direct measurements. Scientists are interested in the vertical profile of gases, that is, how the gas concentrations change with altitude. To measure this relatively directly, one might use a weather balloon or airplane. But these methods of detection are troublesome: both are expensive, weather dependent, and require significant manual labor. Instead, much of the data on these gases come from remotely installed devices that measure the electromagnetic signature of the gas to infer their vertical concentrations. This method of remote sensing has the advantage of being cheaper, automated, and consistently return results over long periods of time. For example, a spectrometer can be placed in an arctic environment and return trace gas profiles on sunny days for years, often without the intervention of researchers. Such information is crucial for studying air quality, trace gas movement, and for providing estimates of water vapor that are used in research on cloud dynamics and in some climate models.

Extracting information about the profile of trace gases from the readings of devices like spectrometers is surprisingly difficult and computationally expensive. The difficulty is that the electromagnetic information received by many remote sensing devices underdetermines the vertical profile of the gases. Gases have relatively unique electromagnetic signatures, but the atmosphere can influence the way such signatures are detected by the remote sensing device, permitting the signatures run together. Methane, for example, has eight other chemical species whose signature can overlap with its own, for instance, species such as ozone and water vapor. It is thus possible for there to be two or more vertical profiles of trace gases that could have resulted in the same reading by a remote sensing spectrometer. Thus, there is no equation that can use as input the quantified observations of the remote sensing device and return a unique profile of trace gas concentrations. This is called an “inverse problem” by those in the climate science and remote sensing communities.

The solution to the inverse problem of trace gas detection is to forego attempts to find a mathematical relationship between the output of the device and the trace gas profile, and instead, attempt to recreate the observed profile from existing knowledge. This process is called retrieval, and it has long relied on ML algorithms. To perform retrieval, one needs a forward model, that is, a mathematical description of how the spectral information received by the detector is produced. This forward model includes a radiative transfer model—that specifies how radiation related to the gases propagates through the atmosphere—combined with a model of how the detection instrument functions and its error characteristics. Using this forward model, scientists can then produce synthetic instrument readings; what the instrument would have seen given a particular distribution of trace gases. Scientists then initiate a choice procedure. Starting with background knowledge regarding the most likely trace gas profiles, they repeatedly simulate what the detection device would have seen given certain distributions of gases, and then try to match the simulated profile to the one actually detected. This search procedure is often formulated in Bayesian terms and represents the ML component.<sup>3</sup> Essentially, the procedure is seeking to calculate the best estimate of trace gas concentrations, which is defined as the maximum a posteriori solution. To find this solution, scientists define a cost function which seeks to find the minimal difference between the simulated and the actual instrument readings. The cost function is explored algorithmically until the best match is located. Essentially, the profile that results in the best match (i.e. the maximum a posteriori solution) is the reported result of the observation. The algorithm qualifies as ML in the sense that it “learns” what parameters produce the best fitting profile (see Rodgers, 2000; Lusk, 2021).

## 21.2.2 Pseudo-Observations: Data Assimilation

Before discussing how NNs may change the way scientists approach climate observations, it is worth examining another practice central to climate science that relies on very similar algorithms. While remote sensing via retrieval helps provide scientists with a means to obtain data in hard to access areas, from a global perspective, the area that observations cover is still limited. Measuring instruments are, after all, not uniformly located across the globe and have gone in and out of service over the timescales of interest for climate. For climate scientists this presents some difficulty, as their models give global results on a uniform grid that covers the globe. Thus, they would like to have some way to make a like-to-like comparison between their model outputs and observations. There are other modeling needs as well. Weather forecasters use numerical models to analyze future atmospheric states. Their models, however, require initial conditions for each grid point, and the results are relatively sensitive to these conditions. Traditional observations do not typically have the coverage to provide the needed information to initialize the weather forecasting model. What is needed are datasets with uniform global coverage.

To produce these datasets, scientists employ a ML-based technique called data assimilation, which combines model output and traditional observations to produce a global gridded dataset. Essentially, scientists use a weather model to fill in information that cannot be detected by the observation system and attempt to reduce error by ensuring that data for one grid point is consistent with others nearby that should be causally related to it. To do this, forecasters employ their last or previous forecast as the first guess for the future time they are interested in. They then “assimilate” the observational data that has been gathered since their forecast or more plainly, the model is free to use the information from observations to check and adjust the first guess. This is done using an algorithmic process where the observations are compared to the first guess produced by the forecast. Although there are several different data assimilation techniques, the general approach is much like the one found in retrieval: there is an iterative search for the value of an atmospheric quantity in a particular location that is consistent with nearby observations, observations made before and after, the physics of the model, and minimizes error in some way. This is precisely why it is a ML product: the assimilation process “learns” the atmospheric parameters that respect the given observational and theoretical constraints and result in minimal error. One virtue of this process is that it can produce globally gridded datasets that are uniform in the way climate models are. For areas where observations are sparse, the model can be used to extract information from the nearest observations to produce physically consistent data.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">3 See Rodgers (2000) for an explanation of the theoretical basis of retrieval.</span></small>

The results of data assimilation are often thought of as pseudo observational, and may be called “data products” or “observationally-based” (Parker, 2025). The employment and refinement of data assimilation has resulted in increased skill in medium to long range weather forecasting. When it comes to climate timescales, scientists have assimilated historical observations for most of the twentieth century, essentially replaying this time period in a model constrained by the observations. For example, the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) has reanalyzed 1940 to the present using a data assimilation system to produce a dataset (i.e. ERA5) with gridded global coverage that is physically consistent (Setchell, 2020). Datasets like these are crucial for assessing the performance of climate models.

## 21.2.3 Impact of NNs on Observations and Pseudo-Observations

NNs are poised to have some impact on the way that scientists approach observational data. Though still in their infancy, techniques to use artificial NNs within retrieval and data assimilation are in development. For example, researchers have developed NN-based retrieval processes for aerosols (e.g. see Di Noia et al., 2015; Di Noia & Hasekamp, 2018) and proof-of-concept approaches for atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> column retrievals (Zhao et al., 2022). In the latter, they demonstrate that it is possible to train a multi-level NN with synthetic data produced using the radiative transfer forward model (Zhao et al., 2022). Though these approaches are still new, they seem to demonstrate promising reliability. When it comes to data assimilation, researchers have shown that they can reproduce the main results from one of the EMCWF’s operational forecasting models (Bonavita & Laloyaux, 2020). At present, these NN implementations are not operational; they are for research purposes only. But they show promise that the kinds of problems that climate scientists face can be addressed using NN techniques.

The question is, what should we make of the shift to such techniques? Philosophically, retrieval and data assimilation techniques have been used to help understand the nature of measurement. For example, Lusk (2021) argues that retrievals produce a form of explanation that is unique to certain measurement contexts. Lusk is interested in the way phenomena are detected and the role of data in that process, an issue that was brought to philosophical prominence by Bogen and Woodward (1988). Bogen and Woodward argue that detecting phenomena is a process that proceeds mostly without appeals to theory, that it happens “bottom-up”, starting with data and reasoning to phenomena, and that the crux of reasoning in these cases is establishing the reliability of data. Data, for Bogen and Woodward, are the publicly available records of experiments or measurements. Data are idiosyncratic in the sense that they are the product of specific experimental contexts and typically cannot occur outside those contexts. They are also the result of multiple causes, for example, data are often produced by the target of a measurement, the measurement device, and a whole host of error causing processes. A paradigmatic example of data would be one of Eddington’s photographic plates of the eclipse used to measure the deflection of starlight in 1919 to test the theory of general relativity. Phenomena, on the other hand are (usually unobservable) effects or processes that are stable enough to reoccur under different sets of conditions. Phenomena are the result of fewer causes than data. A paradigmatic phenomenon would be the amount of starlight deflection that Eddington measured. Such a phenomenon would be explained “topdown” by theory (in this case general relativity).

Bogen and Woodward describe the process of phenomena identification as proceeding largely without appeals to theory; instead, what a scientist attempts to do is find reasonable ways of handling and reducing error. For example, scientists may attempt to ensure that their observational devices are screened from error producing sources. This helps ensure the data produced are reliable and are amenable to statistical analysis in ways that will help control or compensate for the sources of error that do exist. Crucially, they claim that scientists do not attempt to explain data: theory-based explanations of data are too difficult to produce and would be scientifically useless even if such explanation could be given. So, while theory might tell us the kind of thing to screen off, one never tries to give an account of exactly how the causes of error impacted the observational report.

Lusk (2021) takes issue with this picture of data production and handling. He argues that the retrieval process as it is employed for atmospheric trace gases constitutes an attempt to explain data. That is, the process is essentially setup in a way that takes the readings produced by a remote located spectrometer, and attempts to explain them by providing a model-based account of their production. Lusk claims “In the case of retrieval . . . scientists attempt to derive the characteristics of spectra from theory and other assumptions, in order to make inferences to trace gas phenomena” (Lusk, 2021 p294). This detailed account of the data is given by the aforementioned forward model and is a necessary component of retrieval. Essentially, Lusk sees scientists as attempting to simulate what the measurement instrument would produce using the forward model of the measurement process and knowledge about the measurement instrument and the likely distribution of trace gases. At least when it comes to certain notions of explanation, particularly Woodward’s (2003) counterfactual notion, this process appears to constitute a search for an explanation of the instrument reports that can answer crucial whatif-things-had-been-different questions. Only with these explanations does it seem we can identify phenomena like trace gas distributions and movement patterns.

However, what happens when the retrieval process, and the forward model, are replaced by NNs; are scientists still providing, or at least aiming to provide, an explanation of data? NNs are generally acknowledged to be black boxes: once trained, it is difficult to tell what relationships the NN has discovered, and thus, it is difficult to know what inference the NN is making on our behalf (see Creel, 2020; Zednik, 2021; Sullivan, 2022a, 2022b). The worry is that by employing NNs, scientists are black boxing a crucial component of the process that does the explanatory work. For example, Zhao et al. (2022) demonstrate the viability of performing satellite retrievals of atmospheric $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ columns using NNs. Their retrieval system employs a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) NN, which is not only one of the most popular forms of NNs, it is one known to lead to the black boxing of inferential steps. In MLP, there is an input layer, and output layer, and then several hidden layers placed in between. Each layer has one or several neurons that serve as nodes that connect to neurons in the next layer. The connections between neurons have weights and bias, and the object is to train the network “by repeatedly updating the weights and bias between neurons to minimize the loss function so that the output values generated by the network are matched with the actual corresponding values” (Zhao et al., 2022, p. 6). It is often the case, when trained, that the weights and biases in the hidden layer connections will not be known to researchers, and thus, exactly what function the MLP-NN is estimating will also not be known. This is when the NN becomes a black box; researchers simply do not know how the MLP-NN is producing the outputs given certain inputs. Zhao et al. employ two linked MLP-NNs that each have two hidden layers. As we will see, there are benefits to employing techniques like MLP-NNs in retrieval, but doing so partially obscures central aspects of the retrieval process.

Does this opacity result in diminished explanatory power, or reduced justification? I’ll argue here that it does not, or at least, not to any large degree given the suggested methods of implementation. Let us consider justification first. Would the black boxing of certain steps in the retrieval process result in a weaker justification for the outcomes? That is, would we have greater reason to think that the estimates of trace gas distributions would unknowingly depart from the values that would have been gathered using the traditional retrieval method?

In many sciences, there is (sometimes) legitimate worries that certain AI methods may be trained in ways that the inferential patterns involved are opaque to researchers. This may be extremely problematic in instances where a trained human is being displaced by an AI process that is directly trained on observations. For example, replacing a judge’s expertise by an AI trained to predict recidivism for the sake of determining bail or sentencing (Ryberg & Roberts, 2022). One reason to worry is not only that the new process is opaque, but it takes a different form from the previous process. Thus, the end-users’ knowledge of how to read results, what the error characteristics are, and the practices of challenging or double-checking a result, may all be different.<sup>4</sup> And this difference creates room for error.

But there is some reason to believe moving from Bayesian optimization to NN techniques does not represent a large departure from existing methods when it comes to retrieval. The difference between the nascent NN techniques and the more traditional ML techniques that use Bayesian optimization is not as large as moving from a human to an algorithm. In fact, the two techniques share some crucial similarities. This is broadly suggested by the way that Zhao et al. describe the function of training for their NN method: they explain the process as the minimization of a loss function, the same basic mechanism at work when Bayesian optimization is operationalized.

In fact, as some have shown, NNs are quite good at estimating the solution to inverse problems. Mohammad-Djafari (2021) points out that many of the steps performed in retrieval, when performed by regularization or Bayesian optimization, can be easily replaced with trained NNs. Certain deep learning NNs can be constructed where each layer is equivalent to one iteration of the search for convergence in more traditional methods. This is not surprising, after all, while I have drawn a distinction here between NNs and other traditional computational techniques like Bayesian optimization, they are both forms of ML.

Still, there are differences between optimization techniques and the proposed MPL-NN technique for retrieval that might be relevant to whether there is a loss of explanation or justification when it comes to remote atmospheric measurement. Bayesian techniques are often most suitable when researchers believe they have a good model but limited or extremely noisy data. A lot of information comes from the model, which is augmented by information about the likely state and device indication. NNs, including the MPL-NNs, are often most suitable when there is a significant amount of data that can be used for training the NN and discovering the relevant relationships. In many applications—especially when trained through unsupervised learning or implemented without constraints—lots if not all the information is coming from the training data. Thus, one might believe the grounds of justification in retrieval has shifted from model to data, and if the relationship identified by the NN is black boxed, that the justification is no longer accessible. After all, it is the first situation—where we have a good model and noisy data—that climate researchers often find themselves.

Climate researchers, however, can deploy the NNs in ways that does not jeopardize their justification or significantly prevent them from understanding what function the NN is estimating. That is, the way that climate scientists train and use the NN can help ensure that they maintain knowledge of what inference the NN performs, and therefore retain their justification. One advantage that climate scientists have is that the retrieval process is extremely well known. For example, all of the steps to obtain the maximum a posteriori solution via Bayesian inference can be written precisely. Since the job of the NN is replacing some of the operators or steps in this process, there isn’t a significant shift in how one would justify the outcome. This is in part because the NN does not end up becoming an opaque black box. Because the steps are well known, scientists are able to train the NN to perform the desired operations, and scientists can be reasonably sure that the NN has not learned a different pattern of inference. For example, Zhao et al. train their two-step MPL-NN on synthetic data produced by their theoretically informed retrieval algorithm. One step of the NN performs the equivalent of one operation in the retrieval, while the second step performs a second operation, whose results are known to be linked by a particular equation. Given this setup, researchers can train the NN on synthetic data produced using the legacy retrieval process, which guides the NN towards the same inference.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">4 See Duede (2022) regarding how the belief in the reliability of scientific AI models cannot be reduced to other familiar epistemic categories of justification.</span></small>

Therefore, there seems to be very little of what philosophers have called “link uncertainty” (Sullivan, 2022a, b): uncertainty about the connection between a NN inference and the target phenomena. Since scientists can identify the operations that the NN performs and can constrain its learning using data produced by known processes, there is good reason to think that the NN is performing the operation as described. Furthermore, scientists can compare accuracy and error characteristics with the traditional retrieval methods. There is no significant shift in how the process is justified.

It is less clearcut whether claims about explaining data continue to hold with the introduction of NNs into the retrieval process. Lusk’s argument about explanation relies on scientists’ ability to use the retrieval process to answer counterfactual questions about what indications the instrument would produce given certain atmospheric concentrations. But counterfactual manipulability is an area where AI and NNs sometimes falter. For example, Jebeile et al. (2021) argue that NNs are not robust with respect to manipulability, and this decreases the intelligibility (i.e. our understanding) of the process containing the NN, and in turn, decreases our intelligibility of the process we try to understand with the NN. They support the claim that NNs are not robust with regards to manipulation by citing the existence of adversarial examples: inputs specifically designed to fool AI systems. For example, in image recognition applications of AI, one can add a layer of pixels to an image that can trick an AI into classifying what appears to be a clear picture of a school bus as an ostrich (Demetrio et al., 2022).

However, it is not clear that the existence of such examples is sufficient, or particularly relevant, to undermining claims regarding explanation. There are, as Freiesleben and Grote (2023) point out, and Jebeile et al. recognize, different notions of “robustness” employed in the AI literature. It is unclear why a lack of robustness with regards to adversarial examples should significantly worry the research scientist. Adversarial examples are (by definition) designed by an adversary and often highly artificial exploits. Such examples take advantage of the NN architecture in order to produce an inaccurate output. Climate scientists, however, are unlikely to be (unknowingly) using the contrived inputs or be targeted by malicious actors for manipulation in this way (i.e. in the way a self-driving car might).

Furthermore, whether a NN retrieval scheme is sensitive to input perturbation generally is an empirical question, and it is one that scientists should be able to answer given their knowledge of retrieval and the availability of the traditional algorithm for comparison. That is, the robustness with respect to what Freiesleben and Grote (2023) call “natural distribution shifts” seems assessable. Given that the fundamental operations remain the same between Bayesian and NN retrieval schemes, it is likely that the number or kind of counterfactual questions that can be answered remain the same as well, and this is a testable assumption.

A loss of explanation may come if, for example, the forward model was to play no role in the retrieval or the training of a NN, and thus, there would be no account regarding why or how the instruments indication was related to the atmospheric state, but given the current use of NNs in retrieval, that situation is not likely. The worst-case scenario would be that the NN is using some shortcut to estimate the output of certain steps of the retrieval. This would be problematic if the shortcut result could not be interpreted as an approximation of the correlate step in the retrieval. But again, since the retrieval process is well known, whether the NN result is an adequate approximation can be assessed. It therefore seems to be an empirical question whether explanations of data are maintained when NNs are introduced into retrieval, but there’s no obvious reason why they would not be.

Why rely on NNs in retrieval then, if in fact the NNs simply end up performing similar operations? The answer is computational efficiency. The use of NNs changes where the computational load rests in the retrieval process, and what kinds of resources can be used for the computation. The traditional retrieval process requires solutions to radiative transfer equations at each iteration, which makes the process computationally expensive and slow. While training a NN is computationally expensive as well, once trained, retrieval would be much more efficient than the standard process. Also, ML is much easier for scientists to parallelize on multiple CPU’s, which provides a significant performance boost.

The impacts of NNs on data assimilation (DA) and reanalysis might be more significant than on retrieval. Since retrieval and DA are similar, it’s unsurprising that the lessons from retrieval hold for DA as well. Geer (2021) shows that one can demonstrate equivalences between a specific kind of DA technique (4D-VAR) and a recurrent NN using Bayes nets. Greer also points out several general similarities. Both DA and NNs are attempting to learn about the world via data using an inverse method, the cost function in variational DA is equivalent to the loss function when training NN, both often employ gradient descent, and specifically, the adjoint method often employed in DA is mathematically identical to the NN training technique called backpropagation. They conclude that from a general enough perspective these two approaches can be unified under a Bayesian framework.

While the similarities between the DA methods currently employed and emerging NN methods might be similar, the epistemic status of DA produced products and atmospheric retrievals is very different. Retrievals are often (though not always) thought of as bona fide observations or measurements. DA products, like reanalysis datasets, are however not generally thought of in this way. These products are acknowledged to be empirically informed, and often play the role of observations or measurements, but the climate community is very aware that imperfect models play a significant role in generating these data products. Scientists often include words of caution when a DA produced reanalysis dataset is employed in research.

Wendy Parker (2017) argues that data assimilation systems are a kind of complex measurement system that is in development. She follows Eran Tal (2012, 2013) in thinking about measurement as a model-based activity, where a precondition on the possibility of measurement “is the specification of an abstract and idealized model of the measurement process. To measure a physical quantity is to make coherent and consistent inferences from the final state(s) of a physical process to value(s) of a parameter in the model” (Tal, 2012, p. 17). Parker has a tripartite view of measurement that includes direct, derived, and complex measurement. Direct measurements are those where no symbolic calculation is performed on the outcome of a measurement device, e.g. a rain gauge for the measurement of rainfall depth or a pre-calibrated mercury thermometer. A derived measurement involves one or more layers of inference, usually taking a direct measurement as input and using a well-known relationship (e.g. a law of nature) to arrive at the measured quantity. Parker defines a complex measurement as one that utilizes many direct or derived measurements together to obtain a result that is more informative than any of the measurements independently.

Ordinarily, the results of a computer simulation would not be candidates for measurement, except in special circumstances (see Lusk, 2016), as they lack any kind of physical interaction with the measured quantity. However, it is tempting to see reanalysis data produced using DA as a case of complex measurement because the DA system is ingesting measurements of direct or derived forms that resulted from interactions with physical systems. After all, the whole idea is to use numeric weather prediction models in combination with past data to produce a consistent time series of quantities of interest. In this sense, it looks as if it is a form of complex measurement in the way that Parker specifies.

Parker, however, argues that DA should be seen as something short of a measurement system, and therefore, reanalysis data are also something short of measurements. She claims that data assimilation seems to be a measurement system that is under development. As Parker puts it: “Ultimately, this is because today’s data assimilation systems are not subjected to a rigorous process of calibration that provides well-motivated uncertainty estimates” (2017 p294). Calibrating the DA system would require identifying and correcting for sources of error. There are at least two ways of doing this. The first is called “white box calibration” and essentially requires breaking the measuring system down into components and crafting an uncertainty budget, demonstrating how each component contributes to the overall uncertainty. The other is to perform black box calibration, which can be thought of as treating the entire measurement system as a singular component, the outputs of which are compared directly with a set of known quantities in a way that enables statistical determination of an uncertainty range.

Both types of calibration look daunting in the context of DA. For most implementations of DA, scientists rely on the assumption of a perfect model, an assumption known to be false (Farchi et al., 2023). As a consequence, reanalysis products often come with cautions regarding the uncertainties involved, and how the uncertainties may vary even for different data points within the same product. As the ERA5 reanalysis documentation points out “ . . . the accuracy of the analyses is not uniform throughout each assimilation window. If the model and observations are unbiased and their errors follow Gaussian distributions and if the observations are homogeneous in space and time, then the analysis error will be smallest in the middle of the assimilation window.” However, it helpfully adds “ . . . none of these assumptions are actually true . . . ” (Hersbach et al., 2023).

The difficulty comes from the varied sources of error, and the lack of a standard against which to calibrate the system. After all, the observations contain their own errors, which become larger and less well known as one goes further back in the twentieth century. There is also no complete gridded dataset that comes from pure observations; if such data existed, the need for DA would be significantly diminished. This makes the straightforward comparisons between DA products and standards with known uncertainties needed for black box calibration difficult. White box calibration perhaps fares even worse. The way different components of the model, for example, contribute to the error are not well known at this point. The ERA5 documentation indicates that their product accounts for some uncertainties in observations and sea surface temperature, they make plain a significant problem: “Other uncertainties are not accounted for, such as uncertainties in radiative forcing due to greenhouse gases, or systematic errors in the model or the way in which observations are used” (Hersbach et al., 2023).

The hope is that NNs can help with this task of clarifying the uncertainties involved in a DA system. Though speculative, the success of this project could make progress towards a more rigorous quantification of error and thus the establishment of DA products as bona fide measurements. There are different ways that this might be done.

Some, for example, have attempted to train a deep NN in an attempt to learn the entire assimilation process (Arcucci et al., 2021). In this example, the NN is trained through a comparison of the extant observational data (the input into the DA system) and the products of DA (the outputs) to learn the DA process. The thought is that, in theory, a NN can learn the traditional DA process and improve upon it using the ability of NNs to update their models as new data is introduced. That this could result in reduced error compared to traditional DA systems has been proven in theory, and some limited proof of concept experiments have been carried out (Arcucci et al., 2021). Still, there are some potential downsides to such methods, for example, there is no guarantee that the purely NN assimilation system will produce physically consistent data, though the hope is that it will produce data as consistent as the DA products it is trained upon. It’s also an open question under what conditions an operational NN assimilation system would outperform a traditional one, or whether such a system could be implemented within existing weather and climate systems for prediction or projection.

Another way NNs might result in better DA techniques is through hybrid assimilation, which attempts to deploy a NN alongside the traditional DA process in order to curtail error. This process starts with a set of observations. The DA system attempts to “update” the observations by finding their optimal states, and filling in areas of sparse observations, using a physically based model that has a fixed set of model parameters. It is essentially asking what the observations should look like given the model, essentially as is done in traditional DA. The products (i.e. updated observations) are then handed to the NN. In this case, the NN has already been trained to learn the DA process, so it is supposed to be a surrogate model of the DA system. The purpose of the surrogate, however, is to update the model based on the data products. That NN then specifies what the model should look like given the observations. From this, information can be passed back to the DA system, for example, updated parameters to use. This cycle continues until there is convergence between the two systems (see Brajard et al., 2020). This process can be used to probe and reduce parameter error and other forms of structural model error. Using surrogate models like this has reached a state of maturity in which they perform at least as well as the extant ways of handling model error in operational data assimilation and appears close to operational implementation for research purposes.

The above suggests that NNs might be a virtue for climate scientists when it comes to processing observational data. When it comes to remote sensing, NNs promise enhanced efficiency without much loss of explanatory power due to their opaqueness (at least, if deployed in the way explored above). When it comes to DA, NNs promise to help scientists curtail and quantify error, and in doing so, DA products move one step closer to genuine measurements.

## 21.3 Climate Models and AI

The kind of models that I’ll refer to as climate models—which include general circulation models (GCM) and earth system models (ESM)—attempt to depict the evolution of the Earth’s climate system. A modern GCM will contain representations of the ocean, atmosphere, land mass, and sea ice, whereas an ESM may additionally include components that represent atmospheric chemistry, ocean chemistry, and perhaps soil and flora. These components are often divided into different modules or components that are then linked together by a coupler, which specifies how information passes between them (see Parker 2025 for more details). Many of these modules are operationally similar in that they approximate solutions to a set of equations that represent the evolution of Earth’s atmospheric systems over successive timesteps. These equations contain much of our theoretical knowledge of the factors that drive climate’s behavior. The equations are discretized, and numerical methods are employed to estimate solutions at regular points on a threedimensional grid. Typically, supercomputers are needed to generate these solutions. Available computer power to perform the estimations has been a significant limitation, but as this power has increased, the resolution of climate models has as well. Our best models currently produce results on a grid of 50–100 km with 50 or more vertical layers.

Climate models are used for a variety of different purposes, including gaining an understanding of the way the Earth system operates (see Held, 2005). Climate models are crucial in providing evidence for anthropogenic climate change. To detect the signal of climate change, we need to have some indication of how the planet would behave in its absence. Yet, there is only one planet, and there is good theoretical reason to think climate change is happening. Thus, climate models provide us with what the counterfactual case would be like, that is, how the planet would naturally behave without anthropogenic interference. Only with this information could we detect a departure from that baseline. Additional support for anthropogenic climate change comes from signatures: telltale signs in models of atmospheric phenomena that is unlikely to occur if anthropogenic interference were not present.

In addition, climate models provide projections of the future climate. To provide these projections, scientists run the models into the future under different emission pathways. These models then provide estimates of how climate behavior may change with ongoing greenhouse gas and land use changes. We can also detect changes in phenomena that are likely to impact human health and well-being, for example, extreme weather events. For these reasons, it’s obvious why the results of climate models are so important for policy and addressing the risks that arise from climate change.

Climate models of the sort described above, however cannot do it all. They are relatively coarse grained and there are lots of physical processes and geographic features that are not fully resolved, and the timesteps may remain long (they are often a day) to make runs of the model over the time periods of interest tractable. To gain insight as to how more local climate might behave, scientists run regional variants of climate models. These “regional climate models” (RCMs) employ the same theory-based representations of the climate system, but they cover a smaller area of the globe, often a country or region. Representing a smaller area allows for increased resolution under the same computational constraints when compared with a global climate model. Thus, regional climate models can represent areas with greater detail and are able to resolve smaller geographical features on shorter timesteps than a global model. These models are thus often used to learn how smaller scale features impact local climate and thus are important for informing regional planning.

It is precisely on these tradeoffs between scale of resolution and computational resources that NNs are poised to have the greatest impact. Researchers have focused on two issues that NNs might be helpful to address: parameterization and dynamical downscaling. Let us now examine these in turn.

## 21.3.1 Parameterization and Neural Networks

Unfortunately, due to computational limitations, one cannot resolve all features of the climate. Those features that cannot be resolved are often called “sub-grid” in that they are too small to be realized on the grid of a climate model. However, scientists are aware that these features are relevant to the climate dynamics that they do want to capture. For example, cloud formation—which has important components that occur on the molecular level—is extremely important for precipitation and storm creation. But such fine-grained processes could not be resolved on the scale of a climate model. But leaving out such processes is likely to result in an inaccurate picture of climate.

Instead of explicitly representing these processes, scientists end up substituting a complex fine-grained picture of their operation with a cruder and coarser one. Scientists divide the way they represent the climate within their model into two broad categories: the dynamics and the physics. For example, in the atmospheric component of a climate model, the dynamics refers to the fluid dynamical and thermodynamical equations that capture large-scale atmospheric behavior. These equations come from physical theory and express the conservation of momentum and mass among other relations. The “physics”, somewhat counterintuitively, represents the sub grid processes that impact large scale behavior, but are too small to be represented explicitly. Instead, these processes are parameterized and expressed as functions of the elements that are computable in the dynamics (often temperature, pressure, wind, etc.). In this sense, parameterizations are often simplified representations of complex small-scale processes. They are engineered to be adequate substitutes (Katzav, 2013) for explicit representations of sub-grid processes.

Parameterization is recognized as a particularly difficult problem within climate modeling. After all, parameterizations are seemingly attempts to find a representation that is simple enough to be efficient but rich enough to capture complex and important components of the system. What a parameterization should look like, or which parameterizations are good ones, is often highly uncertain. In addition to uncertainty, and often times because of it, parameterizations are also a central focus for climate model tuning. Model tuning is akin to measurement calibration discussed above: aspects of the model are adjusted so that the model results agree with observations to within some specified degree. Parameterizations are frequently altered to ensure agreement with observations. One chooses these alterations based on how uncertain one is of the accuracy of the parameterization and the kind of observations one is trying to fit. It should be noted that how to tune a parameter is also a contentious process, as the adequacy of particular parameterizations may rest on other parameterizations in the model, to at least some degree.

There are several different methods of parameterization. The simplest is representing the sub-grid process deterministically by finding, often through data-driven investigation, what the average contribution of the process might be, or using a crude physical relationship or heuristic rule. The most complex might be what is called a super-parameterization. Super-parameterization uses a separate, high resolution and short timestep, model of the sub-grid process, which runs alongside a climate model with much coarser resolution and longer timesteps. When the climate model requires information about the sub grid process, the parameterization model provides it. For example, convection, the movement of less dense air through cooler more dense air, is a sub-grid process that is crucial for correctly describing cloud formation, precipitation, and storm formation. Parametrization of cloud related processes is a significant locus of disagreement between climate models and a significant uncertainty related to climate projections (Bony et al., 2015). In a super parameterization scheme, one would employ a fine-grained model of convection and cloud formation. These cloud resolving models are based primarily on physical theory. Each climate model grid box would have its own implementation of the resolving model. But while the climate model might run with a timestep of 1 hour, the resolving model might run with a timestep of 10 or 20 seconds. Each hour, when the climate model requires convection information, the resolving model provides it, and the information from the climate model is then used to constrain the next run of the resolving model.

The virtue of a super parameterization scheme is that it provides a more detailed account of sub-grid processes than other parameterization schemes. Super parameterization is also heavily informed by physical theory, meaning that what is happening in the model is (relatively) transparent or surveyable by scientists interested in those processes. There are downsides, however, that might by now be obvious: running such a small-scale model for a sub-grid process alongside a climate model is computationally costly, and it is infeasible for many of the long term and global investigations that climate models are used for.

Is there a way to harness the benefits that may come from using super parameterization while not incurring the high costs? This is what scientists examining the use of NNs for climate model parameterization hope to achieve. There have been several attempts to harness the power of super parameterization, particularly of cloud resolving models (CRMs), while trying to cut computational costs. In these attempts, scientists attempt to replace the super parameterization with a NN. For example, in Gentine et al. (2018), researchers used the SPCAM-3 climate model (simplified for an aqua-only planet) that employed a super parameterization in the form of a cloud resolving model. They recorded two years of the input and output for each instance of the cloud resolving model, and then divided it according to year. The first year of data was used to train a multilayer NN to see if it could learn the relations that the cloud resolving model was relying on to give information to the climate model. Researchers then coupled the trained NN to a climate model and ran it for a year in an analogous situation to their original two-year SPCAM-3 run. They validated their NN by comparing the results to the second year of the SPCAM-2 data, which the NN had never seen, to determine if it successfully learned from the super parameterization scheme.

In some ways the results are extremely promising. They found good agreement between the climate model using the super parameterization scheme and the one that employed the NN. The most promising result, however, was the efficiency gains of employing the NN: the climate model using the NN parameterization performed ten times faster than the original SPCAM-3 using the super parameterization. But Gentine et al. also point to two obstacles. First, the NN was in no way constrained by physical theory, and thus some physical processes, like energy and moisture conservation, were not respected. Second, given that this NN was trained on an aqua only planet, it is unclear how it would perform in novel situations, for example, areas with significant landmass.

Philosophers express concerns about these precise limitations. For example, Suzanne Kawamleh (2021) examined several attempts to emulate cloud resolving models for the purposes of parameterization. What she finds is that they fail to generalize outside their area of training and may in fact find relations that overfit the trained data. She also argues that by employing NNs, scientists loose access to one of the crucial ways of building confidence in their models: process evaluation (see Kawamleh, 2022). She indicates that “the neural network remembers and reproduces the mapping between the input and output variables of that particular CRM data set instead of learning the general physical or causal relations that underlie the CRM output data” (Kawamleh, 2021, p. 2014).

For Kawamleh, the causal relations and the processes that they give rise to are central to assessing the quality of our climate models and improving their reliability through process evaluation. However, with a NN parameterization these processes are “black boxed” and obscure; we don’t know what relations have been learned. Furthermore, if performance in novel situations is bad, we can be assured that whatever relationship was posited by the NN, it is not capturing a set of underlying stable physical relations that hold across contexts. By employing NNs then, scientists limit their ability to examine the climate processes, thus placing the weight of justification for model reliability on predictive success or fit with the data.

The claim that physical processes relevant to assessing the reliability of a climate model are obscured when a NN is employed for parameterization is a fairly general feature of many NNs. Barring the success of explainable AI, which climate scientists are keenly interested in (see Mamalakis et al., 2022), it is likely that NNs will remain black boxes. Thus, it may be hard to point to why they are successful, even when they are, or to discern what relationships they have learned. The question, however, is whether this lack of representational transparency is in fact troubling.

To address the question, it is worth comparing NN parameterizations to the two other kinds of parameterization schemes on offer. When compared to a super parameterization, it seems clear a researcher’s ability to survey the way relationships are represented within the NN scheme is much reduced. However, the ability to survey the relationship may not completely prevent scientists from employing process validation. Climate scientists can still analyze the way that a process looks dynamically within the model output that employs a NN parameterization scheme. This is often how climate scientists build confidence in their models via processes: they compare the visualized outputs of the model to other sources (e.g. observations or data assimilation products) to see if characteristic atmospheric patterns are present in both. This kind of pattern matching gives an indication that the model and parameterization scheme are able to capture processes that contribute to atmospheric phenomena of interest. This is one way to build confidence in a model. Even if the parameterization scheme is opaque to researchers, all is not lost. It is also worth noting that super parameterization schemes are too costly to implement for large models and long runs, so even though they might allow for enhanced ability to examine how scheme structure relates to model behavior, the ability to do so is quite limited.

But super parameterizations are not the typical case, and more often climate models employ parameterizations that consist of simplifications or empirical statistical properties to save on computational costs. While these parameterizations are representationally transparent to scientists, they are often inaccurate. Still, such parameterizations may be reliable, not because they are accurate, but because they nicely compensate or balance out other sources of error, including other parameterizations. When compared to this style of parameterization, a NN scheme does have possible advantages. First, it shares many similarities with traditional parameter schemes: they are both (often) data-driven and may not accurately capture physical processes. However, a NN scheme trained via super parameterization could have the ability to capture a more intricate relationship than a rule of thumb or statistic. If so, then it can reasonably be expected to provide better performance if it can be trained for the relevant situation, which in turn could result in more realistic model behavior and better climate projections, without the high computational costs of super parameterization. Thus, relative to the way climate parameterizations presently work, a NN scheme may provide the same level of representational transparency while offering better results.

## 21.3.2 Downscaling

Downscaling is the process by which information from a GCM is enhanced to produce higher resolution climate information and projections for specific geospatial areas. While the term “downscaling” gets used in many ways throughout the climate literature, there are two main forms of downscaling: dynamical downscaling and statistical downscaling. Dynamical downscaling involves using the coarse information from a GCM as a constraint on a higher resolution RCM, that then “zooms in” on regions of interest. Essentially, the RCM is nested within the GCM to obtain information with higher detail. Much of this kind of work is done through the Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX), which uses several RCMs to create localized data and projections for 14 regions spanning most of the globe. Statistical downscaling is much simpler: it involves finding an empirical statistical relationship between the low-resolution information provided by a GCM and higher resolution information obtained by observations, for example. This relationship is then applied to the data from the GCM to obtain the regional resolution information.

Climate scientists are beginning to deploy NNs to emulate the dynamical downscaling process. The training set for the NN is gathered from dynamical downscaling experiments. For example, scientists might obtain 10 years of data for a region via the standard downscaling process, and then use that data to train the NN in conjunction with local land features not present in the GCM. The NN then becomes what these scientists call an emulator: it is supposed to approximate the function of the RCM in downscaling. By now, the advantage of employing a NN in this context should be clear: running the emulator is more computationally efficient than dynamical downscaling using an RCM. It also happens to be a wellunderstood problem in this domain. NNs have been employed extensively to upscale video: taking low resolution television and film and interpolating the necessary information to bring them up to modern 1080p or 4 k resolution standards. The downscaling problem is essentially the same: a GCM creates a low resolution “film” of the atmosphere, and the job of the NN is to enhance it.

A similar situation to the use of NNs in parameterization is observed when it comes to downscaling: the NN technique seems to have some of the advantages of both previous methods. The NN technique is computationally cheap, like the statistical downscaling method. However, some of the virtues provided by dynamical downscaling can also be retained. In particular, statistical downscaling often assumes that the empirical downscaling relationship is stationary through time, which often leads to poor performance when examining future climate scenarios, as the climate is known to be nonstationary because of anthropogenic change. The dynamical downscaling approach need not assume stationarity, enabling it to perform better when making future projections of the sort requested by policy makers and insurance companies for climate adaptation. A NN downscaling approach trained using a RCM need not assume stationarity, and thus may perform better under changing conditions than statistical downscaling (Hobeichi et al., 2023). NNs therefore may represent a cheap approximation of dynamical downscaling.

Along several epistemic criteria of goodness—for example representational accuracy, empirical adequacy, and physical plausibility—a NN emulator will fall short of full-fledged dynamical downscaling. However, the computational cheapness of the NN approach has one significant advantage: it is possible to perform many more downscaling operations with the same resources. This enables scientists to explore uncertainty with greater confidence. Previously, when making future projections of how regional climate might behave under different scenarios, the computational costs would restrict scientists to making a limited, or only a single, projection. Thus, they could only offer decision makers a “best guess” as to what the future regional climate might tend towards. Using a NN and making downscaling much more efficient, scientists may now run ensembles of downscaling experiments using different RCMs or different GCMs. In doing so, they would be better able to explore the spread of uncertainty in their results and offer decision makers better information about the range of conditions that might occur under a projection scenario. In this way, NNs permit scientists to trade accuracy and plausibility to probe the space of possibility more deeply and gauge uncertainty.

## 21.3.3 Conclusion: Could AI Replace Current Theory-Based Methods of Climate Projection?

Thus far we have examined the various ways that NNs are being implemented to help improve the capacities of climate observation systems and climate models. The instances we have examined take a hybrid or embedded approach where NNs complement (or are trained by) existing systems that have significant theorydriven components. Could scientists just forego these theory-driven methods and completely start over with only data-driven NNs?

On the spatial and temporal timescales that climate operates, there is skepticism that a purely NN projection system could be successful. First, NNs are most successful when there is ample training data. As was pointed out in the discussion of data assimilation, the available observational data on climate timescales is severely limited. High quality global climate datasets only go back to the late 1950’s and the launch of early satellites, and even these may be spotty and incomplete. Given the multi-decadal timescales on which climate can operate, this is not enough data to expect a NN to extrapolate meaningful predictive relationships given current technology.

Additionally, the problem of assessing future climate change is not one that is tailored to the strengths of AI or NNs (see Chantry et al., 2021). As the downscaling discussion above mentions, the atmospheric system is not thought to be stationary. That is, the description of the climate regime our planet once inhabited is unlikely to continue to be accurate into the future because of changes brought on by anthropogenic forcings. Climate change means that the future climate is unlikely to resemble the past. The type of problem that results—inferring from a historical state to a new unseen state—is exactly the kind of problem that AI and NNs struggle with. In short, the future pattern may not be in the historical training data, and if it is not, there is no easy way for the NN to learn it. Furthermore, it is likely that any errors that the NN representation does contain will build up over climate-relevant timescales. As we have seen, climate scientists could train NNs on existing climate models, but it is likely that the existing models would represent the upper limit of accuracy and reliability. Given present technology and knowledge, it looks unlikely that NNs will soon make theory-informed climate modeling obsolete.

There are, however, climate-adjacent modeling tasks where NNs are already demonstrating their promise, and perhaps superiority (Ebert-Uphoff & Hilburn, 2023). These tasks tend to be short to medium term weather forecasts. Nowcasting—making weather and storm forecasts up to 6 hours—seems to be better suited to NN style analysis than global long-term climate projection (Chantry et al., 2021). Nowcasts extrapolate from the current weather patterns to near-future weather, helping to predict the movement and intensity of heat, rainfall, and storms. Such information is often used in disaster response, aviation, and even planning for events like the Olympics. Unlike long-term analyses, the short time scales involved do not permit errors to build up over time, which indicates that the NNs need not identify a physically realistic pattern to successfully nowcast. Furthermore, there is significant weather data from satellite, ground stations, and remote sensing devices available to train a NN, and the availability of this data is only growing as smart devices proliferate. Recent attempts to use NNs for nowcasting look promising: Zhang et al. (2023) have created a system trained on both observations and physical equations that outperforms traditional systems on many forecasting tasks.

AI systems may be useful for medium range forecasts (up to two weeks) as well. Bi et al.’s (2023) Pangu-Weather forecast system has been entirely trained on observational data and seems capable of forecasting quantities like temperature, wind speed, and pressure (though it hasn’t been tested on precipitation, which is often most difficult to predict). Like with most of the implementations discussed in this chapter, what is particularly impressive is the computational savings: Bi et al. estimate that their AI powered system produces forecasts 10,000 times faster than numerical weather prediction with a theory driven model.

Here again, we see another instance of what makes climate science special as a case for examining the deployment of NNs. Climate scientists often face tradeoffs between theoretical rigor and computational efficiency. This methodolog ical concern arises when gathering data, dealing with existing climate models, or even considering scrapping existing models and starting over with data-driven technologies. This concern will not soon go away, regardless of the success of AI. As many of the above examples show, NNs promise to capture some of the complexity of our best climate tools, without the computational costs. AI therefore offers a new tool to face this tradeoff, one where hybridization of theory-driven models with data-driven NNs is a promising way forward.
